en: The Gṛhyasūtra composed by the venerable great sage Āpastamba,
accompanied by the Anākulā commentary written by Śrī Haradatta.
The domestic practice is unconfused;
now the rites beginning with customary conduct (ācāra) are taken up. 1.1.
Homage to Rudra! This unconfused commentary on the *Gṛhya-sūtra* composed by Āpastamba is now being produced by Haradatta.

Ritual acts (*karman*) are of two kinds: those characterized by *śruti* (Vedic revelation) and those characterized by *ācāra* (traditional practice). Among these, those characterized by *śruti* have already been explained. Now, we shall explain those ritual acts beginning with marriage which are understood and known from *ācāra*—that is, from practical application—and not from direct *śruti*. What is the purpose of this *sūtra*? It is to provide the introduction to the rituals based on tradition (*smārta*). By means of this, rules such as the requirement of the northern solstice (*udagayana*) and others like "in every case, when the fire has spontaneously ignited" (ĀpGṛ 8.5) apply only to the domestic (*gārya*) rituals, and not to the Vedic (*śrauta*) ones. Here, by the word *atha* ("now"), the author indicates that he will provide the instruction on the traditional rituals immediately after the instruction on the Vedic ones, thereby showing its dependence upon the former. In this regard, those general rules (*paribhāṣā*) such as "he [performs] for the three castes" (ĀpPari 1.2), "one should join the beginning of the ritual acts with the ends of the mantras" (ĀpPari 2.1), "the Raudra and Rākṣasa [offerings]" (ĀpPari 2.9), and "this is the expiation for all" (ĀpPari 2.10), and so forth, also apply here. These are the things to be done.
Rites should be performed during the northern course of the sun, on the first day of the lunar fortnight, and on auspicious days. 1.2.

The prescription of the northern solstice (*udagayana*) and so forth is for the purpose of prohibiting the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*) and the like. There is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the northern solstice and the other factors, not an option (*vikalpa*). "Auspicious days" (*puṇyāha*) and "divine asterisms" (*devanakṣatra*) are well known in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*); "Yama-asterisms" (*yamanakṣatra*) are not prescribed therein.
With the sacred thread worn over the left shoulder. || 1.3 ||
The word "duties" (kāryāṇi) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. || 1.3 ||
Circumambulation. || 1.4 ||

And those [acts] should be performed clockwise; that which is directed toward the right hand is "clockwise" (*pradakṣiṇa*). An example is the ritual strewing (*paristaraṇa*) and so forth. Now, one might object: "Both of these are already prescribed for *śrauta* rites by the rule 'those pertaining to the gods' (*daivāni*, ĀpPari 2.15). To this it is replied: This undertaking is for the purpose of ensuring that these two [rules] apply here too, even to human rites such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) and others. 1.4.
The commencement is from the east or from the north. 1.5.

This statement is for the purpose of establishing a rule where there was no fixed rule; it is intended to prevent the commencement from the south or from behind. The spreading of grass and so forth serves as the illustrative example. 1.5.
Likewise, liberation [is attained]. 1.6.

Their completion (*apavarga*) should also be understood in the same way; that is to say, "towards the east" or "towards the north. *Apavarga* means conclusion. Here, this rule is not applied identically to both the beginning and the conclusion—namely, that if something begins towards the east, its conclusion must also be right there, or if it begins towards the north, its conclusion must likewise be right there. Rather, the application proceeds according to what is possible. For example, in the case of the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*), since a conclusion towards the east is impossible once it has begun towards the east, its conclusion is towards the north. In that case, the injunction regarding the conclusion would be redundant, as it has already been prescribed for Vedic rites in the rule: "They are either ending towards the east or ending towards the north" (ĀpPar 2.15). It is replied: If the injunction regarding the conclusion were not restated here, then in the case of the rule "having made two huts to the west of the fire" (ĀpPar 19.14), the conclusion towards the south would result, because of the rule restricting the beginning to the northward direction. Therefore, this [new] statement is made so that, in the event of a conflict, the priority of the conclusion may prevail. Otherwise, by the general rule of circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*), the specific rule would be sublated; however, it has been specified therein that this applies to "certain divine rites. Consequently, this restriction on the conclusion is intended to apply even to human rites and the like. (1.6)
The rites for the ancestors are performed during the dark fortnight. || 1.7 ||
With the sacred thread worn over the left shoulder and under the right arm. || 1.8 ||
Counter-clockwise. || 1.9 ||
The completion [of the ritual] is toward the south. 1.10.

Rites dedicated to the ancestors (*pitṛdaivatyakarman*) are to be performed during the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*). As it is taught there: "The monthly *śrāddha* is in the dark fortnight" [ĀpGṛ 21.1], and "That which occurs after the full moon of Māgha is the *vyaṣṭakā*" [ĀpGṛ 21.10]. This restriction, however, is intended to ensure that even for those rites—such as the *gayāśrāddha* and others—which are prescribed for specific locations or specific recipients, or which are performed out of desire (*kāmya*), and which we have accepted as being of the *pārvaṇa* type such as the *krānta* and so forth, the dark fortnight must be observed. Therefore, for one who has died during the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*), the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should be performed in the dark fortnight, and not on the eleventh day. Furthermore, the performance [of the *ekoddiṣṭa*] takes place on the eleventh day; we shall explain this very point later in connection with the rule regarding the dark fortnight for the monthly *śrāddha*.

Furthermore, the rule for the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) is an exception (*apavāda*) to the entire procedure beginning with the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*) and so forth, rather than being restricted to what precedes it or to the northern course alone, as the case may require. An example is the ritual strewing (*paristaraṇa*) and other such acts. Now, this triad beginning with "wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder" (*prācīnāvītī*) is not an injunction, because it has already been prescribed specifically for Śrauta rites. It is replied: the rules "with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*) one proceeds clockwise" (ĀpGṛ 1.3–4) and "likewise the completion" (ĀpGṛ 1.6) are recited here in this context without qualification; since they are general rules, they would apply even to rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*). This present rule is intended to set aside that [general application].

And in this context, this rule for the *prācīnāvīta* applies only to those ancestral rites that proceed independently at their own time; it does not apply to those performed as subordinate parts (*aṅga*) elsewhere. Therefore, in rites for the gods and for humans, such as the formula "O fathers, O grandfathers," the *yajñopavīta* alone is used.

Another says: because of the observation in the *Taittirīya Saṃhitā* (3.4.5), “Therefore, the *Abhyātāna* offerings belong to the *Vaiśvadeva*,” and because the formula “the fathers, the grandfathers” also pertains specifically to the ancestral rites (*pitr̥ya*), there is no occasion for the *prācīnāvīta* [wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder]. Likewise, under the heading “In the dark fortnight, the ancestral rites,” it is stated that the *prācīnāvīta* applies without distinction to all ancestral rites along with their constituent parts. Therefore, in the ancestral rite, from the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings up to the *jaya* and subsequent rites, the *prācīnāvīta* alone is used. (1.7–10)
The contingent [phenomena] depend upon the observation of signs. 1.11.

The connection with the preceding sūtra is as follows: "with the sacred thread over the right shoulder, moving from left to right, ending toward the south. Those occasional rites which have specific causes must be performed immediately upon observing those causes; there is no requirement for them to wait for the northern solstice or other such times. Examples include the rule: "when a pillar of the house sprouts" (ĀpGṛ 23.9). In that case, because of the statement "on the night of the new moon," there is a postponement only to that extent. Some maintain that entering the house is an occasional rite; others say it is not. 1.11.
Having kindled the fire, he strews grass around the fire with the tips pointing eastward. || 1.12 ||
Or with their tips pointing eastward or northward.

The general rules for the *pākayajñas* have been stated. Now, their common ritual procedure (*tantra*) will be explained: "Kindle the fire" (*agnim idhva*). This is called the "kindling of the fire," and it is an integral part of the rite. But what fire is intended here? In rites connected with the wife, it is the *aupāsana* (domestic) fire. Regarding this, some desire that the fire be taken over from the time of the birth-rite (*jātakarma*) onwards; others, however, from the initiation (*upanayana*); and others still, from the return home (*samāvartana*), according to the rule: "One should take possession of that fire where one would place the final fuel-stick. Where, however, no well-known fire exists, there the fire is brought from the house of a learned *śrotriya* or produced by friction. As for the phrase "wherever [one places] the fire," this is a consecration of the site which applies everywhere, provided the site has not already been consecrated. The repetition of the word "fire" in the phrase "kindle the fire"—though it was already the subject—ensures that the strewing around (*paristaraṇa*) also takes place even in those cases where the common procedure does not otherwise apply: "He strews around the fire on all sides. The kindling of the fire, however, is established there by the sense of the context. Or else, with blades pointing eastward or northward. Alternatively, the strewing is not necessarily on all sides with blades pointing only eastward; rather, it is with blades pointing both eastward and northward. In that case, the blades pointing northward are placed at the back and at the front. (1.12–13)
In rites for the ancestors, [the grass] has its tips pointing southward. || 1.14 ||
Or with the tips pointing south-east. 1.15.
In that regard, the tips [of the grass] should face south, both behind and in front. 1.14–15.
Having strewn darbha grass to the north of the fire, he arranges the vessels, joined in pairs and facing downwards, beginning with those associated with the gods.

Immediately after the strewing [of grass], he spreads *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward to the north of the fire for the purpose of arranging the vessels; this is the "spread" (*staraṇa*). He arranges them, that is, he places them down. "Tilted" (*nyaṇci*) means turned downwards. And all materials that have a specific purpose are included by the term "vessels" (*pātra*). Therefore, even the girdle (*mekhalā*) and other items are placed down at the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and similar rites. Among those, he arranges in pairs those connected with the gods—meaning two by two—in rites such as the *Pārvaṇa*, which are rituals for the gods. The mention of "fire" (*agni*) is redundant because it is not modified, as in the phrase "having kindled the fire. However, this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), signifying that this rule prescribed for the strewing around the fire does not apply to the arrangement of vessels. When, then, does it apply? It applies when there is a distinction regarding the tips of the *darbha* grass and when there is no overarching ritual framework (*tantra*). Consequently, even in rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*), the strewing is with tips pointing eastward to the north of the fire, and there is no overarching framework due to the absence of the arrangement of vessels. However, by virtue of the context, it applies only to the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the fire. Both of these [distinctions] must be understood to apply precisely because of that context. (1.16)
In that regard, concerning certain matters of human conditioning, karma, and objects, he states an exception regarding vessels:
"Those associated with humans [are purified] by a single [application]. (1.17)

Those vessels associated with humans he employs all at once, not in pairs. "Human rites" refers to marriage and the like. The particle *eva* (only) is for the purpose of prohibiting repetition of the action. Because there are many vessels, even if one is unable to set them down using both arms simultaneously, they are nonetheless set down all at once by some means. Some maintain that only those items associated with humans, such as the girdle (*mekhalā*) and so forth, are to be employed all at once, but not those intended for the oblation (*homa*). We, however, have stated that "associated with humans" means associated with human rites. 1.17.
Each one is connected with its respective father. 1.18.
Those [rites] connected with the ancestral ceremonies he performs one by one; that is to say, each one individually. || 1.18 ||

The consecration of the two strainers consists of their measurement according to length; the consecration of the *prokṣaṇī* water and the sprinkling of the vessels are performed silently, as in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice. 1.19.

The consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the two strainers (*pavitrayoḥ*) consists of [preparing] grass, wood, and so forth. Their measurement in length—that is, their long dimension—is that they are "a span (*prādeśa*) long," as stated in Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 1.11.9. The consecration of the sprinkling water (*prokṣaṇī*) begins with the words, "In the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle covered by the two strainers" (ĀpŚr 1.11.9). Since the *agnihotrahavaṇī* is not present here, another vessel is employed. The sprinkling of the vessels begins with the words, "The vessels are turned face upwards," and so forth. This indicates these four ritual acts. Just as the action regarding the vessels was prescribed for the sprinkling, the loosening of the fuel-stick (*idhma*) is established by its inclusion therein. However, this statement is for the purpose of restriction: that the measurement in length applies only to the two strainers, so that it does not apply to the fuel-stick or to the tips of the *darbha* grass when they are being thrown into the clarified butter (*ājya*). But how could there be any occasion for such an application there? This very point makes it known: that here too, as in the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the consecration is performed silently (*tūṣṇīm*). By the mention of "length," this rule of measurement in length for the two strainers excludes the number and measurement of the fuel-stick belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices. Therefore, since the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) are absent here, the fuel-stick does not consist of twenty-one pieces of wood; rather, the supplementary offerings (*upahoma*) serve the purpose of the after-offerings. 1.19.

To the west of the fire, having poured water into a vessel over which a strainer has been placed, having purified it three times with two strainers whose tips point northward, having carried it across level with his breath, having set it down on *darbha* grass to the north of the fire, and having covered it with *darbha* grass. 1.20.

After sprinkling the vessels, having placed the *pavitra* strainers upon the *praṇītā* water-pot to the west of the fire, and having poured water into them while placing the *pavitra* strainers with their tips pointing north over that [water], he purifies [the water] three times with the two north-pointing *pavitra* strainers, ending toward the east. The mention of "fire" [in the sūtra] is because the context concerns the vessels. A specific detail seen in another ritual manual (*kalpāntara*) is that [he should do so] with both hands turned upward, using the thumb and the ring finger. Having purified [the water], he carries that water level with his breaths; the meaning is that it is equal to [the level of] his mouth. Having carried it, he places it on the Darbha grass spread out to the north of the fire. The mention of "fire" is so that there may be no intervention by other vessels. Having set it down, he covers it with Darbha grass. He performs all of this with the *pavitra* strainers in his hand. 1.20.
Having seated the Brahmin to the south upon Darbha grass.

Because of the context, [the seat] is to the south of the fire. There, others desire that he sit down after silently casting away a blade of grass, having passed to the south behind the fire; others, however, prefer to go around the front of the fire. Regarding the duties of the *hautra* and *brahmatva*, another ritual manual (*kalpa*) states: "The *brahmā*, performing his own duties, should sit upon the *brahmāsana*; having placed there his umbrella, upper garment (*uttarāsaṅga*), or water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), he may then perform the other rites" (Khādira Gṛhya Sūtra 1.1.26). Āśvalāyana says: "In offerings of clarified butter (*ājya-homa*), the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*) is both performed and not performed; likewise for the two *ājyabhāga* portions and the *brahmā*" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.3.4–6). 1.21.

Having melted the clarified butter, having poured it out into a butter-pot over which two purifiers have been placed to the west of the fire, having pushed the embers toward the north, having placed [the pot] upon them, having removed the flames with a pair of tongs, having thrown two tips of *darbha* grass into it, having carried fire around it three times, having pushed the embers back toward the north, and having purified it three times by drawing [the butter] back and forth through the two northward-pointed purifiers, he does not remove the purifiers. 1.22.
Thus ends the first section in the Gṛhyapraśna of Āpastamba.

Now follows the preparation of the clarified butter (*ājya*). In this regard, the melting of the *ājya* takes place in whichever fire is available, because of the subsequent mention of "taking the *ājya*" (*ājyagrahaṇa*). "Pouring out" (*nirvāpa*) means bringing it forth. The repetition of the term "taking the *ājya*" is so that the preparation of the *ājya* may take place even in a rite where there is no formal *āghāra* libation; for it is said, "Having poured out the *ājya* everywhere, one offers. "Setting aside" (*nirūhaṇa*) means separating it. The mention of "toward the north" (*udag*) is so that it may apply even to rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*). By this, the "removal from the fire" (*udvāsana*) is explained. "Illuminating" (*avadyotana*) is the kindling with a burning blade of grass. In that context, having prepared two tips of *darbha* grass like purifiers (*pavitra*), he throws them into the *ājya*, i.e., he casts them in. The mention of "two" or "one" is for the purpose of prohibiting the option seen in the *Agnihotra* ritual; therefore, even in the *Agnihotra* procedure, there are exactly two *darbha* tips. Then he carries fire around that *ājya* three times clockwise; he causes the fire to revolve all around the *ājya* using either a blade of grass or a fire-brand (*ulmuka*). In that regard, they desire the carrying of fire around to be clockwise even in rites for the ancestors. "Removal" (*udvāsana*) means taking it out. "Pushing back" (*pratyūhana*) is the mixing together with the fire. "Bringing back again" (*punarāhāra*) means having brought it back repeatedly. These three [acts]—the upward purification (*utpavana*)—are completed toward the west. "Throwing into the fire" (*anupraharaṇa*) refers to the fire, because of the context and because of another ritual manual (*kalpāntara*) which says, "having loosened it, he should touch it with water. (1.22)
Thus ends the first section in the *Anākula*, a commentary on the *Gṛhyasūtra* composed by the venerable Haradatta.
Now begins the second section.

That with which he offers, having heated it over the fire, mixed it with *darbha* grass, heated it again, sprinkled it, and set it down, he touches with water and throws the *darbha* grass into the fire. 2.1.

The cleaning (*saṃmārjana*) is as previously described. "Heating" (*pratitapana*) means heating [the spoon] while it is held downwards. The mention of "fire" (*agni*) is redundant, because heating is impossible elsewhere. It is performed here for the purpose of extending those properties that belong to the cleaning during the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; thus, the heating prescribed for the *Āhavanīya* or *Gārhapatya* fires occurs in this fire. Only the specific fire is different; everything else is the same, starting with the rule: "The *sruva* [is heated] over the fires" (ĀpŚr 2.4.4). The second mention of "fire" in the phrase "he throws it into the fire" (*agnau praharati*) is so that the optional throwing into the fire seen during the cleaning of the *sruk* does not apply here. From this also, it is understood that the properties of the *sruk*-cleaning apply here. Furthermore, in the *pākayajñas*, the oblation is offered with a ladle (*darvī*), because it is seen in other ritual manuals (*kalpa*) and because of direct observation. When the text says, "At the *samāvartana*, having taken a ladle and pouring clarified butter into it... (ĀpŚr 10.9.1), it shows that the ladle is obtained even in that context which is focused on something else. And when it says, "having struck once" (*sakṛd upahatya*), it shows the striking from the *sthālīpāka*; that too would not be possible without a ladle. In those cases, there is one ladle for *ājya* offerings, and two for *sthālīpākas*—one for the offering and one for the cutting (*avadāna*). There is cleaning for both, because the cutting is for the sake of the offering, just as with the *sruva* at the *Agnihotra*. Where it is necessary to say "he heats the ladle in the fire," why is it said "with which he offers"? This is so that it may apply here as well as in the case of "with the middle or the last leaf of a *palāśa* tree," and so that it may apply in the *Agnihotra* and the *Āgnihotrika* ritual procedure (*tantra*). If that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of using the hollowed palms (*añjali*) as well. This is established by an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) regarding the wedding, the *Sarpayajña*, and others. When the text makes an effort by saying "like the *Pārvaṇa* in the *Aupakārya*," it indicates that offerings made with the hollowed palms do not adopt [all] the ritual properties (*adharma-grāhaka*), but possess only those properties explicitly stated. Therefore, the triad beginning with "placing" (*sādana*) does not apply to the hollowed palms. 2.1.1.2.1.10–13.1.1.15.1.10–13.1.1.16.1.10–13.1.1.17.1.10–13.1.1.18.1.10–13.1.1.19.1.10–13.1.1.20.1.10–13.1.1.21.1.10–13.1.1.22.1.10–13.1.1.23.1.10–13.1.1.24.1.10–13.1.1.25.1.10–13.1.1.26.1.10–13.1.1.27.1.10–13.1.1.28.1.10–13.1.1.29.1.10–13.1.1.30.1.10–13.1.1.31.1.10–13.1.1.32.1.10–13.1.1.33.1.10–13.1.1.34.1.10–13.1.1.35.1.10–13.1.1.36.1.10–13.1.1.37.1.10–13.1.1.38.1.10–13.1.1.39.1.10–13.1.1.40.1.10–13.1.1.41.1.10–13.1.1.42.1.10–13.1.1.43.1.10–13.1.1.44.1.10–13.1.1.45.1.10–13.1.1.46.1.10–13.1.1.47.1.10–13.1.1.48.1.10–13.1.1.49.1.10–13.1.1.50.1.10–13.1.1.51.1.10–13.1.1.52.1.10–13.1.1.53.1.10–13.1.1.54.1.10–13.1.1.55.1.10–13.1.1.56.1.10–13.1.1.57.1.10–13.1.1.58.1.10–13.1.1.59.1.10–13.1.1.60.1.10–13.1.1.61.1.10–13.1.1.62.1.10–13.1.1.63.1.10–13.1.1.64.1.10–13.1.1.65.1.10–13.1.1.66.1.10–13.1.1.67.1.10–13.1.1.68.1.10–13.1.1.69.1.10–13.1.1.70.1.10–13.1.1.71.1.10–13.1.1.72.1.10–13.1.1.73.1.10–13.1.1.74.1.10–13.1.1.75.1.10–13.1.1.76.1.10–13.1.1.77.1.10–13.1.1.78.1.10–13.1.1.79.1.10–13.1.1.80.1.10–13.1.1.81.1.10–13.1.1.82.1.10–13.1.1.83.1.10–13.1.1.84.1.10–13.1.1.85.1.10–13.1.1.86.1.10–13.1.1.87.1.10–13.1.1.88.1.10–13.1.1.89.1.10–13.1.1.90.1.10–13.1.1.91.1.10–13.1.1.92.1.10–13.1.1.93.1.10–13.1.1.94.1.10–13.1.1.95.1.10–13.1.1.96.1.10–13.1.1.97.1.10–13.1.1.98.1.10–13.1.1.99.1.10–13.1.1.100.1.10–13.1.1.101.1.10–13.1.1.102.1.10–13.1.1.103.

2.2. Shamyas are used in place of enclosing sticks (paridhi) at weddings, initiations, return home from study, the parting of the hair, the tonsure ceremony, the clipping of the beard, and expiatory rites.

Then he lays the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) around [the fire]. Everything is done silently, as in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; after that, the two *āghāra*-offerings and the fuel-sticks (*samidh*). Why is this so? Because they are authorized as being established, and because the *śamyā*-sticks serve the purpose of the enclosing-sticks. "For the purpose of the enclosing-sticks" means for the function of the enclosing-sticks. The *śamyā*s are well-known wooden pegs used at the ends of the yoke-ends in their holes. Their binding is performed together with the fuel-sticks. The expiation (*prāyaścitta*) refers to the expiation for extraordinary portents. And in marriage, *śamyā*s are used everywhere for the purpose of joining the hearts. Except for marriage and the like, in all cases such as the *Pārvaṇa* offerings, only enclosing-sticks are used. The mention of the *caula* ceremony is redundant, as it is already established by the extension (*atideśa*) from the *sīmanta* rite. However, it serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*); it indicates that in marriage and the other rites mentioned here, *śamyā*s are used, but not in those rites where they are extended from elsewhere. Therefore, in the *puṃsavana*, which is extended from the *sīmanta*, only enclosing-sticks are used. And just as in the *Pārvaṇa* and other cooked-offerings (*pakvahoma*), so too is there an application [of the rule] "from this point forward" (ĀpGṛ 7.19), based on the observation [in the Sūtra] "starting from the wedding *sthālīpāka*" (ĀpGṛ 7.20). 2.2.

He sprinkles water around the fire: with "O Aditi, give your consent," from the south toward the east; with "O Anumati, give your consent," from the west toward the north; with "O Sarasvatī, give your consent," from the north toward the east; and with "O God Savitṛ, impel [the sacrifice]," all around. 2.3.

*Pariṣecana* is sprinkling with water. The mention of *agni* (fire) is for the purpose of ensuring that the sprinkling does not take place outside the boundary of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), since the section concerning the *paridhis* is currently in effect. It is stated "towards the east" and "towards the north" so that the act of sprinkling may extend eastward and northward; thus, the completion (*apavarga*) of the rite is already established by the general rule (*paribhāṣā*). The mantra is simply "O God Savitṛ, impel," as this much is seen in many other ritual manuals (*kalpa*). And in the *Baudhāyana Gṛhyasūtra*, this is made explicit: "He joins those mantras together, saying 'Thou hast assented' and 'Thou hast impelled'" [BauGṛ 1.4.7]. However, for the Chandogas alone, this is the beginning of the mantra. *Samantam* means "equally. Therein, having commenced from the front, one pours water everywhere while moving clockwise, reciting the mantra at each step. 2.3.
In the rites for the ancestors, one should remain silent throughout. || 2.4 ||

If the particle *eva* were being enjoined, this would be for the purpose of prohibiting the mantra during the sprinkling all around; however, because of the particle *eva*, there is the exclusion of the triad beginning with "to the south" and "eastward. (2.4)
Having kindled the fuel, he pours the two libations silently, as in the New and Full Moon sacrifices. 2.5.

Because the term *idhma* (fuel) refers to the whole collection, one places the fifteen-wood fuel-pile on the fire all at once. Regarding the instruction "having sprinkled [the ghee]," there is an alternative ritual procedure (*kalpāntara*) which says "like the Darśapūrṇamāsa," meaning that one proceeds by moving along the northern junction of the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) and then along the southern junction of the enclosing-sticks, and so forth; in this injunction, the phrase "silently" prohibits the utterance of mantras. Consequently, even the rule "meditating upon Prajāpati in the mind" does not apply here. Since the mental recitation of mantras is prescribed therein, the optional (*kāmya*) procedures for the *āghāra* libations do not apply here, because they pertain to the archetype (*prakṛti*). Some desire the first *āghāra* with the *sruva* ladle; others, however, perform both with the *darvī* spoon alone, since the *vedā* and *upabhṛt* spoons are absent. He offers the other *āghāra* while remaining seated and does not breathe out toward the fire. We shall state the authority for this later. 2.5.107–108.

Then he offers the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga): with "To Agni, svāhā! on the eastern part of the northern half, and with "To Soma, svāhā! on the eastern part of the southern half, equal to the former. 2.6.

The northern part is the *uttarārdha* (northern half) of the fire; the eastern part is the *pūrvārdha* (eastern half); the space between those two is the *uttarārdhapūrvārdha* (northeastern quarter). "Equally" (*sama*) refers to location; the meaning is that those two should be offered equally, not unequally. Since the connection with the *āghāra* offerings is already established by the direct instruction (*upadeśa*), the word "then" (*atha*) is for the purpose of formal introduction. What is thereby established? The commonality (*sādharmya*) between the two *āghāra* offerings and the two *ājyabhāga* offerings is established. Consequently, the oblation in the *jyotiṣmatī* fire follows the well-known rule of the *āghāra* offerings; thus, the procedure of the *āghāra* offerings is extended to the *ājyabhāga* offerings as well.

Likewise, the well-known rule for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings is that they are performed while seated and without exhaling; this same rule applies to the two *āghāra* libations as well. Therefore, what was stated—that in the latter *āghāra* there is neither fixing the position nor breathing out—is established. "The two *ājyabhāgas*" is the designation for the two oblations. Its purpose consists of such matters as the rite beginning with the kindling of the fire and ending with the two *ājyabhāgas*. (2.6)

Having offered the principal oblations according to the instruction, he offers the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations, followed by the *prājāpatyā*, the *vyāhṛti*s recited separately, and the *sauviṣṭakṛtī* oblation, with the formula: "Whatever in this rite I have done in excess or whatever I have done here deficiently—may Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the wise one, make all of it well-sacrificed and well-offered, Svāhā! (2.7)

"According to the instruction" means: whatever principal oblations are instructed for whichever specific ritual action—for example, "the subsequent oblations while [the sacrificer] maintains contact" (ĀpGṛ 1.2*)—it refers to those very ones. The *jayas* are those beginning with "Thought and Intelligence" (TS 3.4.4). The *abhyātānas* are those beginning with "Agni of beings" (TS 3.4.5). The *rāṣṭrabhṛts* are those beginning with "The conqueror of truth, the upholder of truth" (TS 3.4.7*). The verse "O Prajāpati, none other than you... is the one dedicated to Prajāpati (*prājāpatyā*). The *vyāhṛtis* are well known. The mention of them individually is for the purpose of excluding their collective recitation; they are not explicitly taught here because they are already established. The two *sauviṣṭakṛtī* verses are recited because they are not otherwise well known.

But is this not also recited in the Sūtra during all expiations (*sarvaprāyaścitta*)? “Whatever of this rite I have done in excess, or whatever I have done here deficiently—may Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the wise one, make all that well-offered and well-sacrificed; Svāhā! If this is so, then this indicates that this procedure for the *pākayajña* is common to some others as well. And the practice of the Kālagireyas is seen in this regard regarding marriages and other rites: this [sūtra] is intended to ensure the application of this [mantra] to those oblations (*homa*) enjoined in those [rites], and for the purpose of teaching their timing. It does not mean that the principal oblations (*pradhānāhuti*) are to be performed before the *jayā*-oblations and after the two *ājyabhāga* offerings. For this purpose, both are taught in that very context by this [rule]: “Having performed the rites from the kindling of the fire up to the end of the *ājyabhāgas*, and having offered the subsequent oblations,” and because of the extension (*atideśa*) from the rule “he offers from the *sthālīpāka*,” its application there is established. As for the *pārvaṇa* [rite], we shall explain it in the same way in the section on the procedure for the *āgneya-sthālīpāka*.

Now, in cases such as the *paṇyahoma* (the offering of merchandise), where there is no statement that "the *jayā* offerings and so forth begin after the *ājyabhāga*s" or that "one proceeds with the *jayā* etc.," this [rule] is stated for the purpose of obtaining [the application of the ritual procedure]. In rites such as marriage (*vivāha*), the prescription of the procedure (*tantra*) would otherwise be redundant because of the statement: "One proceeds with the *jayā* etc. at the end of the *ājyabhāga*s. Therefore, the *paṇyahoma* and similar rites are *apūrva* (unprecedented) and possess only those characteristics explicitly mentioned. However, the purpose here is this: if the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*) rites prescribed in other ritual manuals (*kalpa*) are performed by people like us, then the application of this same procedure (*tantra*) should also occur in them. One might object: "But isn't this already established by the observation of the *pārvaṇa* and other rites, since it is understood that whatever is practiced through tradition is included? True, this is established for cooked-offerings (*pakvahoma*), but not for offerings of clarified butter (*ājyahoma*) such as those with the *kūśmāṇḍa* mantras using ghee, because that [tradition] pertains to non-cooked substances. The rule regarding the prescription of the procedure (*tantravidhāna*) in rites such as marriage is for the sake of restriction: in those rites where the *gṛhamedhin* (householder) is enjoined, the application of the procedure occurs only where there is a specific statement such as "from the kindling of the fire up to the *ājyabhāga*s" or "one proceeds with the *jayā* etc. By this, it is established that the *paṇyahoma* and others have only the characteristics as stated. The mention of the "principal oblation" (*pradhānāhuti*) is for the sake of establishing the sequence of the *jayā* etc. and the portion ending with the *ājyabhāga*s therein. The word "upa-" in "he offers additionally" (*upajuhoti*) signifies immediate succession. Thus, the subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*) follow immediately after the principal oblation. Consequently, in the *īśānayajña*, the *baliharaṇa* (food offering) takes place at the end of the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*). In the *śrāddha*, there is no instruction [to offer] the *barhis* grass, whereas in the *sthālīpāka*, it is said "he offers the *sauviṣṭakṛtī*" (the portion for Sviṣṭakṛt); this is for the purpose of making known that Sviṣṭakṛt is the deity. Therefore, the Sviṣṭakṛt offering of clarified butter occurs in cooked-offerings. (2.7)
As before, there is the sprinkling with water; the mantra for the naming is "You have consented; you have given leave. (2.8)

"As before" means: in the rites for the ancestors (*paitṛka*), everything is performed silently; elsewhere, there are four sprinklings accompanied by mantras. "Sannāma" (modification) means adaptation, that is, modification. For the [formula] *anusanyasva*, the modification is *anvamaṃsthāḥ*; for *prasuva*, it is *prāsāvīḥ*. Prior to the sprinkling, the throwing away of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) is done silently. Before the secondary offerings (*upahoma*), twenty-one fuel-sticks (*samidh*) are placed on the fire. There is no throwing of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) in the offerings of clarified butter (*ājyahoma*), because the [formula] *lepayoḥ* pertains specifically to cooked offerings (*pakvahoma*). At the end of the sprinkling, there is the release of the *praṇītā* water. And the Brahman priest exits by the same way he came at the conclusion of the rite. The inclusion of the word "mantra" in the term *mantrasannāma* is so that this rule of modification (*ūha*) applies specifically to mantras; otherwise, one might suppose that even the name of Agni could be modified. This is because the word *sannāma* is seen used elsewhere as well, for example: "He modifies or wipes [the vessel]. (2.8)
The term *pākayajña* refers to the sacrifices of worldly people. 2.9.10.

“Worldly” (*laukika*) means those that exist in the world, characterized by worldly tradition (*lokasmṛti*). By the word “world” (*loka*), the cultured (*śiṣṭa*) are meant. The term “cooked sacrifice” (*pākayajña*) is prescribed as a designation for marriages and other such rites. The word *pāka* signifies “small,” as in: “One should sacrifice quickly; Pāka is the deity” (ĀpGṛ 20.15). If one were to derive the term as “a sacrifice characterized by the quality of being cooked” (*pākaguṇaka*), then this designation would not apply to offerings of clarified butter (*ājyahoma*). The purpose of this designation is so that these rites may be included under the heading “We shall explain the sacrifice” (ĀpPar. 1.1), and so that ritual rules (*dharma*) may be extended to them by the rule “One should worship Nirṛti with a pākayajña. (2.9)
In that regard, the rule is dependent upon the Brahmins. 2.10.
He offers twice, wipes [the vessel] twice, eats twice, moves away, sips water, and licks [the vessel] clean. Thus [it is said]. 2.11.

Regarding those *pākayajñas*, they speak of another procedure called the "Brāhmaṇāvekṣa" (dependent on the Brāhmaṇa). It is called *brāhmaṇāvekṣa* because one regards the Brāhmaṇa as the authority for oneself; the meaning is that it is seen [prescribed] in the Brāhmaṇa. "Procedure" (*vidhi*) means the performance; that which was previously mentioned, characterized by the *āghāra* libation and having the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as its archetype, is this [former] one. However, this [latter] one has the *agnihotra* as its archetype and is the *brāhmaṇāvekṣa*. It is stated that there is an option between the two in that context—for the purpose of showing that its application occurs optionally only in those *pākayajñas* where the ritual framework (*tantra*) of the *āghāravat* type proceeds. Consequently, this procedure does not apply to the *paṇyahoma* and similar rites.

In this context, by the rule "he offers twice," it should be understood that the ritual procedure (*dharma*) pertaining to both oblations of the *agnihotra* is prescribed for *pākayajñas*, specifically with reference to the principal oblation and the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. Likewise, "he wipes twice" refers to the wiping of the smearings as in the *agnihotra*. "He eats twice" refers to the eating from the fingers. And regarding "having stepped aside, he sips water," that which is enjoined there—namely, the third sipping of water after having taken hold of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and turned toward the north—is also indicated here. Furthermore, regarding "he licks [the spoon]," that which is enjoined there—"having licked the ladle twice"—is also indicated here. To whatever extent the accomplishment of the oblation and other rites is achieved through the prescribed rules, all that should be understood as being derived from the *agnihotra* itself, but without mantras. For example: pouring out [the ghee] with the *sruva* ladle; the fuel-stick (*samidh*) made of *palāśa* wood for the purpose of supporting the oblation; and the taking of four or five portions (*caturgṛhīta* / *pañcagṛhīta*). The practical application (*prayoga*) is as follows: Having kindled the fire, swept around it, strewn grass around it, and sprinkled water around it; having prepared the clarified butter (*ājya*) for the *ājya* offerings, or the cooked rice (*sthālīpāka*) for the cooked-food offerings; and having cleansed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, he takes portions of the material for the principal oblation, whether four or five portions. Where there are two types of sacrificial food (*havis*), he takes portions of both, as in the monthly *śrāddha*. Then, having placed the *palāśa* fuel-stick upon the sacrificial grass behind the fire, and having recited all the mantras together, he offers the principal oblations all at once. Afterward, having wiped away the smearings as in the morning *agnihotra*, he wipes them on the sacrificial grass if the rite is performed during the day; if at night, as in the evening *agnihotra*. Then he offers the second oblation for *Sviṣṭakṛt* like the subsequent oblation: "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā! in the case of cooked-rice offerings; "Whatever of this rite... in the case of *ājya* offerings; and in the *Īśāna-yajña*, the action is performed with the mantra prescribed therein. Then, having wiped away the smearings as before, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he wipes on the ground to the south. Then, having set down the *sruk* ladle, the sequence from the eating from the fingers until the final wiping is like the *agnihotra*. Then follows the washing of the *sruk* with *darbha* grass, and then the sweeping and sprinkling. This ritual framework known as the *āgnihotrika-tantra* is optionally combined with the *āghāra-vat* framework in all *pākayajñas*. (2.11)

Since the mantras for marriage are recited earlier in the section on the rules for the single sacred fire (*ekāgni-vidhi-kāṇḍa*), he intends to explain marriage first; thus, he states its time by setting aside the restriction regarding the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*) and other such rules:
"All seasons are suitable for marriage, except for the two months of the dewy season (*śiśira*) and the last month of summer (*nidāgha*). (2.12)

Now follows the procedure for marriage, which takes place before initiation (*upanayana*). Although one should have said "excluding the cold season" (*śiśiraṃ parihāpya*), the phrase "the two months of the cold season" (*śaiśirau māsau*) is used; and in the case of the expression "and the last month of summer" (*uttamaṃ ca naidāgham*), this is for the purpose of identifying the specific month. Otherwise, the day itself might be understood [as the time for marriage]. The injunction regarding all seasons is an exception to the rule concerning the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*). As for the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*) and so forth, these are established in the context of marriage by virtue of general rules (*paribhāṣā*), just as the injunctions for spring and other seasons apply to initiation; so say some. Others, however, consider that even the bright fortnight and so forth are exceptions [to the general rule]. According to them, marriage is not prohibited during the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) or at night. (2.12)
All the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) mentioned as auspicious for meritorious deeds. || 2.13 ||

Since the rules for all seasons constitute a general exception [to the prohibition], this [statement] is for the purpose of prescribing auspicious days (*puṇyāha*). Thus, there is a prohibition against marriage during the night and the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*). Even so, the mention of the "specified" [days] would otherwise be redundant; it is made, however, for the sake of selecting the specific hour (*muhūrta*)—so that all those lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) which are auspicious, and all those hours which are declared auspicious, may be available for the marriage. Among these, the lunar mansions are to be understood from the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*). Morning, the time of the *saṅgava* (the second period), midday, afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), and evening—these are the hours (*muhūrta*). 2.13.
Likewise, [one should perform] auspicious rites. 2.14.

“Having fed the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce blessings,” and so forth—these are well-known from one’s own scriptures (*svaśāstra*). Auspicious acts such as bathing, wearing unwashed garments, being anointed with perfumes, wearing garlands, and having eaten, as well as the barber’s work, the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), and so forth, are well-known from worldly custom (*lokaprasiddha*). All these are to be understood [as included]. 2.14.
And when they have returned from the sciences, they should be recognized [as having completed their studies]. || 2.15 ||

Ritual actions devoid of mantras are called *āvṛta*. In whatever country, village, or family these *āvṛta* rites are well-known, they remain established exactly as they are understood; this is not the case everywhere. (2.15)
By means of the Invakās, those boons are released, being joyfully welcomed.
Thus ends the second section in the *Gṛhyapraśna* of Āpastamba.

A verse praising the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) has been cited here in the section on marriage for the sake of the context concerning the bridegroom (*vara*). If the bridegrooms—the suitors of the girl—are sent forth by the *ivakas* for the purpose of choosing the maiden; [then this verse applies].

Those suitors, being welcomed by those who possess daughters, become successful in their purpose. Therefore, in the context of choosing a bridegroom, the lunar mansion named Invakā is praised. He himself will explain later that "the word *invakā* refers to Mṛgaśiras" (ĀpGṛ 3.4). From this it is known that this verse is merely a worldly proverb well-known from other Smṛtis, and is not the composition of the author of the Sūtra. 2.16.
Thus ends the second section in the Anākula commentary on the Gṛhyasūtra composed by the venerable Haradatta.
Now begins the third section:
under the asterism Maghā, cattle are seized. 3.1.
If cows are acquired through purchase or other means under the asterism Maghā, and those cows become well-pleased, therefore the Maghās are praised for the acquisition of cattle. 3.1.
It is arrayed under the two Phalgunīs. || 3.2 ||

If an army is arrayed under the two Phalgunīs at the time of battle, it becomes victorious; therefore, the two Phalgunīs are praised for the arraying of an army. Since there is no distinction specified, both the former (Pūrva-phalgunī) and the latter (Uttara-phalgunī) are intended. In all these cases, the third case ending is used in the sense of location according to Pāṇini 2.3.45: *nakṣatre ca lupi*. 3.2.
“If one should desire that a daughter be beloved, one should give her away under the Niṣṭyā asterism;
she will indeed be beloved, but she does not return again. This rule is based on the Brāhmaṇa texts. 3.3.

A father who desires for his beloved daughter that she may be dear to her husband should give her away under the constellation Niṣṭyā. Given in this manner, she indeed becomes dear to him. Furthermore, this is another virtue of this constellation: she does not return from her father’s house to seek [him] again; rather, all her desires are fulfilled within her husband’s home alone.

Others, however, consider this to be a censure; for since it is stated that "the rule depends on the Brāhmaṇas," there are other rules regarding the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) that also depend on the Smṛtis. Otherwise, just as Tiṣya is [prescribed] for the *puṃsavana* rite, this very same mansion would have to be used for the marriage ceremony as well. (3.3)
The word *invakā* refers to Mṛgaśiras; the word *niṣṭyā* refers to Svāti. || 3.4 ||
Because these two are employed in the Veda, their meaning is now explained. 3.4.
At a wedding, a cow [is the fee]. 3.5.
At the place of the wedding, a cow should be sacrificed by one who has a daughter.
A cow in houses. 3.6.
And in the household, a cow must be sacrificed by that very same man who has a daughter; this is the application for those two. 3.6.
To the question "For what purpose?", he says:
"With that [milk], one should honor a guest as is fitting. (3.7)

One should honor the bridegroom with the cow given at the wedding as one would an *atithi* (guest). Because of the expression "as an *atithi*," he is also honored with the *madhuparka*; for there is the rule: "A student of the Veda is worthy of the cow and the *madhuparka*" [ĀpDh 2.8.5]. 3.7.
Whoever has shown him honor, he [honors] with the other [hand]. 3.8.102.

The teacher who has come together with that honored guest (*apacita*)—who is worthy of worship—is to be honored by means of the cow that is seized in the houses for the other [guest]. When the question arises as to "in what manner?", it is simply this: one should honor them like guests. At a wedding, a separate preparation of food takes place on a different fire for the groom and his companions; and the offering of the omentum (*vapā-homa*) occurs right there. For the honored guest and his companions in their own homes, there is a separate preparation of food; and the roasting of the cow's omentum and its offering take place specifically on the *aupāsana* fire. This is the method of performance. (3.8)
These are the occasions for the immolation of a cow: a guest, the ancestors, and a marriage. (3.9)

The sacrifice of a cow (*gor ālambha*) is to be performed only in these three instances and not elsewhere, such as in the *pākayajñas*. By the word "guest" (*atithi*), the rite of hospitality is designated, as in the passage beginning, "where they offer him honor" (*ĀpGṛ* 22.3). By the word "ancestors" (*pitṛ*), the *aṣṭakā* rite is meant, as in the passage beginning, "on the following day, with *darbha* grass, a cow... (*ĀpGṛ* 22.3). By the word "marriage" (*vivāha*), the rite mentioned immediately preceding is included. In other ritual manuals (*kalpa*), the sacrifice of a cow is also prescribed for the *īśānayajña* and others; this restrictive rule is intended to prohibit that. By speaking thus, other specific details observed in other ritual manuals are permitted. (3.9)
Now, regarding the girls who are to be avoided at a wedding, he says: One should avoid a girl who is asleep, weeping, or absent at the time of the formal proposal. (3.10)

When suitors have arrived for the purpose of choosing a bride, if a girl sleeps, weeps, or departs from the house, she should not be chosen; these are inauspicious signs. The word *pari* signifies an absolute prohibition, meaning that this applies even when there is already restraint of her mind and eyes [by the suitors]. (3.10)

One should avoid a woman who has been given away, one who is protected, one who is radiant, one who is like a bull, one who is like a śarabha, one who is bent, one who is deformed, one who is shaven-headed, one who is like a frog, one who is of mixed origin, one who is red, one who is a guardian, one who is a friend, one who is her own younger sister, and one who brings rain. || 3.11 ||

*Datā* means one who has been given away to another. *Guptā* means one who is guarded and protected with great effort. She may be of bad character or possess inauspicious marks. *Dyotā* means one of perverse vision. *Ṛṣabhā* means one of bovine disposition. *Śarabhā* means exceedingly beautiful. *Jārāḥ* means those who would lust after her, and she likewise [lusts after them]. *Vinatā* means one with bent limbs or a hunchback. *Vikaṭā* means one with broad shanks. *Muṇḍā* means one whose hair has been removed. *Maṇḍūṣikā* means having skin like that of a frog; the meaning is "rough. Others say it means "dwarf. *Sāṃkārikā* means one born into another family or who has become the offspring of another family, or one in whose womb the mother was like a heap of bones. *Rātā* means one whose nature is for sexual pleasure. *Pālī* means a protector of calves and so forth. *Mitrā* means "possessing friends," i.e., having many friends, or being herself a friend. *Svanujā* means one whose younger sister is beautiful or herself beautiful to behold; others say it means one born only a short time after her elder sister, or born in the very same year. *Varṣakārī* means one who is superior by a year; others say it means "one whose nature is to perspire. It is said "one should avoid" (*varjayet*) so that this [term] does not follow [only] the act of choosing (*varaṇe*); therefore, there is a prohibition against these [women] even in those forms of marriage such as the *brāhma* where no formal choosing takes place. Furthermore, if that term were to follow, there would be the undesirable consequence of an absolute prohibition. (3.11)
Those named after constellations, rivers, or trees are censured. || 3.12 ||
And one should completely avoid all [names] that have *ra* or *la* as penultimate letters when choosing a name.

Those whose names are [derived from] constellations (*nakṣatra*) are called *nakṣatranāmāḥ*; those with names of rivers or trees—such as Rohiṇī, Gaṅgā, Karañjā, and so forth—are likewise [to be avoided]. These are censured in marriage. Furthermore, all those whose names end in the letters *ra* or *la*—meaning names of such a nature—such as Karā, Kālā, Suvelā, and so on; one should avoid them at the time of choosing a bride, meaning that even the formal selection (*varaṇa*) of them should not be performed. (3.12–13)
Having placed objects within the range of his power but concealed from view, he should say, "Touch them. (3.14)
Various kinds of seeds mixed together, soil from a threshing floor, a clod of earth from a field, dung, and a clod of earth from a cemetery. (3.15)

“He should marry one endowed with the auspicious marks (*lakṣaṇa*)” (ĀpGṛ 3.19)—thus he will state later. Since the marks are not yet known therein, the means for their examination is now taught. Furthermore, this is not an obligatory rule (*nityavidhi*), because of the statement “within the scope of one’s ability” (*śaktiviṣaye*). Ability means capacity; that is, if it is possible. The meaning is: if the bride’s kinsmen should give their consent, then it should be performed, and not otherwise. How is it to be performed? It is said: having made five substances to be mentioned later hidden within lumps of clay, and having placed them near the girl, the groom should say to her: “Touch one of these lumps. What, then, are those substances? They are various seeds mixed together, such as rice and barley; dust brought from the sacrificial altar (*vedi*); a clod of earth brought from a field rich in crops; cow dung (*śakṛt*); and a clod of earth brought from a cemetery—these are they. Although seeds do not deviate from being substances, they are called “substances” here so that other substances seen in another treatise may also be optionally included here. For example: “From a pond that does not dry up, a woman who has borne all [her children]; from a gambling ground, a gambler’s wife; from barren soil, an unfortunate woman” (ĀśGṛ 1.5–6). 3.14–15.
By touching the [images of] ancestors, there is success according to their respective characteristics. 3.16.
They declare it to be the highest. || 3.17 ||

In this regard, by touching seeds one gains offspring; by touching the loose earth of the altar (vedipurīṣa), one gains sacrifices; by touching a clod of earth from a field, wealth and grain; by touching cow dung, cattle; and by touching a clod of earth from a cremation ground, death—such is the meaning according to the respective signs. They "proclaim" the final substance as "supreme," meaning they despise it or avoid it. 3.16–17.
One should marry a woman who is endowed with noble lineage, good character, and auspicious marks, and who is free from disease. || 3.18 ||

The girls to be avoided have been described; now those to be accepted are described. By the word *bandhu*, "family" (*kula*) is meant. As Āśvalāyana has stated: "One should first examine the family—those on the mother's side and on the father's side—as previously explained" [ĀśGṛ 1.5.10]. "Endowed with good character" means possessing noble conduct. "Endowed with auspicious marks" means possessed of the characteristics of a woman, being free from disease and free from consumption, epilepsy, and so forth.
Now he states the qualities of the bridegroom:
"Endowed with noble lineage, good character, auspicious marks, learning, and freedom from disease" constitutes the excellence of the bridegroom. (3.19)

"Learned" means endowed with the study of the sacred scriptures. "Excellence of the groom" refers to his excellent qualities. The meaning is that a daughter should be given to one who possesses such qualities.

Now, regarding the determination of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), he states the opinion of some: "In that [direction] where the binding of the mind and the eye occurs, there the supernormal power exists; one should not pay heed to anything else," so say some. (3.20)

Thus ends the third section in the *Āpastambīya Gṛhyapraśna*, and the first chapter is completed. Regarding a maiden in whom the bridegroom’s mind and eyes find their attachment and in whom satisfaction arises, success with her is certain; not otherwise. Some learned authorities state that one should not pay heed to the examination of qualities or defects, such as whether she has been previously given in marriage or not. According to this view, even if a girl is endowed with every excellence, she is to be rejected if his mind and eyes are not bound to her. Even under this view, those women forbidden by the scriptures must certainly be avoided, such as one who is of a different caste (*asavarṇā*) or of the same lineage (*sagotrā*). 3.20.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Anākula*, a commentary on the *Gṛhya-sūtra* composed by the venerable Haradatta.
Now begins the second chapter.
And let him send forth as messengers his friends who have assembled, who are wise in counsel, and who are excellent. 4.1.

Now follows the procedure for the selection of a bride (*kanyāvaraṇavidhi*). It has been stated that "they set out under the *invakās* (the Pleiades). On that [asterism] or on another auspicious lunar mansion, having fed the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce blessings, he should dispatch—meaning send forth—the suitors who are seeking a bride: friends, kinsmen, who have assembled and gathered together, who possess the sacred mantras, and who are accomplished in Vedic learning and study. He should send them with the instruction: "From such-and-such a family, you shall choose a girl for me. Even though in such a matter only friends are expected, they are nevertheless called "friends" so that, in the absence of those possessing the mantras, the status of being a friend alone may suffice. By the term "possessing the mantras," only Brahmins are intended; therefore, even for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, only Brahmins serve as the suitors. (4.1)
One should consecrate them from the beginning with two [verses]. 4.2.

Immediately after those suitors have departed, he should consecrate them with the two verses beginning with *prasugmantā*, which are recited at the beginning of the collection of mantras (*mantrasamāmnāya*). Consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) is the utterance of a mantra directed toward a specific object. Then, having gone to the girl’s family, they should say: “We choose your daughter for such-and-such a person of such-and-such a lineage, for joint performance of rites. Thereupon, they should reply: “It is well; we shall give her accordingly. In that regard, in the *brāhma* and *daiva* forms of marriage, there is an omission of the formal choosing (*varaṇa*) because the purpose [of the rite] is already accomplished and because other ritual manuals (*kalpa*) prescribe: “In this case, one should not send forth suitors. The same applies to the *gāndharva* and *rākṣasa* forms of marriage. (4.2)
Regarding what the bridegroom should do immediately after this, he says:
"Having seen her himself, he should mutter the third [verse]. (4.3)

Then, once the marriage has been decided upon, having performed the *nāndī-śrāddha* on the preceding day and having fed the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce benedictions on the following day, the groom goes to the bride’s family. Having offered him the *madhuparka*—beginning with the gift of the *kūrca* grass mat and ending with food—he bestows the girl upon him, saying: "I give this woman to you for the duties of procreation and shared life. Then, having personally seen her, the groom should mutter the third verse, "Not a slayer of brothers," etc. By the word "personally" (*svayam*), the meaning is that he should see the groom, since he is the subject under discussion; however, because of the inclusion of the word "personally," the meaning here is that he should see the girl herself. In that regard, in the *brāhma* form of marriage, the bestowal is preceded by the pouring of water; but in the *gāndharva* and *rākṣasa* forms, there is no such formal bestowal at all. (4.3)
On the fourth day, he should examine [the student]. || 4.4 ||
Observing by means of the parts is "samīkṣaṇa. "Aghoracakṣuḥ" is the fourth [verse]. 4.4.

Having grasped a blade of *darbha* grass with the thumb and the ring finger, and having wiped the space between her eyebrows with the following *yajus* formula, he should cast it away toward the west. 4.5.

"Near the middle finger" means *upamadhyamā*; by that finger, that is, by the ring finger (*anāmikā*). "Between the eyebrows" means in the middle; [this is done] with the subsequent *yajus* formula, namely, "here I... This is a mantra for wiping (*saṃmārjana*), not a mantra for casting away (*nirasana*). "Westward" means directed toward the west. He should cast it out over the head. Then there is the touching of water. Although the term "finger" is already established by the mention of the "near-middle" finger in connection with the thumb, the specific designation of the "finger" as the subject is for the sake of clarity. The qualification "with the *yajus*" is so that there may be no suspicion that the word "subsequent" (*uttareṇa*) refers to a direction. 4.5.107–108.
When the occasion arises, one should recite the subsequent [verse]. 4.6.

The weeping of the bride and her kinsmen is the occasion [for this rite], because of the indicative mark [in the Vedic text]: "They weep for the living. Regarding the subsequent verse, "They weep for the living," this recitation occurs on every such occasion at the conclusion of the *samāveśana* rite within this marriage ceremony. When the occasion recurs, the mantra is repeated. 4.6.
He should send out pairs of men assembled together, accompanied by the sacred formulas, for the waters with the next [verse]. 4.7.

The fetching of water for the purpose of bathing the bride is performed with the following verse: "vyukṣat krūram" (MP 1.1.7). He should send forth—that is, dispatch—those who are learned in the Mantras and have heard the sacred tradition. Although the rule "likewise auspicious things" (ĀpGṛ 2.14) already establishes this, the mention of "an even number" is made because he will later prescribe bathing with five mantras; in that case, there would be a repetition of the bathing for each mantra. Furthermore, since the bathing there consists of an uneven number [of acts], the water-jars intended for it would also be uneven. The same applies to the Brahmins who fetch the water. Therefore, the word "even" is used. By this, it is established that there is a different jar for each mantra and a different Brahmin for each jar. In that regard, if there are four jars, the consecration is performed with the fourth jar using the fourth and fifth mantras. But when there are eight, then [the first] five are used with the mantras and the others silently. The mention of "together" regarding the fetching of water is for the purpose of their acting in unison. The phrase "learned in the Mantras" refers to the Brahmins, as seen in the mantra: "O Brahmins, for her... (MP 1.1.7). 4.7.

With the following Yajus formula, having placed a piece of lead upon her head, he fixes the southern end of the yoke-pin through its hole with the next verse; having placed a piece of gold within the hole with the next verse, he bathes her with the five subsequent verses, covers her with a new garment with the next verse, and binds her with a girdle with the next verse. 4.8.

Then, when those waters have been brought, he places upon the head of that bride a circle fashioned from *darbha* grass upon the *iṇva* (the wooden pin) with the *darbha*-grass, using the following Yajus formula: "Of Aryaman... (*aryamṇo agnim*, MP 1.1.8). Having fixed the southern hole of the yoke—the outer hole of the southern yoke-pole—into that *iṇva* with the next verse, "In the hole of the cart... (*khe 'nasaḥ*, MP 1.1.9), he places a piece of gold within that hole, covering it with the next Ṛc: "May gold be auspicious for thee... (*śaṃ te hiraṇyam*, MP 1.1.10). He then bathes her with those waters, using each of the five subsequent verses beginning with "Gold-colored... (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, MP 1.2.1), reciting one mantra for each bath. But how is bathing possible by means of covering the hole? He covers it in such a way that the water flows through. Then he covers her with a new garment with the next Ṛc: "Around thee, O lover of songs, the songs... (*pari tvā girvaṇo giraḥ*, MP 1.2.6). Having himself uttered the mantra, he causes her to put it on. Having covered her and caused her to sip water, he girds her with the waist-belt (*yoktra*) with the next Ṛc: "Bestowing... (*āśāsānā*, MP 1.2.7). The specific details regarding the bride sitting with her knees raised (*ūrdhvajñu*), as prescribed in the *Dārśapaurṇamāsa* ritual (ĀpŚr 2.5.2), are intended here as well. 4.8.

Then, having taken her by the right hand with the following [verse], and having led her toward the fire, he spreads a mat with its ends pointing north behind the fire; they both sit upon it, the bridegroom to the north. 4.9.

Then, immediately after the donning of the garments, he prepares the fire according to the options beginning with "wherever there is a fire" (ĀpDh 2.1.13). Having either churned the fire or brought it from the house of one learned in the Vedas, he then leads the bride toward the fire with the following verse: "Pūṣan, lead her hither" (MP 1.2.8). This is the mantra for leading her forward; the grasping of the hand, however, is done silently. The mention of "northward-pointed" is for the purpose of excluding those pointing southward. || 4.9 ||
From the kindling of the fire up to the end of the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga), he should then consecrate her with the first two [verses]. 4.10.

Then, having sat down in this manner, he undertakes the ritual acts beginning with the kindling of the fire. Having kindled the fire with grass-blades pointing eastward, and once the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* (the butter-portions) have been performed, he immediately thereafter rises and addresses the bride as she sits with two verses from the beginning of the third *anuvāka*, namely, “Soma was first” (*somaḥ prathamaḥ*) [MP 1.3.1]. The mention of the kindling of the fire and so forth is for the purpose of establishing the general ritual framework (*tantra*). The inclusion of the limit “up to the *ājyabhāga*” is for the purpose of indicating the timing for the subsequent rites, such as the addressing with mantras. The word “then” (*atha*) is intended to show a change of state: having performed the rites while sitting until the end of the *ājyabhāga*, he then stands up and proceeds with the addressing and the rest. Thus says Baudhāyana: “Then, having risen near her, [he addresses] her heart-region” [BauGṛ 1.4.1]. And Āśvalāyana says: “Standing, facing east, he addresses her who is seated and facing west” [ĀśGṛ 1.7.3]. She is referred to as “her” (*enām*) so that one might not suspect the addressing is directed toward the fire. Although it would have been sufficient to say “with the following two,” the phrase “with the first two” is used to demonstrate the arrangement of the *anuvākas* within the collection of mantras; by this, in passages such as “he should recite the remainder at the wedding” [ĀpGṛ 8.10], the term refers to the remainder of the *anuvāka*. 4.10.
Then he should take her right hand with his own right hand held downwards, while her hand is turned upwards. 4.11.

Then, remaining in that very position, he should take her right hand with its palm turned upward while she is likewise seated, using his own right hand held low and downward-turned. This is the rite called *pāṇigrahaṇa* (taking of the hand). The word "with the right" (*dakṣiṇena*) need not be stated, because in rites to be performed with a single hand, the right hand is already established by convention. If it were not so established, there would result a lack of restriction regarding which hand to use elsewhere, as is the case here and previously in the *upanayana*. If this is so, then the right hand is not being prescribed here. What then? It is restated for the purpose of prescribing the downward-turning (*nyakta*). That is to say: "That which is the right hand, well-known for all rites—with that, the taking of the hand should be performed here in a downward manner. And from this very restatement, it is established that the right hand is to be used everywhere. (4.11)
Now he states two optional rules:
"If he should desire, 'May I give birth only to females,' he should grasp only the fingers. (4.12)

It is indeed the fingers, not the thumb, nor even the palm. This is a specific rule connected with desire for that which was previously mentioned; therefore, here too, there are such particulars as "with the right hand held low," and so forth. (4.12)
If he should desire, "May I procreate only males," [he should touch] the thumb alone. 4.13.
He grasps it as if by the big toe, as if by the hairs. 4.14.
The word "should take" (gṛhṇīyāt) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. 4.13–14.
He states the mantras for the previously mentioned obligatory rite and for the optional ones with these four verses beginning, "I take hold of you" (gṛbhṇāmi te). 4.15.

He who does not desire the pleasure at the taking of the hand should grasp the hand so as to touch the thumb and the hair on the back of the hand; such is the meaning. The word *abhi* denotes "above," and the word *iva* denotes "slightly. The sense is that he should grasp the thumb and the hair on the hand in such a way that they are slightly touched, just as the hairs growing on the hand are slightly touched. Regarding this, Āśvalāyana says: "One who desires both [pleasure and progeny] should grasp the hand together with the thumb at the edge of the hair" (ĀśGṛ 1.7.5). 4.15.
Then, to the north of the fire, he makes her step forward with her right foot toward the east or the north direction, saying: "One for food. (4.16)

Now, having raised this bride, he causes her to step forward seven steps with her right foot from the place north of the fire toward either the eastern or the northern direction, using these mantras: “One for food,” [MP 1.3.7], and so forth. The meaning is that he causes her to set down the steps either directed eastward or northward. In this case, he himself takes hold of her foot, recites the mantras, and causes her to set it down, as in the ritual procedure for stepping upon the *saṃbhāra* materials. The specification “with the right foot” is intended to establish a connection with the right side for the mantras and to ensure their precedence; therefore, the other foot follows silently behind.

Regarding the statement, "In this case, with these [formulas], 'To Soma, the knower of birth, svāhā!'—one mantra for each," the phrase "one mantra for each" need not have been stated. We shall explain how this is so in that very place. Therefore, the connection [of the formulas] occurs here by their being drawn down [from their original positions]. [The rule is: "With these, 'One for food,' one mantra for each. Otherwise, the connection of the mantra with every individual word would not be established. Furthermore, there is a restriction to the number seven of the words; just as in the case of the rule "with the three following verses, turning to the right," the commencement of the circumambulation occurs at the end of the three verses, so it would be here as well. He mutters the formula "May Viṣṇu follow you" as an addition (*anuṣaj*) everywhere, because it is recited in the first and last [verses]. (4.16)
At the seventh step, he mutters: "A friend. (4.17)

Thus ends the fourth section in the *Gṛhyapraśna* of Āpastamba. It has been stated that he causes [the bride] to take seven steps, reciting a mantra for each step. Therein, once the seventh step has been taken, having clasped her foot, he mutters the mantra beginning with "Sakhā saptapadā" (MP 1.3.14). The meaning is that he mutters those mantras which occur prior to the *homa* mantras. This is seen in another ritual manual (*kalpa*) as: "having clasped the seventh step. (4.17)
Thus ends the fourth section in the *Anākula*, a commentary on the *Gṛhya-sūtra* composed by the venerable Haradatta.
Now begins the fifth section.
"It is said 'before the oblation' for the purpose of defining the extent of the recitation.
Before the oblation, having circumambulated the fire clockwise... (5.1)
Having sat down in the proper place while she maintains contact with him, he offers the subsequent oblations with these mantras, one by one: "To Soma, the knower of births, svāhā! and so forth. 5.2.

Having completed the recitation (*japa*), he then circumambulates the fire together with her; the meaning is that they both walk around it keeping it to their right. In every instance, the circumambulation is performed while holding her by the right hand. Then they sit down in their respective places; the meaning is that each sits in the place assigned to him, such as "the bridegroom sits to the north. Having sat down, while the bride has taken hold of him (i.e., while she is holding on), he offers the sixteen principal oblations (*pradhānāhuti*) with the subsequent formulas, one by one, beginning with: "To Soma, the knower of births, svāhā! Since sitting is already established by the fact that this is a *darvīhoma* (an offering made with a ladle), the word "having sat down" is stated for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtham*): namely, that one offers these sixteen subsequent oblations while seated, whereas the others are offered while standing. Therefore, the parched grain (*lāja*) offerings must be offered while standing. This is seen in many other ritual manuals (*kalpa*), such as those of the Bodhāyanas, the Bahvṛcas, the Chandogas, the Vājasaneyins, and the Ātharvaṇikas. Regarding the subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*), the seating remains as previously prescribed; this we shall explain later. Others, however, desire the offering to be made while both are seated. The citation of the mantra "To Soma, the knower of births" is for the purpose of indicating the beginning of the oblation-mantras; therefore, the *japa* mantras precede them. This was stated previously: "before the oblation. By the phrase "the subsequent oblations," it is established that the offering is performed with each mantra individually, as is the case with other offerings. However, it has been said that the rule "with these, one by one" is drawn forward [to apply to the preceding section]. Among those, the first four mantras are recited ending with *svāhā*. Then follow twelve verses (*ṛca*); at the end of these, the *svāhā* occurs as an injunction for the *juhoti*—that is, the offering is made with the utterance of *svāhā*. (5.1–2)
Then, to the north of the fire, he makes her step upon a stone with her right foot, saying: "Step upon! (5.3)
The preparation of the footprint and the placing of the footprint-stone; that stone, along with its son—the mortar—is already established together with the vessels. || 5.3 ||
Then, having spread a base of ghee in her joined palms and having twice poured fried grains into them, he pours clarified butter over them. 5.4.
Some say that her uterine sister should scatter parched grains [over her]. 5.5.

The word *atha* (now) indicates a connection with the [preceding] position. Thus, it means "as soon as he has stood up" and "as soon as she has stood up. Therefore, from the time of the cutting of the portions (*avadāna*) onwards, there is indeed standing. In that regard, the ritual procedure for the cutting of portions belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) has been demonstrated, not another procedure. Consequently, here too, the re-sprinkling (*pratyabhighāraṇa*) and the fivefold cutting (*pañcāvatta*) occur for those who follow the fivefold division. Furthermore, the preparation of the parched grains (*lāja*) is according to worldly custom. The placing down (*sādana*) and the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) take place together with the vessels. However, it has been stated that for the joined palms (*añjali*), there is no placing down and so forth. (5.3)

Because of the statement, "The sister pours the fried grains," the spreading [of the base] and the sprinkling [of clarified butter] belong to the bridegroom alone; however, according to the alternative view, everything belongs to him alone. 5.4–5.
"This woman offers the oblation," [he says]. || 5.6 ||
The act of offering the oblation belongs to the groom alone; the bride’s cupped hands serve as the vessel. (5.6)
Having circumambulated the fire clockwise with the next three verses, he causes him to step upon a stone as previously described. 5.7.

With the three subsequent verses beginning with "They have led you around first" (*uttarābhis tisṛbhis tubhyam agre paryavahan*), he circumambulates the fire from left to right. Taking her by the hand, he begins the circumambulation at the end of the three verses. Because of the rule that "a single action may be accompanied by many mantras," the use of the plural "with the subsequent ones" (*uttarābhiḥ*) alone would have sufficed to establish the number three; however, the explicit mention of "with three" (*tisṛbhiḥ*) ensures that there is only one circumambulation performed with all three verses together, so that the ritual act does not repeat with each individual mantra. (5.7)
And the oblation is performed with the following [verse]. 5.8.
The phrase "as before" is understood here; [the rite is performed] with the following verse, "Aryaman, the god... [MP 1.5.7]. || 5.8 ||
Again, the circumambulation, the administration [of medicine], and the fire-oblation are performed with the following verse.

Furthermore, the circumambulation of the fire must be performed, as well as the placing of the stone. The word "furthermore" (punar) is intended to indicate the repetition of the action; by that, the phrase "with the three subsequent [verses]" and so forth occurs. With the subsequent verse, namely the *ṛc* "Thou art Aryaman" [MP 1.5.12]. || 5.9 ||
Again, the circumambulation. || 5.10 ||
The word "again" (punaḥ) is as before. 5.10.
One undertakes [the practice] beginning with victory. 5.11.
