The application of the *tantra* (the common ritual framework) was previously shown by the mention of the kindling of the fire and so forth. However, this present statement is for the purpose of prescribing the time, so that the *jaya* and other offerings may take place after the circumambulation (*parikramaṇa*). Otherwise, based on the rule "he offers the *jaya* and others," the subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*) would occur immediately after the *lāja* oblation, and the third circumambulation would follow thereafter. || 5.11 ||
Having performed the rites up to the final sprinkling, he should unfasten the yoke with the two subsequent verses; then he should either drive her forward himself or cause her to be driven. 5.12.

The mention of "ending with the sprinkling" (*pariṣecanānta*) is an indication of the remainder of the ritual procedure (*tantra*). By this, the unloosening of the *yoktra* (the cord) also occurs at the end of the release of the *praṇītā* water. Although it would have been established simply by saying "one proceeds with the *jaya* offerings and so forth," the specific mention of "ending with the sprinkling" is so that the unloosening of the *yoktra* occurs immediately after that, and not at the time of departure. The unloosening is performed with the two subsequent verses, namely “*pra tvā muñcāmi*” [MP 1.5.16]; for according to the rule, “a single action may have many formulas,” the unloosening consists of two formulas. The expression “then” (*tataḥ*) is intended to ensure that there is no restriction regarding the time of departure for the unloosening of the *yoktra*, so that one may set out either on the following day or immediately, as the case may require. *Pravāhaṇa* is leading [the fire] by means of a chariot or similar vehicle; *prahāraṇa* is leading it by means of a palanquin or similar vehicle carried by men. In both cases, the word “or” (*vā*) is for the purpose of indicating the equality of both options. Otherwise, since the leading by chariot is taught here as if it were directly perceived, the human-carrying vehicle—which is not explicitly taught—might be understood as being indicated only as a secondary option, like the ritual procedure for the *Āgnihotra*. Therefore, the word “or” is used in both instances; thus, even when leading by human carriers, the mantras such as “she mounts” (*ārohatī*), “with the subsequent ones,” and “with the subsequent one, O auspicious one” [MP 1.5.17–19] become applicable. 5.12.
Having brought [the fire] together, they carry it after [the horse]. || 5.13 ||

Having deposited this marriage fire into the mouth of the fire-drill (*araṇi*), his men carry it behind the departing couple. The word "having deposited" is intended to exclude the procedure of formal re-depositing (*samāropaṇa*) seen in the case of the *śrauta* fires. By making this exclusion, he shows that in the rule "the fire is to be churned after [the departure]," the churning is to be done from the fire-drills as in the *śrauta* rites. The word "after" (*anu*) is for the purpose of prohibiting carrying the fire ahead. 5.13.
It should be worn constantly. 5.14.
This is the perpetual and eternal nuptial fire, which is to be maintained for the sake of the rites related to the wife. 5.14.
The fire to be produced by friction is to be followed. 5.15.

The *udvāta* fire is that which is produced by churning (*manthaya*), generated through the act of rubbing. According to this view, even in the case of marriage, its source is this very same one. Furthermore, the maintenance of the two churning-sticks (*araṇī*) begins from the time of the marriage ceremony. In that context, it has been stated that at the wedding, the churning is performed with two new sticks, whereas in the case of the *anugata* fire, it is performed using the very same churning-sticks [as those used for the original consecration]. In the absence of those, one should touch the churning-sticks with ashes and then perform the churning. (5.15)
Or it may be brought from the house of a Vedic scholar. 5.16.

A *śrotriya* is a Brāhmaṇa endowed with learning, conduct, and Vedic study; from the domestic cooking fire of such a person, [the fire] is to be fetched. According to this view, even in the case of marriage, its source is precisely this. (5.16)
He states the penance:
"And there shall be a fast for either the wife or the husband when [the other] has followed [in death]. (5.17)

In this case, the connection between the words is established by supplying an intermediate term: "When the fire has been followed [into death], there is fasting for both the wife and the husband, or for one of the two. The word *ca* (and) serves to conjoin the fasting of both; that is, "of the wife and of the husband. The word *vā* (or) expresses an option regarding one of the two; that is, "or for one of the two. Fasting (*upavāsa*) means non-eating at both times, according to common usage. Furthermore, immediately after the following [into death], the preparation of the fire and the *sarvaprāyaścitta* oblation are to be performed.

[Objection: Is it not the case that "the fire has gone out" (*anugata*) was the subject under discussion; why then is there this mention of the cause by saying "if [the fire] has gone out"? [Response: It is said: The departure of the couple is the subject here, as in the rule, "Then he should have her carried away. The rules regarding the sacred fire (*agnidharma*), however, are incidental (*prāsaṅgika*). Consequently, even the injunction for fasting would be understood as a mere supplement to the departure. And thus, rules such as "for three nights both must sleep on the ground and observe celibacy" would not have a connection with the incidental matter, but rather only with the primary subject (*prākaraṇika*). Since it would already be established that if the fire goes out, both must fast or else one of them, the separate mention of "of the wife and of the husband" serves a specific purpose. By that [mention], it is shown that in certain rites where the wife does not participate (such as the *upākaraṇa* and *samāpana*), the fire is not employed. Furthermore, in rites such as the "subduing of co-wives" (*sapatnībādhana*), although the husband does not participate, the fire is employed precisely because of its connection to the wife. (5.17)
Or rather, one should offer an oblation with the following verse; one need not fast.

With the following verse, "And with this, O Agni" (MP 1.5.18), he should offer one oblation. This oblation does not involve the ritual framework (*tantra*). The strewing of grass, the consecration of the clarified butter, and the wiping of the ladle are performed. Since the optionality is already established by the word "or" (*api vā*), the prohibition against fasting is intended so that this oblation may serve as a substitute specifically for the fast. Therefore, even here, there is a combination with the *sarvaprāyaścitta* homa. This expiation should also be understood to apply when the fire is destroyed by theft or other causes. Regarding the intentional abandonment of this very fire or its interruption after twelve days, an expiation is prescribed in another Smṛti; in those cases as well, the re-establishment of the fire (*agnisaṃskāra*) is exactly the same. 5.18.
Uttarā is the prop of the chariot. 5.19.

Now, the specific duties for the departure of the couple are taught. [The verse] "The north is supported by truth" (RV 10.87.21) is used; the meaning is that the support of the chariot must be performed with this verse. By what means? By the bridegroom, since he is the one authorized [for the rite]. 5.19.
With the next two verses, he yokes the two draft-animals. 5.20.
The right [hand] first. || 5.21 ||

The two by which the chariot is drawn are the two draft animals, whether horses or oxen. With the following two verses, "They yoke the ruddy one" and "In every yoking," he yokes them; that is, he fastens them to the yoke and the pole. With the verse "They yoke," he yokes the right [ox], and with "In every yoking," the left. Some desire the yoking of each with both verses. By implication, this means the left is done first. Furthermore, if the chariot faces westward, the rule does not apply. In other cases, it is established that the completion [of the yoking] occurs in that manner. 5.20–21.
As she ascends, he addresses her with the following verses. 5.22.

Then the bride mounts that harnessed chariot. As she is mounting, he consecrates her with the subsequent verses beginning with "The auspicious bird, the bright one" (MP 1.6.4). Because of the use of the plural number here, there would otherwise be the contingency of using three or more verses without restriction; however, by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, the rule is fixed at four. On the other hand, the entire procedure beginning with the propping up (*uttaṃbhanādi*) applies to the vehicle. And it has been stated that the acts of consecration and so forth, which are duties pertaining to the couple, also apply to horses, men, and the like. Some hold that the mantras apply to the chariot alone because of the indicative mark of the mantra "the one with good wheels" (MP 1.6.4). Others hold that since the mantra is intended for the bride's conveyance, its reference to the chariot is merely a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*). 5.22.
On the two paths, he spreads out [the grass] with the next [verse]: blue on the southern [path], red on the northern. 5.23.

There are two threads, blue and red, on both sides of the chariot’s tracks. This is a future reference (*bhaviṣyannirdeśa*) to those two tracks upon which the chariot wheels will roll; it would have been more appropriate to read *vartinyoḥ* (on the two tracks). Thus, the feminine gender in the subsequent mention of *dakṣiṇasyām* and *uttarasyām* becomes logical. The word *vi-* in *vyavastṛṇāti* has the sense of "across" (*tiryak*); he spreads [the threads] across. With the latter [verse], namely "blue and red," he spreads that which is blue of those two threads across the southern track. "On the northern" means on the track of the left wheel. Having taken hold of the two threads simultaneously, he spreads them while reciting the mantra only once, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra despite the difference in location. Another says: "Because of the difference in location, there is a repetition of the mantra. However, the approach should be understood as being like the *sānnāyyakumbhī* (the milk-pot): "I place the two *ukhā* vessels for the non-falling of the sacrifice. There is no spreading of threads in the case of horses and other animals, due to their lack of connection with a chariot. 5.23.
He approaches them with the following verses. 5.24.

He approaches and passes over those [verses] in the Sūtra; he passes over them with the three subsequent ṛcs beginning with "ye vadhvaś candram. While traveling there by chariot, he goes over [them]. Others, however, say that the mantras should be recited even when going on horseback and so forth, because their purpose is simply "going. No, say others; for there is a restriction to the number three based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantras. The commencement of the journey takes place at the end of the three. 5.24.
And when passing by a sacred ford, a standing pillar, or a crossroads, one should mutter the following verse.
Thus ends the fifth section in the Gṛhyapraśna of Āpastamba.

*Atikrama* means passing by; *vyatikrama* is simply *atikrama*, the prefix *vi-* being redundant, just as *abhyupāya* is the same as *upāya*. The bridegroom should recite the next verse, namely, "Tāmandasāna... (*RV* 10.85.39). There is a repetition of the recitation whenever the occasion arises. The word *ca* (and) serves to connect the recitation with each [offense] individually. Otherwise, based on the indicative power of the mantra, the recitation would have to be performed only when all three offenses coincide; however, the Tīrthas and others are not praised in the mantra. Rather, the Aśvins are praised; therefore, one should not object that the mention of the other two [Tīrtha and Soma] would be useless in the event of an offense against only one, nor should one suspect that those words [referring to the others] were omitted [from the original]. (5.25)
Thus ends the fifth section in the Anākulā, composed by the venerable Haradatta.
Now begins the sixth section: He consecrates the boat with the next verse. 6.1.

Now, if on the way there should be a river, a pond, or a lake to be crossed by boat, he addresses the boat with the second verse, "May this [boat] carry us to the further shore in safety," with this [mantra]; the meaning is that he should address it. Addressing (anumantraṇa) means the recitation of the mantra while standing behind and looking toward [the object]. Once the addressing has been performed, the bridegroom and the bride board it. 6.1.
And while crossing a boat, the bride should not look about. 6.2.

Those who carry one across by boat are "boat-people" (*nāvyāḥ*), namely fishermen; "crossing them" means crossing at the time of fording. Although the feminine gender alone would have sufficed [to indicate the bride], the mention of the word *vadhū* (bride) is so that the prohibition against looking may apply specifically to her. Consequently, the rule "having crossed, he should recite the subsequent [verse]" applies to the groom alone. The word *ca* (and) is intended to show that the bride and the groom cross together. Both cross together. However, there is this further distinction regarding the bride. Some explain that "boat-crossable waters" (*nāvyāḥ*) refers to waters to be crossed by boat; according to them, the use of the masculine gender [in the compound] would be untenable. (6.2)
Having crossed over, one should recite the Uttara. || 6.3 ||

Having crossed and reached the further shore, the bridegroom should mutter the next verse, "On its further shore" (asya pāre) [MP 1.6.14]. If it is not a river, then he should also mutter "The plants which... (yā oṣadhayaḥ) [MP 1.7.9]; for the author will state later that this applies to the crossing of rivers and deserts. 6.3.

If there is an accident involving the cremation ground, or if a vessel or a chariot is damaged, one should kindle the fire; at the conclusion of the *yājyābhāga* offerings, while [the wife] maintains contact [with him], he offers the subsequent oblations, proceeds with the *jaya* and following rites, and performs everything up to the final sprinkling of water. || 6.4 ||

If one passes over a cremation ground, or if a vessel, a bowl, or the like, or a chariot is broken or lost—“chariot” being used here as an illustration for other such ill omens—the oblation to be described below must be performed. Therein, the ritual procedure (tantra) beginning with the kindling of the fire is undertaken. Because of the use of the word *adhi* (“over”), this applies specifically when passing over a cremation ground; however, it also applies when passing near sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*) and the like. He offers the subsequent oblations. The meaning is that he offers seven oblations with these subsequent mantras beginning with “*yad ṛte cid*. The restriction to seven is established by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra. Having offered them, he undertakes the remainder of the ritual procedure beginning with the *jaya* offerings. The vessels are employed only once. The *śamyā* sticks serve the purpose of enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). The mention of the kindling of the fire and so forth is for the purpose of introducing the ritual procedure (*tantra*), while the mention of the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings is for the purpose of instructing on the time for the *anvārambha* (the wife’s joining). The phrase “he undertakes the *jaya* offerings and so forth” is intended to exclude the *anvārambha*. Thus, he undertakes the *jaya* offerings and so forth as they have been established. Whatever ritual act was previously mentioned as occasional (*naimittika*), beginning from the kindling of the fire and ending with the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*), he performs that immediately thereafter. The meaning is that he does it only once, not repeatedly. Even if there is a repetition due to differences in place or time regarding the aforementioned occasions, this final oblation occurs only once at the end. 6.4.

When crossing milky trees or other trees that bear auspicious marks, as well as rivers and desert wastes, one should mutter the appropriate mantra over the northern side according to its specific characteristic.

The meaning is: of well-known boundary trees such as the *nyagrodha* and others that bear milky sap and are auspicious, as well as other famous boundary trees that possess auspicious characteristics (*lakṣaṇya*). Even with the reading *lakṣmaṇyānām*, the meaning is the same. Regarding rivers—both those containing water and those without—and deserts (*dhanvan*) and forests: upon crossing them, one should recite the two subsequent verses according to their respective gender; that is, whichever verse has the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) corresponding to whichever object is being crossed, that one should mutter. In this regard, for crossing a tree, one uses "Those Gandharvas... (MP 1.7.8); for crossing a river, "The herbs which... (MP 1.7.9); and for crossing a desert, "Those deserts... (MP 1.7.10). The instruction to follow the gender is so that both verses are not used in both cases. Thus, even when crossing a river, the entire verse is used, and likewise when crossing a desert. 6.5.
He causes [the disciple] to look at his own home with the *uttarā* mantra. || 6.6 ||

Then, having reached her own home and helped her descend from the chariot, he brings the wealth that came as her dowry into the house; thereafter, with the following verse beginning "I cause to appear," he causes her to see it clearly. The mantra should be applied to this purpose in some way or another: "I cause to appear—that is, I show—the dowry brought from the bride’s father's family, with a friendly and non-terrible eye—not merely with a non-terrible one, but with a friendly one—along with my own houses; and my house as well. In this [verse], the ornament called *viśvarūpa* which is fastened upon her belongs to the husbands (the plural is used for the singular); "may Savitṛ make my face pleasant for my husband. 6.6.
With the two following [verses], he unyokes the two draft-animals, the right one first.

With the next two verses, "We two have come" and "This god Savitṛ for us," [he performs] the unyoking with each mantra individually, as in the case of yoking; that is to say, the left [side] last. 6.7.

Having spread out in the middle of the house a red bull’s hide with the neck pointing eastward and the hair side up, while leading her into the house, he makes her recite the next verse as she steps forward with her right foot.

Having unyoked the two draft-animals, the bridegroom first enters the house himself; there, in the middle of the dwelling where the husband and wife reside, he spreads out a hide with the following verse, “A shelter and a shield,” and that hide belongs to a bull and is red in color. The manner of spreading it is such that the hair is directed toward the north and the neck toward the east. Having spread it, he then causes the bride to step forward into the house with his right foot; he causes her to enter. While causing her to step forward, he makes her recite the next verse, “The houses. Since the context was already the houses, the word “houses” is stated again—otherwise, because the chariot had also been mentioned in the context, one might suspect the mantra refers to entering the chariot. This very point indicates that the spreading of the hide takes place in the middle of the interior of the house. Because of the statement “while causing her to step forward, he makes her recite,” the commencement of the mantra and the action coincide; the delivery of the gift does not occur at the end of the mantra. 6.8.
And he does not stand upon the threshold. || 6.9 ||

The *dehalī* is the wooden threshold at the bottom of the door; others say it is the surrounding platform (*paryantavedikā*). The meaning is that at the time of entering, neither he nor she should step over it. Once they have both entered, he leads them toward the fire. Having entered the house, he should then eat his meal at that time. Then, having established the wedding fire in the northeast corner of the room where the skin-covers are spread, he proceeds with the ritual procedure beginning with the kindling of the fire. The vessels are used only once; the *śamyā* sticks serve as the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). 6.9.

In the north-eastern part of the house, having kindled the fire and offered the two *yājyābhāga* oblations, while she maintains contact with him, he offers the subsequent oblations; then he proceeds with the *jaya* and following rites, and having performed everything up to the sprinkling around, they both sit upon the skin with the next verse, the bridegroom to the north.

The bridegroom alone offers the thirteen principal oblations of the latter part, beginning with "āgan goṣṭham" (MP 1.8.3), even though there is a conflict with the indicative mark (*liṅga*), because the injunction (*vidhi*) is more powerful. The indicative mark is not intended to be significant here, since mantras serve the purpose of recalling the deity. It has been stated that this distinction—that the bridegroom is the one who acts in the latter part—applies to all the oblations. Regarding the rule "in the north-eastern part of the house," this should be understood to apply to the fire in every case. He performs the offering with the subsequent verse, "iha gāvaḥ prajāyadhvam" (MP 1.9.1). The statement that they both sit down at the end of the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*) is for the sake of immediate sequence; sitting down must be performed immediately after the sprinkling and nothing else. By this, it is established that the meal takes place prior to that. In that sitting, the mantra belongs to both of them. Since there is no connection with the fire here, it was stated that the bridegroom is the one who acts. And they both sit facing the east. 6.10.

Then, having seated the son of this woman who has sons living upon her lap with the [first] Uttarā [verse], having given fruits to him with the following Yajus, and having murmured the subsequent [verses], they remain silent until the stars appear. 6.11.

That woman who gives birth only to males and not to females is a *puṃśū* (male-bearer). Regarding her, the reading is *puṃsvaḥ puṃsvo jīvaputrā yā*; the letter *repha* (the visarga) is not to be recited, or if it is recited, it should be regarded as Vedic (*chāndasa*). She whose sons are indeed living and not dead is *jīvaputrā*, and she may also be regarded as *jīvapatyā*. Likewise, regarding "auspicious things" (*maṅgalāni*). For such a woman of the three higher castes, having seated the son on the lap of this bride with the subsequent verse, "With Soma, O Ādityas... [MP 1.9.2], and having given fruits to that boy with the subsequent *yajus*, "You are the breaths; go forth... [MP 1.9.3], he then mutters the two subsequent verses, "What is dear here... [MP 1.9.4] and "The auspicious one... [MP 1.9.5]. Then both, sitting upon that very skin, restrain their speech until the stars appear—that is, until the rising of the constellations. And the boy, having taken the fruits, goes according to his purpose. 6.11.

When the stars have risen, having gone out toward the eastern or northern direction, he shows her the Pole Star and Arundhatī according to their respective characteristics with the two following [mantras]. 6.12.
Thus ends the sixth section in the Gṛhyapraśna of Āpastamba.

Because of the statement "when the stars have risen," their sitting upon that very hide while restraining speech occurs prior to that; afterwards follows the departure. Although the rising of the stars alone would suffice, the specific mention of "stars" is for the sake of clarity. With the two subsequent verses, namely *dhruvakṣitiḥ* (MP 1.9.6) and *saptarṣayaḥ* (MP 1.9.7), the bride's act consists in looking at both with the recitation of the mantra. However, the groom, while looking, first causes her to recite the former verse by pointing out the Pole Star (*dhruva*), and afterwards the latter verse by pointing out Arundhatī. Then follows the release of speech. Since the viewing according to the respective signs is already established by the indicative power of the mantras themselves, the explicit mention of "according to the signs" is for the purpose of allowing an option. Thus, it is understood that with the two subsequent verses he shows her the Pole Star and Arundhatī either according to their respective signs or not. Consequently, in the case of the latter verse, the bride's act may optionally consist in the simultaneous viewing of all the Seven Sages starting from Kṛttikā as well as Arundhatī, or of Arundhatī alone. 6.12.
Thus ends the sixth section and the second chapter in the *Anākula*, a commentary on the *Gṛhya-sūtra* composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the third chapter, the seventh section:
Then he causes her to sacrifice with a *sthālīpāka* offering dedicated to Agni. 7.1.

By the word *atha* (now), it is indicated that on this very night the *sthālīpāka* (pot-cooked offering) takes place. It is called *sthālīpāka* because it is cooked in a pot (*sthālī*). The rule for its deity is given by the words *āgneyena* (with the offering to Agni). But one might object: "Is it not true that it will be prescribed later that 'Agni is the deity, with the *svāhā*-utterance as the primary element' [ĀpGṛ 7.5]? True; however, there is another rule there as well: "Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the second. Consequently, if that were the sole rule for the deity, this oblation would have two deities. And in that case, at the time of the pouring out (*nirvapaṇa*), the formal dedication (*saṅkalpa*) would have to be made to both of them. Even though in reality the sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is subordinate, it is nevertheless enjoined there as if it were primary: "Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the second" [ĀpGṛ 7.7]. Therefore, the dedication would have to be made to him as well. Thus, this *sthālīpāka* belongs exclusively to Agni. (It must be stated: thus, of the offering to Agni alone... if the rule regarding the expiation for "when the deity has not been assigned" applies, then for the Sviṣṭakṛt, the rule "when the deity has been assigned" applies. Because of the statement "he causes her to sacrifice," there is no joint status for both in this ritual act. This ritual belongs to the bride alone, while for the groom it is merely the office of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). Therefore, this serving of the *sthālīpāka* and the gift of rice and other items as a fee (*dakṣiṇā*) belong solely to the bride's property. As it is said: "For the wife is the mistress of the household goods" (TS 6.2.1). || 7.1 ||
The wife husks [the grain]. 7.2.

Immediately after seeing the Arundhatī star, he enters the house and pours out fresh rice or barley intended for the fire-offering, as much as he deems sufficient for the oblation and for the feeding of the Brahmins. He also sprinkles them silently with consecrated water. Then the wife threshes them. Although one could have used the pronoun "she" (sā) in the reference "threshing [it] with this husband" (*enā patyā*), the specific mention of the word "husband" (*pati*) is made so that it may be understood that this is a duty of the wife; otherwise, it would be understood as a duty of the sacrificer. For if the wife were considered here to be the sacrificer, it would follow that the threshing would belong to the husband in the *Pārvaṇa* and other such rites. 7.2.

Having cooked [the rice], having sprinkled it with clarified butter, having removed it from the fire toward the east or the north, and having sprinkled it again once it has been set down, he offers oblations from the *sthālīpāka* while she maintains contact with him, beginning from the kindling of the fire and ending with the *yājyābhāga* portions. 7.3.

Then the bridegroom washes those [grains] which have been husked three times and cooks them. The mention of the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire (*upasamādhāna*) is for the purpose of establishing the *tantra* (the common ritual framework) and for the purpose of fixing the time; it indicates how the *tantra* is to be undertaken after the sprinkling over the cooked oblation (*pratiṣṭhitābhighāraṇa*), and not before. Therefore, the sprinkling is performed with unconsecrated clarified butter (*ājya*). Here too, the employment of the vessels occurs only once, because the yoke-pins (*śamyā*) belong to the remnants of the wedding ceremony. Others, however, say "no" [to this].

The statement ending with the *ājyabhāga* offerings is intended to indicate the time for the *anvārambha* (the taking hold of the wife). The phrase "from the *sthālīpāka*" is redundant, because that [offering] is for the purpose of the *homa*. Nor should it be argued that the *sthālīpāka* is for the purpose of feeding the Brahmins, while the *homa* would follow from the clarified butter (*ājya*) alone; for this is because of the prescription of the sacrifice and the prescription of the deities. In that case, this is the style of our teacher: wherever there are both types of oblation—clarified butter and vegetable food—he provides a qualification for the principal offering, such as "an offering of clarified butter from the *sthālīpāka* food, from the cake, or from the *ājya*. By this, it is established that where no such qualification exists, there is only a single oblation. Consequently, in the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, there is an absence of clarified butter. Therefore, in that case, only the method of a single direct striking (*sakṛdupaghāta*) applies, since spreading under (*upastaraṇa*) and pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*) are impossible due to the absence of clarified butter. And regarding the marriage rite, in the passage "having sat down in their respective places" (*ĀpGṛ* 5.1), because of the absence of the qualification "an offering of clarified butter," it is established that in that context clarified butter alone is the sacrificial material (*havis*) possessing its ritual properties (*dharmavat*), whereas the parched grains (*lāja*) are without such properties (*adharmaka*). 7.3.
The under-spreading of the base and the sprinkling of clarified butter are performed once; the cutting of portions is done twice. || 7.4 ||

By this [rule], the procedure for cutting portions (*avadāna-kalpa*) pertaining to the sacrificial cake (*pauroḍāśika*) is to be understood as demonstrated here. Thus, the rule beginning with "Therefore, [the portion] is the size of a thumb-joint" (ĀpŚr 2.18.9) also applies. And there is the fivefold cutting (*pañcāvatta*) for those who practice the fivefold cutting. Furthermore, the second pouring over (*pratyabhighāraṇa*) of the oblation is like the cutting of the parched grains (*lāja*). When it should have been stated, "Having spread a base layer (*upastīrya*), having cut twice, he pours over twice," the singular expression is intended to indicate that the spreading and the pouring over are for the purpose of accomplishing the fourfold cutting (*caturavatta*). Therefore, in the absence of the fourfold cutting, there is also an absence of both the spreading and the pouring over, as in such cases as "Having offered once, he should sacrifice" (ĀpGṛ 7.7) and "With the hollow of his hands, [he offers] only curds" (ĀpGṛ 22.10). || 7.4 ||
Agni is the deity; the offering is made with the utterance of "svāhā. || 7.5 ||

Because there are two primary subjects, this is a restatement of what is already established for the sake of what follows. *Agni* alone is the deity of the former oblation, which was prescribed by the rule "that which belongs to Agni" (*āgneyena*); for the latter, another deity is now prescribed. That in which the offering—the act of pouring—is performed with the utterance of *svāhā*, is called *svāhākārapradāna*. This refers to the oblation of the *sthālīpāka*. Since no distinction is made, it applies to both the former and the latter. In that context, because of the connection with the word *svāhā*, the name of the deity takes the dative case—e.g., *agnaye svāhā* or *agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā*. Although this is already established by the rule "An oblation enjoined by the verb *juhoti* is one where the offering is made with *svāhā*" (ĀpPar 3.4), this statement is intended to exclude the practice found in certain other ritual manuals (*kalpa*) where the offering is enjoined to be made with a mantra, such as "One should offer with 'svāhā to so-and-so'," or "Or with a *ṛc* addressed to that deity," or "Having recited the *puronuvākyā*, one should offer with the *yājyā*. Even so, one might think that for the *sthālīpāka* one should simply say "to Agni, svāhā," and for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, "to Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā. However, this specific statement is intended to exclude the use of mantras in cases where the deities are extended from the *Pārvaṇa* sacrifice by the rule "The deities are according to the instruction" (ĀpGṛ 7.24). Consequently, it is established that in cases such as "At the full moon, the Full Moon [deity]" (ĀpGṛ 7.28), where the deity of the *sthālīpāka* itself is enjoined, the oblation is to be made using the name of the deity itself, and not with a mantra dedicated to that deity. 7.5.
Or alternatively, having offered it all at once, he should sacrifice. 7.6.

With the same ladle with which the oblation was taken, one should offer it after having scooped it out once. In this view, it is established that there is also an absence of the under-layering (upastaraṇa) and the sprinkling over (abhighāraṇa). Some, however, perform these. The explicit statement "one should offer" is intended to ensure that the rule applies even to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. || 7.6 ||
Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the second. || 7.7 ||

Agni Sviṣṭakṛt becomes the second [deity] by virtue of being a deity. The mention of "second" is for the purpose of making known that he shares the same ritual characteristics as the preceding [deities]. By means of this, there is an inclusion of the Sviṣṭakṛt even in such rules as “one should offer the principal oblations according to the instruction” (ĀpGṛ 2.7). Likewise, there is the application of the two rules: “having dipped [the ladle] once, one should sacrifice” (ĀpGṛ 7.7) and “the offering is accompanied by the utterance of svāhā” (ĀpGṛ 7.5). || 7.7 ||
There is a single spreading [of clarified butter] and a single cutting [of the portion], and a double sprinkling [of clarified butter]. || 7.8 ||

Here too, the procedure for the portions to be cut for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the *puroḍāśa* should be understood as demonstrated [in the preceding section]. The specific details—“By that [procedure], one who cuts five portions [cuts] twice; each subsequent [portion] is larger; he does not pour clarified butter over the oblation again” (*ĀpŚr* 2.21.3, 4, 5)—are also to be observed here. || 7.8 ||
The portion to be cut off is from the middle of the eastern side. 7.9.

This refers to the primary *pradhāna-homa* of the preceding [offering]. This statement is for the sake of the *upaghāta* (dropping) method of offering. However, in the case of the four-portion (*caturavatta*) method, the rule is already established because it pertains to the cake-offering (*pauroḍāśika*). One might object: "In that case too, would this not be for the purpose of prohibiting those two specific locations, namely 'the second from the eastern half' and 'the third from the western half'? If that were so, then the rule "from the northern half for the subsequent [offering]" regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* should not have been commenced, as there would be no distinction [between the two cases]. Therefore, in the case of the four-portion method, the injunction belongs solely to the cake-offering ritual; this present statement, however, is for the sake of the *upaghāta* method. 7.9.
The fire-oblation (homa) is performed in the center. || 7.10 ||

The middle point is the junction of the *āghāra* libations. Here too, the place for the oblation (*homadeśa*) should be understood as being exactly that prescribed in the *Pauroḍāśika* section. Therefore, when there is a plurality of oblations, the specific rules such as "the preceding one joined with the preceding one" (ĀpŚr 2.19.9) and so forth apply here as well.
From the latter half [of the preceding word], [the augment] of the following [word]. 7.11.
This undertaking also has the purpose of refuting the position of those who hold to the view of injury. 7.11.
The oblation is performed in the eastern half of the northern half. 7.12.

Here too, the ritual procedure (*dharma*) of the *pauroḍāśika* *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is to be understood. By that [procedure], the specific rule “not touching the others” (*asaṃsaktām itarābhiḥ*, ĀpŚr 2.21.6) applies here as well. If the term “oblation” (*homa*) were relied upon, then the phrase “in the eastern part of the northern half” (*uttarārdhapūrvārdhe*) might also be construed with what follows, namely “like the *prastara* [grass-bundle] regarding the two smearings” (*lepayoḥ prastaravat*). || 7.12 ||
He states the disposal of the two ladles smeared with the remnants of the *upastaraṇa* and other offerings, as well as of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) spread for the purpose of using the vessels:
"Having silently anointed the two smearings with the sacrificial grass as in the case of the *prastara*, he throws them into the fire. (7.13)

Having taken a small portion from that sacrificial grass (*barhis*) upon which the oblation and the clarified butter (*ājya*) are placed, he silently anoints that grass with the remnants of the food and the clarified butter—just as one does with the *prastara* bundle—and then silently casts it into the fire just like the *prastara*. Precisely because this is prescribed as a disposal (*pratipatti*), the spreading of the *barhis* takes place behind the fire, and the placing of the oblations occurs there as well; this is also clear in another ritual manual (*kalpa*). [It says: "Having sprinkled the cooked oblations, having moved them northward, and having placed them on the *barhis*. Some consider the anointing to take place after the surrounding of the fire. Because of the statement "like the *prastara*," the anointing occurs at three places. In the case of the four-fold portion (*caturavatta*), the anointing is done with the ladle used for the offerings at the tip [of the *barhis*], with the one used for the under-layer and the sprinkling at the middle, and with the clarified butter vessel at the root. In the case of the "direct-contact" method (*upaghāta*), since there is no ladle for the purpose of the under-layer and the sprinkling, the anointing of the middle part is done in the clarified butter vessel and the root part in the pot of cooked rice (*caru*). There is also the instruction: "having taken a blade of grass from what has been anointed. Likewise, he himself performs the placing of the ladle used for the offering and the duties of the *āgnīdhra*.

In this case, since there is no explicit statement [to that effect], even though the *jayā* and other offerings are discontinued, the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*) which follows their sequence is not discontinued, because it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the fire-sacrifice; thus he says: "The subsequent sprinkling is established. 7.14.

The meaning is that the subsequent ritual (*uttaraṃ tantraṃ*), beginning with the *jayā* offerings and so forth, should be performed here exactly as established [in the archetype]. And how is it established? From the statement "he offers additionally" (*upajuhoti*). Following the principal oblations (*pradhānahoma*), the throwing of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) into the fire occurs after those additional oblations (*upahoma*). Otherwise, because of the instruction [that it follows] immediately after the principal oblations, the throwing would occur before the additional oblations.

In this context, the word *kṛtvā* (having performed) must be supplied. The meaning is: "having performed the sprinkling," that is, "having completed the ritual up to the sprinkling. For what purpose is this? It is for the purpose of establishing that only the rites beginning with the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas are to be performed at the end of the sprinkling, and nothing else. Others, however, reading the entire section as a single rule—*siddham uttaram pariṣecanam* (the subsequent sprinkling is established)—explain it thus: by this, in the case of the *sthālīpāka*, after the principal oblations (*pradhānahoma*), only the sprinkling from the remainder of the ritual procedure (*tantraśeṣa*) is established, while everything else is not established. Therefore, they argue that the omission of the secondary oblations (*upahoma*) is enjoined here. For them, the term *uttaram* (subsequent) would be redundant. 7.14.
With that [food] mixed with clarified butter, he should feed a Brāhmaṇa. || 7.15 ||

The word "with clarified butter" (*sarpiṣmatā*) is used for the sake of emphasis, since it is already possessed of clarified butter by virtue of the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*); the meaning is that one should pour over it abundant worldly clarified butter. The Brāhmaṇa who sits to the south—him the bride or the groom should feed.
He gives a bull to one who has honored him. || 7.16 ||

To that teacher who is honored and worthy of respect for this groom, the bride gives a bull as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) from the *sthālīpāka*. Although the sacrificial fee should be given by the bridegroom to the officiating priest after being brought from her own family, because there is no mutual giving or receiving between husband and wife, it is therefore enjoined that it be given to the teacher. By this, he becomes fully rewarded. And this principle is seen in the Dharmaśāstra: having stated such things as, "A father shall not perform a sacrifice for his son, nor a son for his father," it concludes, "they should give the sacrificial fee to the teacher. (7.16)
Thus, from this point forward, on the festival days (parvan), the rite should be performed by those who have fasted, with the exception of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

Therefore, after the *sthālīpāka* and excluding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the two householders—having observed the fast according to the rule, “On the *parvan* days there is fasting for both” (ĀpDh 2.1.4)—should perform the *sthālīpāka* on the *parvan* days, that is, on the full-moon and new-moon nights, in this very same manner according to the procedure for the *āgneya-sthālīpāka*. This is an extension of the ritual procedure (*kalpātideśa*): the meaning is that the *sthālīpāka* is to be performed on the *parvan* days, and its procedure begins with “He causes him to sacrifice with the *āgneya-sthālīpāka*” (ĀpGṛ 7.1) and ends with “He gives a bull as the fee. Here, because of the dual number in the expression “by the two who have fasted,” both are entitled to the rite; however, in that context, it is the wife alone [who is the primary agent]. Furthermore, the distinction here is that no sacrificial fee is given. In that *pārvaṇa* rite, the specific details occasioned by the marriage, such as the single set of vessels and the *śamyā* peg, are not to be performed. Nor should the *anvārambha* (the touching of the wife by the husband) be performed, because it is an act belonging to the sacrificer, and in this case both are the sacrificers. [Objection: Let there then be another officiating priest, and let the *anvārambha* be performed by both. [Reply: That too is not so, because of an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*). When the text prescribes the *anvārambha* involving the touching of the heart, it indicates that the *anvārambha* does not occur in the *pārvaṇa* and similar rites. Otherwise, the *anvārambha* would already be established through the extension (*atideśa*) from the *pārvaṇa*. In passages such as “From the taking of the hand onwards, the vow of the two householders” (ĀpDh 2.1.1), the marriage rite is intended to include all its constituent parts. Therefore, once the marriage rite is completed at the end of the *saṃveśana* (the ritual cohabitation), the duties of a householder, such as the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), commence. The status of being established in the *pārvaṇa* rites might occur even before the *saṃveśana*; however, the commencement occurs after the cooking when the *parvan* day arrives. To that effect, he says: “After this” (ĀpGṛ 7.19). And the beginning of that rite is on the full moon, not on the new moon, because we see it so in the Śrauta texts, and because these two rites take the place of those. The Chandogas also recite: “If the new moon falls first, one should perform the full moon sacrifice and then do that; some say one should wait without having performed the full moon sacrifice” (KhāGṛ 2.1.2). Although the status of being established in the *pārvaṇa* is already established by the rule “On the *parvan* days there is fasting for both,” the explicit statement “by the two who have fasted” is for the purpose of showing that both are entitled to this particular rite. Even so, one might argue that it should simply say “by the two” instead of “by the two who have fasted. Therefore, having taken up the fasting already established by the rule “On the *parvan* days there is fasting for both,” the entitlement of both is shown by the dual number in the phrase “by the two who have fasted. By this, it is established that the *sthālīpāka* is to be performed on the very day of the sacrifice. The ritual action takes place on the fourteenth day, the day before the full moon. Thus says Āśvalāyana: “Now the *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka*. Its fasting is like that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). And there is the binding of the fuel and the sacrificial grass” (ĀśGṛ 1.10.1, 2, 3). If it were merely stated that it is to be done on the *parvan* days by both, then the *sthālīpāka* and the fasting would apply only to the *parvan* days, since the reference is identical. 7.17.
Some, however, say that a full vessel is the sacrificial fee. 7.18.

The word *pātra* has both genders. They say that a vessel full of a hundred handfuls of grain is a "full vessel" (*pūrṇapātra*). And this sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is to be given to the Brahman priest. 7.18.
From that time forward, he should offer these two oblations every morning and evening with his own hand, using either rice grains or barley.

After this *sthālīpāka* sacrifice, one should offer these two oblations every evening and morning with rice grains or barley. The phrase "after this" has the same application as in the *pārvaṇa* rite; therefore, the commencement of the rite takes place on that very night. After that, the husband and wife may eat their evening meal. These are called "these oblations" in order to indicate that they are the same as the *agnihotra* oblations of one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). Consequently, the ritual rules (*dharma*) pertaining to those oblations apply here, such as the rule regarding the *samidh* fuel-stick: "The *samidh* is made of *palāśa* wood, two finger-breadths long from the root," and so forth, as well as the times for kindling the fire (*prāduṣkaraṇa*) and for the oblation. This has been stated in the *Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra*: "Its times for kindling the fire and for the oblation are explained by those of the *agnihotra*" (ĀśGṛ 1.9.5), and so on. The mention of "with the hand" is an exception to using the *darvī* ladle. Since no specific ritual procedure (*tantra*) is prescribed, this rite is considered new (*apūrva*). However, the spreading of grass around the fire (*paristaraṇa*) certainly takes place. The sprinkling of water (*pariṣecana*), however, is specifically enjoined right here. (7.19)
The deity is the same as that for the *sthālīpāka* offering. 7.20.
The deity itself is the sacrificial object (*daivata*). "Svāhā to Agni" is the first oblation; "Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt" is the subsequent one. 7.20.
"The first oblation in the morning belongs to Sūrya," say some. 7.21.

The *saurī* [offering] has the Sun as its deity; the first oblation consists of "To the Sun, svāhā! The rest is the same. In that regard, one may proceed according to one's desire, but once the procedure has begun, one is bound by the rule. 7.21.
The sprinkling on both sides is as described previously. || 7.22 ||
The sprinkling around this oblation must be performed both before and after; as it was enjoined previously: "He sprinkles water around the fire as before, performing the circum-sprinkling. (7.22)
By this [Pārvaṇa rite], other rites such as those of customary conduct (ācāra) which are included under the Gṛhya [tradition] are explained.

That which occurs on the *parvan* days is *pārvaṇa*. By this *pārvaṇa* *sthālīpāka*, all other rites—which are gathered from traditional practice (*ācāra*) and thus known—are explained. This too is an extension of the ritual procedure (*kalpātideśa*). The meaning is that whatever is the procedure for the *pārvaṇa*—beginning with "After this... (ĀpGṛ 7.19) and ending with "The full vessel is the sacrificial fee, according to some"—that very same procedure applies to all *pākayajñas*. In that regard, fasting does not occur except in connection with the *pārvaṇa*, because it is prescribed in a different context in conjunction with the *parvan* days, and because the phrase "by the two who have fasted" (referring to ĀpGṛ 7.20) is not itself an injunction. Now, one might object: these duties (*dharma*) are taught in the context of marriage, and by that very fact they are extended (*atidiṣṭa*) to the *pārvaṇa*; therefore, the extension to other rites should also proceed from that very source. [Response: However, the extension is made by means of the *pārvaṇa* specifically to include the particularities such as "excluding the sacrificial fee" (ĀpGṛ 7.17) and "the full vessel is the fee, according to some" (ĀpGṛ 7.18). The statement "other than this" (ĀpGṛ 7.23) is intended to include only those of the same class; therefore, this extension applies only to *sthālīpākas* and animal sacrifices characterized by cooked food (*pakvaguṇa*), and not to those characterized by clarified butter (*ājyaguṇaka*). Some, however, desire it even there. Because of the word "rites" (*karmāṇi*), it is only the rites themselves that are explained by the *pārvaṇa*, not the times, the performers, or their specific duties. Consequently, in the rule "one should appease Nirṛti with a *pākayajña*" (ĀpDh 1.26.8), there is neither the presence of a wife nor the restriction to *parvan* days, and there is no fasting in cases such as the touching of the heart. Because of the word "explained" (*vyākhyātāni*), there is only an explanation of other rites by means of the *pārvaṇa*, not a relationship of archetype and modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti*). Therefore, even for one who has not previously performed a *pārvaṇa*, engagement in rites such as the *sarpabali* occurs upon the arrival of the proper time. Because of the statement "those which are gathered from traditional practice," this instruction applies even to rites characterized by cooked food that are not taught in this treatise but are seen in other scriptures—for example, in place of optional (*kāmya*) offerings, there are optional *carus*, such as "the *caru* consists of six oblations," and so forth. (7.23)
According to the instruction, [he should offer] to the deities between [the offerings to] Agni and Sviṣṭakṛt.

It has been stated that the phrase "the others [are performed] by means of the *pārvaṇa* [rite]" constitutes an extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual procedure (*kalpa*). Consequently, whatever deities and whatever *sthālīpāka* are prescribed for the *pārvaṇa*, they apply to all these rites. However, since there arises the possibility of sublation (*bādha*) of the two *pārvaṇa* deities by the deities specifically enjoined in each particular case, this statement is intended to prevent that sublation and to prescribe the location for those deities enjoined therein: "Between that *agni* which belongs to the *pārvaṇa* and the *sviṣṭakṛt*, those deities are to be sacrificed to in the interval between the two. In that regard, the oblation for the *pārvaṇa-agni* is the very same oblation prescribed for the *pārvaṇa* itself; as for what is prescribed in each specific instance, that is what applies there. As for the *sviṣṭakṛt*, however, its oblation consists of the entire remainder of the sacrificial materials (*haviḥśeṣa*), because it is observed to be so elsewhere. Others, however, maintain that the sacrifice to the two *pārvaṇa* deities is also to be performed from the very oblation prescribed for that specific rite.

Another says: "In this [rite], Agni and Sviṣṭakṛt are not merely restated (*anūdyete*) as the deities of the *pārvaṇa* sacrifice. What then? These two are enjoined as adventitious (*āgantuka*) by this very statement. Since no sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is specified there, the oblation for Agni is clarified butter (*ājya*), while for Sviṣṭakṛt, it is the entire remnant of the oblation. In any case, in all rites where the *pārvaṇa* is extended by analogy (*atideśa*), Agni must first be sacrificed to. And so it is seen in the Śrauta rites: "Whatever sacrifice one might desire to perform, one should certainly perform the offering to Agni therein. This is explained according to the Bhāṣya: "In all rites explained under the *pārvaṇa*, one sacrifices to the deities according to the specific instruction; one sacrifices to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt—that which is the second specific deity in the *pārvaṇa*—and one sacrifices to him from that very same oblation which was prescribed here and there. In that context, the phrase "the deities according to the instruction" is a restatement (*anuvāda*), intended to enjoin the inclusion (*samuccaya*) of Sviṣṭakṛt. If there were no such inclusion, his application would not occur in those [rites], because they would have been completed by the deities specifically prescribed for each. For just like Agni, Sviṣṭakṛt is also enjoined as a primary deity, as indicated by the expression "Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the second. However, by the word "between" (*antareṇa*), the location for that very Sviṣṭakṛt is restricted: "One sacrifices to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt between the principal offerings (*pradhānāhuti*) and the secondary offerings (*upahoma*). Therefore, even in cases where, after performing the subsequent offerings, one proceeds to the *jaya* and other rites—as in the rule stating "having performed the subsequent clarified-butter offerings, one proceeds to the *jaya* and so on"—which is concerned with the sequence, there too Agni Sviṣṭakṛt must invariably be sacrificed to in this interval. Furthermore, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), the meaning "between the principal offerings and the secondary offerings" is also obtained. (7.24)
Hospitality is unaltered [by the guest's status]. 7.25.

The rite called *ātithya*—in which a cow is offered to a guest, as expressed by the rule "He says 'cow' regarding the cow" (ĀpGṛ 13.15)—is an unmodified *apūrva* (an independent rite). The meaning is that the *pārvaṇa* dharmas are not to be performed during its offering of the omentum (*vapā-homa*). This very [statement] is the indicator that this extension [of rules] does not apply only to *sthālīpāka* offerings; rather, it applies to all animals characterized by being cooked, including those in the *aṣṭakā* rites and optional animal sacrifices seen in other scriptures. Thus, the *pārvaṇa* dharmas are established for these cases. 7.25.
In the Vaiśvadeva [offering], the Viśvedevas [are the deities]. || 7.26 ||

Regarding the injunction, “The noble ones, being purified, [should perform the rite] at the Vaiśvadeva” (ĀpDh 2.3.1), this instruction concerning the deities is for the purpose of forming a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) at the time of the offering (*nirvāpa*) during the rite known as the Vaiśvadeva. As for those deities therein—such as those mentioned in “With the first six, verse by verse” (ĀpDh 2.3.16)—they are the deities at the time of the actual offering (*pradāna*). Therefore, having resolved, “To the Viśvedevas,” the householder should prepare the cooked food in his own home. From that very cooked food, the oblations (*homa*) and the offerings (*bali*) are to be made to each respective deity. Passages such as “Every day, the *bhūtabali* offerings” (ĀpDh 1.12.15) constitute the originative injunctions (*utpatti-vidhi*) for the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*). However, the rule beginning with “The noble ones, being purified” (ĀpDh 2.3.1) is the procedural injunction (*prayoga-vidhi*) for those very same sacrifices. Consequently, the five great sacrifices are not to be performed separately; they are included within that very Vaiśvadeva rite. That which is performed in the fire is the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*). That which is the offering of the *bali* is the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*). That which is offered to the south with a formula containing the word "father" (*pitṛliṅga*) is the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*). And that which is given to the *agni* (or the guest) and so forth is the sacrifice to men (*manuṣyayajña*). Regarding this, the commentator on the mantras has stated that in the Vaiśvadeva, the second oblation is “To Soma, svāhā. Nor is there a contradiction with the rule “with the first six,” because that refers to the primary deities, whereas the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering belongs to the ritual framework (*tantra*).

Now, why is the complete ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for the Vaiśvadeva not taught here? It is said: if it were taught here, that procedure would not apply to all *caraṇas* (Vedic schools), yet this is desired. Therefore, its teaching is placed among the *sāmayācārika* (customary) rules common to all *caraṇas*. Furthermore, why was the instruction regarding the deities not made right there [in the section on those rules]? The purpose of teaching it here is so that this Vaiśvadeva rite may also be taught within this *Gṛhya-sūtra*. Consequently, for our own school, that very Vaiśvadeva procedure is prescribed, and not those found in other Dharmaśāstras; moreover, the application of the technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*), such as "with the sacred thread over the left shoulder" (*yajñopavītinā*) and "from left to right" (*pradakṣiṇam*), takes effect. 7.26.
Now, as an incidental digression, he teaches the deity of the snake-offering (sarpabali) and its performance:
"On the full moon day" means on whichever full moon day the rite is performed. || 7.27 ||
Thus ends the seventh section in the Gṛhyapraśna of Āpastamba.

Regarding the rule, “On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, at sunset, there is a *sthālīpāka* offering” (ĀpGṛ 19.3), and so forth, the deity for whatever rite is enjoined on the full moon day is that full moon itself. Which one? That full moon on which the rite is performed, as indicated by the mantra, “Svāhā to the full moon of Śrāvaṇa. Thus, from the *sthālīpāka* comes the oblation. Then, according to the instruction, there are *samidh*s of *kiṃśuka* wood and oblations of clarified butter; thereafter, from the *sthālīpāka*, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; and then the *jayā* offerings and so forth. If it were not stated, “on which [day] it is performed,” the oblation would have been offered simply with “Svāhā to the full moon. 7.27.
Thus ends the seventh section in the *Anākulyā*, a commentary on the *Gṛhyasūtra* composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the eighth section.
At both the commencement and the conclusion [of the recitation], the sage who is recognized [should be named]. || 8.1 ||
The Lord of the Assembly is the second. 8.2.

The commencement (*upākaraṇa*) is of two kinds: the commencement of a *kāṇḍa* (section) and the commencement of an *adhyāya* (chapter). The conclusion (*samāpana*) is likewise. Furthermore, this is seen in another passage: “At the commencement of a *kāṇḍa*, one who has no mother; and at the conclusion of a *kāṇḍa*, one who has no father” [ĀpDh 1.11.1–2]. The commencement of an *adhyāya*, however, is well known: “Having commenced the *adhyāya* on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa” [ĀpDh 1.9.10]. Likewise, the conclusion: “One should cease on the full moon of Taiṣya or under the asterism Rohiṇī” [ĀpDh 1.9.20]. In both types of commencement and conclusion, the seer (*ṛṣi*) who is recognized in the *Kāṇḍānukramaṇī* as the seer of the *kāṇḍa* is the deity (*devatā*) there. In that regard, Sadasaspati is the second. The meaning is that after making an offering to the seer of the *kāṇḍa*, one must offer to Sadasaspati. In this context, the *kāṇḍas* are the Prājāpatya, Saumya, Āgneya, and Vaiśvadeva; Prajāpati, Soma, Agni, and the Viśvedevas are the seers of these *kāṇḍas*. Those *kāṇḍas* which are mixed are called Sārasvata.

As Baudhāyana says: “The *pauroḍāśika* [section], the *yājamāna*, the *hautra* of the Hotṛs, and the *pitṛmedha*—these, together with their Brāhmaṇas and Anubrāhmaṇas, belong to Prajāpati. The *ādhvaryava*, the *grahas*, the *dākṣiṇāni*, the *samiṣṭayajūṃṣi*, the *avabhṛthayajūṃṣi*, the *vājapeya*, the *śukriyāṇi*, and the *savas*—these, together with their Brāhmaṇas and Anubrāhmaṇas, belong to Soma. The *agnyādheya*, *punarādheya*, *agnihotra*, *agnyupasthāna*, *agnicayana*, *sāvitra*, *nāciketa*, *cāturhotriya*, *vaiśvasṛja*, and *āruṇa*—these, together with their Brāhmaṇas and Anubrāhmaṇas, belong to Agni. The *rājasūya*, *paśubandha*, *iṣṭis*, *nakṣatreṣṭis*, *divaśyenayas*, *apāghās*, *satrāyaṇa*, *upahomas*, *sūktas*, *upānuvākyas*, *yājyās*, *aśvamedha*, *puruṣamedha*, *sautrāmaṇī*, *acchidrāṇi*, *paśuhautra*, and *upaniṣads*—these, together with their Brāhmaṇas and Anubrāhmaṇas, belong to Viśvedevas. (BauGṛ 3.1.21–24). And our two *mantrapraśnas* of the Gṛhya-sūtra are also to be seen within the Vaiśvadeva-kāṇḍa under the name *ekāgnikāṇḍa*. In that regard, when commencing the section (*kāṇḍopākaraṇa*), one should offer an oblation to the *ṛṣi* of that section with the formula: “To Prajāpati, the *ṛṣi* of the section, svāhā!”

Then, the mantra "tataḥ sadasaspatim adbhutam," which follows in its proper sequence, is recited in this section on marriage for the purpose of private Vedic study (svādhyāya) accompanied by mantras; this sūtra is placed here specifically to demonstrate its application. Otherwise, it would have had to be stated immediately after the initiation ceremony (upanayana).

Thus, upon the completion of each respective *kāṇḍa*, there is an oblation for that specific *kāṇḍarṣi*. A second oblation is for Sadasaspati. There are no *jayā* and subsequent offerings, due to the absence of an injunction [to that effect]. Some perform these oblations by relying on other *sūtras*. These four *vedavrata*s are those which are the introductory rites (*upākaraṇa*) for each *kāṇḍa*; those which are the completion rites (*samāpana*) are the rites for the dismissal of the vows (*vratavisarjana*). However, at the commencement of a full term of study (*adhyāya*), the oblation is made for all the *kāṇḍarṣis*, followed by that for Sadasaspati. The *jayā* and subsequent offerings may or may not take place. In this regard, since the commencement and completion of a *kāṇḍa* are restricted to the northern solstice and so forth, one should immediately after the initiation (*upanayana*) undertake the *prājāpatya-kāṇḍa*. Having commenced it on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, the study of the *prājāpatya-kāṇḍa* proceeds; its conclusion (*utsarga*) occurs on the full moon of Taiṣa. When the *prājāpatya-kāṇḍa* is finished in that much time, the conclusion is performed with it. Then follows the commencement of the *saumya-kāṇḍa*. Until the commencement of the next term, the retention and study of the *prājāpatya-kāṇḍa* takes place during the bright fortnights, while the study of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) takes place during the dark fortnights. On the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, the rite of commencement (*upākarma*) is performed. Then follows the study of the *saumya-kāṇḍa*. Its conclusion (*utsarga*) is on the full moon of Taiṣa, marking the completion of the *kāṇḍa*. The same applies to the other two [the *sāvitra* and *āgneya* *kāṇḍas*]. In all cases, after the conclusion, the first option is the retention and study of the portion previously learned, as well as the study of the auxiliaries, and the performance of the oblation. Now, for those who study the *Sārasvata-pāṭha*, they perform the four *vedavrata*s immediately after initiation in their proper order. At the appropriate time, having commenced the term of study, they study according to the recension; the conclusion (*utsarga*) is on the full moon of Taiṣa. As before, there is the retention and study of the auxiliaries, followed again by the rite of commencement, and so forth. In the first alternative, however, some do not perform the conclusion (*utsarjana*). Having studied from the commencement (*upākaraṇa*), they commence again. Others, however, conclude and then study again. They perform the *vedavrata*s whenever convenient. Their source must be sought. In all these alternatives, the commencement and conclusion of the *Śukriya* sections are performed separately.

The procedure there is as follows: on the full moon day, beginning with the rising of the sun during the northern course and ending with the *ājyabhāga* offerings, one offers oblations with the formulas "To Soma, the Ṛṣi of the section, svāhā! and "To Sadasaspati," and then proceeds with the rites beginning with the touching of the *madantī* water, up to the end of the *pariṣecana* and the *jaya* offerings. The same procedure applies here as well, including the dismissal [of the fires] as before. 8.1–2.

“Whatever is not offered in the fire must not be eaten” (ĀpDh 2.15.13). Because of this statement from the *Dharmaśāstra*, even for the sake of maintaining the body, the meal of a twice-born person must consist only of the remnants of the *vaiśvadeva* offering. According to the statement, “If [the fire] is not invoked for four nights, it becomes a worldly fire,” if the *agnihotra* is not performed, the fire intended for all sacrifices would become a worldly fire. Consequently, even when afflicted by illnesses such as fever, since the *vaiśvadeva*, *agnihotra*, and other rites—or their expiatory offerings—must necessarily be performed, there arises the possibility that even if no officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is available, two persons who have not yet reached marriageable age might perform them in some manner, even by omitting the indicative marks of the mantras. Likewise, regarding the *vaiśvadeva* at *śrāddhas* and other occasions, because of the statement, “Now, for the householder, there are offerings and oblations of whatever is fit for eating” (ĀpDh 2.3.12), there arises the possibility of offering oblations with sacrificial material (*havis*) mixed with *suvarcaka*, barley-alkali (*yavakṣāra*), salt, inferior food, or *kośadhānya* (also known as *māṣa* and other grains, excluding sesame). To prohibit both of these cases, he says:
They prescribe that the oblation (homa) be performed by a woman who has not undergone initiation, and with food that is mixed with alkaline salt and inferior grains. 8.3.

In the section concerning *pākayajña* sacrifices, this prohibition applies everywhere, including *śrāddha* rites and others. "Inferior grains" refers to leguminous crops such as *māṣa* beans, black grains such as chickpeas (*caṇaka*) and *kodrava*, and so forth; these the learned avoid and reject. Although the prohibition is already established by the rules: "A woman shall not offer the oblation; one who has not been initiated shall not; there is no offering with alkaline salt" (ĀpDh 2.15.17, 18, 14), this specific prohibition is for the sake of what follows. Furthermore, since Āśvalāyana’s statement—"From the taking of the hand [in marriage] onwards, one should maintain the domestic fire oneself, or else the wife, or the son, or the daughter, or a pupil" (ĀśGṛ 1.9.1)—might give rise to the suspicion that the wife and others are entitled to perform the *aupāsana* oblations, this prohibition is stated to preclude that. (8.3)
He states an exception to this prohibition:
"The optional offerings and the bali-oblations are according to the instruction. (8.4)

This prohibition regarding women and others is not to be observed in the case of optional rites (*kāmya-karma*); those rites must be performed exactly according to the instruction. Likewise, the offerings (*bali*) must also be performed exactly according to the instruction. The example of the optional rite is: "Whatever merchandise he may have in his house for the sake of success. Thus, from the point "whatever is edible" onwards, since there is no possibility of the prohibition of women and others—which was enjoined for the *homa*—applying to the offerings, this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*): that the rules of the *homa* apply to the offerings. Therefore, [rules] such as "with the other [hand]" and "having bent the right knee" also apply to the offerings. Although it would have been established by the rule "not in optional rites and offerings," the statement "exactly according to the instruction" indicates that their application occurs precisely through the instruction itself—whether by one's own scripture or another scripture—and not as a substitute (*pratinidhi*). 8.4.
When the fire has been kindled by itself in every respect, he should place two fuel sticks upon it with the following two verses. || 8.5 ||

"In all cases" means in all *pākayajña* sacrifices when the fire has ignited itself, that is, without human effort such as blowing [on the embers]. When this occasion has arisen, one should place two fuel-sticks (*samidh*) into the fire with the two following verses: "Flame up! and "Do not harm us! Since this is enjoined by the verb *ādadhāti* ("places"), there is no *svāhā*-utterance. Because of the inclusion of the word "all," this rule applies to all *pākayajñas*; otherwise, due to the context, it would apply only to the marriage ceremony. "In all cases" means in any fire—whether worldly, Vedic, or domestic—others say it refers to times when a single ritual action is being performed. 8.5.
"May Fortune not come to me; may Fortune not go to me," so [he says]. 8.6.
"With these two *yajus* formulas, he should place these two kindling-sticks (*samidh*) upon the fire"—this is an alternative for the mantra. (8.6)
One should recognize this day as the day on which one brings home a wife. 8.7.

One should recognize this day and this lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) and not forget them. The meaning is that one brings [the bride] from her family on the day and under the lunar mansion in which one marries her; that lunar mansion under which the taking of the hand was performed must not be forgotten. By the word "brings" (*āvahate*), the initial taking of the hand is intended. The purpose for instructing not to forget is that every year, under that same lunar mansion, there is a specific ritual act. But what is that? It is that which is taught among the customary rules (*sāmayācārika*) beginning with, "And whatever may be dear to the two of them" (ĀpDh 2.1.7). Nor is that a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*). For if it were a specific modification of the *Pārvaṇa* rite, then the statement "its performance is explained by the *Pārvaṇa*" would be inconsistent. Now, why is that very injunction not taught here? It is said: if it were taught here, it would be understood—by virtue of the context—to be an auxiliary part of the marriage ceremony. Consequently, even the *śamyā*-wood and other such items would become duties of the marriage ceremony. Furthermore, the teaching there is for the sake of all schools (*caraṇas*). 8.7.
For three nights, both shall sleep on the ground, observe celibacy, and abstain from pungent and salty foods. 8.8.

Starting from the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice, for three nights both husband and wife must sleep on the ground, not on beds or similar furniture. There is to be celibacy (*brahmacarya*), which means abstaining from sexual intercourse, and the avoidance of alkaline substances and salt in their food. In this regard, the avoidance of alkaline substances and salt does not apply while they are on the journey prior to the *sthālīpāka*. However, celibacy applies even then. Since the rite of cohabitation (*samāveśana*) is prescribed for the fourth night, this mention of celibacy is for the sake of reinforcement; even though the two sleep together, effort must still be made to avoid sexual intercourse. (8.8)
Between their two beds stands a staff smeared with fragrant substances, encircled by a cloth or a cord. || 8.9 ||

Between the two spouses, in the middle of the bed, a staff made from a milky tree—smeared with fragrant perfume, adorned with flowers, and encircled by a cloth or a thread—should be placed so that there may be no mutual contact. 8.9.

On the fourth [night], during the latter part of the night, having raised her with the two following [verses], washed her, and set her down, he performs the rites from the kindling of the fire up to the end of the *yājyābhāgas*. While she maintains contact [with him], he offers the subsequent oblations and proceeds with the *jayas* and so forth. Having performed the rites up to the final sprinkling (*pariṣecana*), he seats her to the west of the fire facing east. He pours the remainder of the clarified butter over her head with the *vyāhṛtis*, preceded by the syllable *oṃ* as the fourth. With the two following [verses], they look at each other according to their respective characteristics. With the next [verse], he wipes their hearts with the remainder of the clarified butter. Having murmured the three subsequent [verses], he should murmur the rest at the time of sexual union. 8.10.

The latter part of the night is the third portion of the night; [the ritual] is performed with the two verses beginning "udīrṣva" and "ātaḥ". The re-enactment of the placement here is so that the staff might not be placed again on that same bed.

He offers the seven principal oblations of the Uttarā [section], beginning with “O Agni, atonement-maker” (MP 1.10.3). In that context, the phrase “You are the atonement of the gods” (MP 1.10.3) is to be supplied as an *anuṣaṅga* to the first four mantras. The remaining mantras are three in number. The term “portion of clarified butter” (*ājyabhāga*) is an instruction regarding the time for the *anvārambha* (the taking hold of the fire). And the statement “he proceeds with the *jaya*-oblations and so forth” indicates the cessation of those [previous rites].

Having completed the remainder of the ritual procedure, he then seats her to the west of the fire, behind the fire, facing east with her face turned toward the east; taking a portion from the remnant of the clarified butter that has been offered, he pours it onto the head of the bride with the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *svāhā*, reciting each mantra individually with a wooden ladle.

Then, with the two following verses, “I beheld you” (MP 1.11.1), they should look at each other simultaneously according to their respective marks: the bride with the first verse and the groom with the second. Then the groom anoints the hearts of both the bride and the groom with the following verse, “May they anoint” (MP 1.11.3), using that same remnant of clarified butter taken once, reciting the mantra only once. Then he mutters the three following verses beginning with “O Prajāpati, [this] body” (MP 1.11.4). Then he should mutter the remainder of the section, beginning with “Climb onto the thighs,” at the time of *samāveśana*, which is the act of coming together. This *samāveśana* necessarily takes place during that very same latter part of the night; this alone is the *samāveśana* performed with mantras, and not others. The statement that it ends with the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*) is for the sake of immediate sequence, so that this very rite occurs immediately after the sprinkling; therefore, the meal takes place even before that. 8.10.
Or someone else might address him with a mantra. 8.11.

Or someone other than the groom should consecrate the bride and bridegroom as they are about to come together with the remainder of the *anuvāka*; the groom himself should not mutter the *japa*. In that regard, the garment which the bride was made to wear previously by him should be removed at the end of the vow; having put on another garment, the bride touches [him]. Because a fault is seen in touching with that [garment], [the verses] beginning with "Go away, O Śābalya" are used for that hand-touching. However, during the performance of the vow, there is no touching because of the intervention of the staff. On the following day, he should give that garment to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the *Sūryāsūkta* with these four verses beginning with "Go away, O Śābalya. As he will say: "He should give the bride's garment to one who knows this, with the subsequent verses" (*ĀpGṛ* 9.11). Āśvalāyana has also stated: "He should give the bride's garment to one who knows the *Sūryāsūkta*; food to the Brāhmaṇas" (*ĀśGṛ* 1.8.13–14). || 8.11 ||

When she has become one whose clothes are soiled with menstrual blood, he then instructs her in those actions prohibited for a Brāhmaṇa woman, namely those beginning with the words, "Her who is soiled with menstrual blood" (TS 2.5.1).

“*Malavadvāsāḥ*” (the woman with soiled garments) is a designation for a menstruating woman. The expression “*yadā*” (when) is used to indicate that [these rules] apply even after marriage; otherwise, they would apply only during the period of the wedding itself, due to the context. Furthermore, the instruction (*saṃśāsana*) occurs once at the first menses, and that alone serves for all subsequent occasions, just as in the case of the initiation (*upanayana*) of a religious student (*brahmacārin*). If the word “*enām*” (her) were not used, one might understand that someone else instructs them, because of the rule “*anyo vainām*” (ĀpGṛ 8.11), which refers to the subject under discussion. The phrase “prohibited by the Brāhmaṇas” is stated to make known that things prohibited by worldly custom—such as sleeping on high beds or seats—are to be understood from common usage alone. By the use of the word “*karmāṇi*” (acts), it is indicated that these are acts themselves that are made known through other words, rather than being an injunction (*saṃpraiṣa*) issued by a Brāhmaṇa passage. The use of the word “*etāni*” (these) is so that there may be an instruction regarding both the prohibited and the prescribed acts, such as those beginning with “*yāṃ malavadvāsasam*. Consequently, there is also an instruction for the two prescribed acts: “*tistro rātrīr vrataṃ cared añjalinā vā pibet*” (TS 2.5.1). Thus, in the phrase “*brāhmaṇapratiṣiddhāni*,” the mention of “prohibited” is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*).
