In that regard: - In the sentence “*yāṃ malavadvāsasam*,” there is a prohibition against approaching her before she has bathed. - In “*yām araṇye*,” there is a prohibition regarding the location. - Even after she has bathed, in “*yāṃ parācīm*,” there is a prohibition against approaching her while she is facing away. - In “*yā snāti*,” there is a prohibition against bathing during the three nights. - In “*yābhyajyate*,” there is a prohibition against anointing the body with oil. - In “*yā pralikhate*,” there is a prohibition against scratching the head with a comb or similar tool. - In “*yāñjate*,” there is a prohibition against applying collyrium to the eyes. - In “*yā dataḥ*,” there is a prohibition against cleaning the teeth. - In “*yā nakhāni*,” there is a prohibition against clipping the nails. - In “*yā kṛṇatti*,” there is a prohibition against spinning cotton or other fibers. - In “*yā rajjum*,” there is a prohibition against making ropes. - In “*yā parṇena*,” there is a prohibition against eating from a leaf. - In “*yā kharveṇa*,” there is a prohibition against using a broken vessel; *kharva* means something partially shattered. - The phrase “*tisro rātrīḥ*” establishes the time limit for these prohibitions. - The phrase “*añjalinā vā pibet*” and so forth prescribes the vessels for drinking during meals. 8.12.
When the appearance of the menses occurs, at the onset of her fertile period, he consecrates her with the following verses. 8.13.
Thus ends the eighth section in the Gṛhyapraśna of Āpastamba.

Regarding the blood-red menses: when the ritual cohabitation (*samāveśana*) is to be performed during the fertile period (*ṛtu*), one should consecrate [the woman] with the thirteen *ṛc*s beginning with "Viṣṇu [prepared] the womb" (MP 1.12.1). Because of the statement "from the appearance of the menses," the consecration takes place at every manifestation of the menses; it is not restricted to the first fertile period alone, as in the case of the formal instruction (*saṃśāsana*). The word "having bathed" (*snātām*) is intended as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for all those things prohibited by the Brāhmaṇas. Thus, the meaning is that she has bathed and performed auspicious rites (*kṛtamaṅgalā*); by this, the application of collyrium and ointments is also permitted. 8.13.
Thus ends the eighth section in the Anākula commentary on the Gṛhyasūtra composed by Śrī Haradattācārya;
now begins the ninth section.

From the fourth day onwards until the sixteenth, they teach that approaching one's wife during her fertile period on each successive even night leads to the birth of offspring and the attainment of the highest good. 9.1.

The word *ṣoḍaśīm* is used in the accusative case with the sense of the ablative; thus, it means "until the sixteenth. The prefix *ā-* here denotes inclusion (*abhividhi*). Starting from the manifestation of the menses, both the fourth and the sixteenth nights are included, as indicated by the context. From the fourth night until the sixteenth, all nights are times for approaching one's wife during her fertile period (*ṛtu*). Furthermore, among these, one should know that each successive even-numbered night leads to the excellence of progeny. Because of the injunction regarding "approaching during the fertile period," this instruction applies even when the first approach occurs at the time of marriage, provided it is occasioned by the fertile period. On the fourth night, the approach must necessarily take place during the latter part of the night. In that instance, one should recite the *samāveśana* mantra over the remainder [of the ritual]. And because of the rule "he consecrates with the following verses," there is a combination of the mantras for the approach. In this regard, the mantras for the approach during the fertile period come first, followed by the mantras for the act of union; others hold the reverse order. (9.1)
If one who is on his way to obtain wealth sneezes or coughs, he should touch water and mutter the subsequent [mantras] according to their respective indications. 9.2.

*Prādhva* means one who has set out on a journey. *Artha* means purpose. For one who has set out on a journey for whatever purpose, that is "one whose journey is for a purpose" (*arthaprādhva*). When an ill omen occurs, such as sneezing or coughing, he should perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) by touching water and reciting the two subsequent verses, namely, "The call from behind, the call from all sides... and so forth. *Sneezing from all sides* (*parikṣava*) is a sneeze made by people standing all around him. The same applies to *coughing from all sides*. *Touching water* (*upasparśana*) is contact with water using the hand, or bathing, or sipping water (*ācamana*). In that case, he should perform whichever act he considers necessary to become pure. The phrase "according to the indicative mark" (*yathāliṅgam*) is inappropriate here, because there is no indicative mark (*liṅga*) of either sneezing or coughing in these verses. If it is argued that the word "sneezing" (*parikṣava*) in the first verse is an indicative mark due to a partial modification, even then, the second verse lacks any indicative mark of coughing. Therefore, it should be explained thus: when either of these two causes occurs, the recitation of both these mantras must be performed; and also in the case of other ill omens recognized through the indicative marks of the mantras, such as "the call from behind" (*anuhava*), etc. In this context, *anuhava* is a call from behind. *Parihava* is a call from all sides. *Parivāda* is slander or false accusation. *Parikṣava* has already been explained. *Bad dreams* are well known. *Bad speech* (*durudita*) refers to things such as "short-lived," etc. The expressions "called from behind" (*anuhūta*) and "called from all sides" (*parihūta*) refer to the inauspicious voice of a bird. *Aśākuna* refers to an ill omen from birds. *Akṣṇayā sṛtam* refers to the transverse movement of an animal, such as a jackal, or moving from left to right. When even one of these causes occurs, the recitation of both mantras must be performed, even though there is no indicative mark of sneezing or coughing. Furthermore, the word *parikṣava* is not an indicative mark for sneezing, because their forms differ. However, a partial modification is possible even for *parikṣava*. But that should be stated under another cause in a different section. The purpose of mentioning this here is so that this expiation may apply even to one going for the sake of marriage when these omens occur. In other sections, those [rules] heard apply only after marriage. However, because of the expression "for one whose journey is for a purpose," this applies to all purposes. And because of the context, these two mantras are recited here for the sake of regulating the place of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) during marriage as well. (9.2)
In this manner, with the subsequent [verses], according to their respective characteristics, he offers to Citriya, Vanaspati, Śakṛdrīti, Sigravāta, and Śakuni. 9.3.

By the word *evam* (thus), there is a requirement for the phrases *arthaprādhva*, *apa upaspṛśya*, and *japed*. And thus, according to the gender and number [of the object], it is for the sake of clarity. *Citriya* means well-known. In that context, having approached a *citriya* tree while traveling toward one's goal (*arthaprādhva*), and having touched water, he consecrates it with this verse: "May Agni be far from you" (MP 1.13.7). He should worship a dung-heap with the words: "The dung-heap is a blessing" (MP 1.13.8). He should worship a whiffle-wind (*sigvāta*)—a wind produced by another or a wind produced by clothing that has come into contact with oneself—with the words: "Thou art a whiffle-wind" (MP 1.13.9). Although a long vowel would have been expected at the end of the word *sigasi na asi*, the short vowel is used as a Vedic license (*chāndasa*). He should consecrate an auspicious bird with the verse: "O bird, like a singer... (MP 1.13.10). But if the speech is inauspicious, the previously mentioned recitation (*japa*) applies. Some maintain that this [recitation] also applies in that very case. 9.3.

Desiring the union of their hearts, having practiced celibacy for at least three nights, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* (mess of rice), and having performed the rites from the kindling of the fire up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he—while she maintains contact with him—offers the subsequent oblations from the *sthālīpāka*. He then proceeds with the *jaya* and following offerings, performs the rites up to the sprinkling of water around the fire, feeds an even number of Brahmins (at least two) with that ghee-smeared food, and causes them to pronounce words of success (*siddhi*). 9.4.

If the mind of the groom should not be won over by the bride, then this rite must be performed by her father or others who are endowed with austerity (*tapas*), without the knowledge of the groom, for the purpose of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). It is to be performed in the *aupāsana* fire. This has been stated previously regarding the rule of celibacy (*brahmacarya*): it is for a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), and therefore as much austerity as one considers necessary for the accomplishment of the goal should be performed. Furthermore, this rite takes place under the *punarvasu* nakṣatras, according to the statement, "on the morrow" (*śvastityena*, ĀpGṛ 9.5). What, then, is that rite? It is the *sthālīpāka* and the worship of the sacred texts (*pāṭha*). The entire ritual is like the *pārvaṇa*. However, because it is taught within the section on marriage, the vessels and the *śamyā* sticks are used only once. There is no fixed time [for its performance]. Its conclusion within the marriage section is to be understood from the fact that the giving of the garment (*vāsodāna*), which is a subsidiary part of it, is taught after it. And it is for this very purpose that it is taught after that. There are seven principal oblations (*pradhānāhuti*) beginning with "In the morning, to Agni" (*prātar agnim*). Then the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, then the *jaya* offerings and so forth. Since the *pārvaṇa* rules extend here, when only one *brāhmaṇa* would normally be fed, the plural number is prescribed; thus, a large *sthālīpāka* must be prepared. The mention of "containing clarified butter" (*sarpiṣmat*) is for the sake of a restrictive rule: after the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*), the *pārvaṇa* duties involve only the use of clarified butter. Therefore, the rule "some say the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a full vessel" (ĀpGṛ 7.18) does not apply here. He should have them recite for success (*siddhi*); that is, having them recite, "May there be the fulfillment of our resolve" (*saṃkalpasiddhir astu*) while they are eating. The statement that it ends with the sprinkling is for the purpose of restricting the agent. How? The same person who performs the oblation should also perform the feeding of the *brāhmaṇas* and the recitation for success. Thus, the bride is the agent for whatever rites follow, such as the scattering of grain (*parikiraṇa*). 9.4.

With the verse, "May there be well-being through the sacrifice," he scatters *pāṭhā* around [the fire] with twenty-one barley grains, saying: "If you belong to Varuṇa, I redeem you from Varuṇa; if you belong to Soma, I redeem you from Soma. (9.5)

Thinking that the rite which is to be performed tomorrow shall be accomplished under the asterism Tiṣya, the father or another officiating priest, acting as the sacrificer, goes on the previous day—after the ritual act has been performed at the conclusion of the recitation for success—to the place where the *pāṭhā* plant stands; having gone there, he scatters twenty-one barley grains (three times seven) around that *pāṭhā* with the two verses beginning, "Thou art of Varuṇa. The expression "three times seven" is a Vedic usage. *Pāṭhā* is a specific medicinal herb; however, the followers of the Atharva Veda read it as *pāśā*. 9.5.

When the next day has dawned, having caused her to rise with the [next] verse and having consecrated her with the three following verses, she should tie it on, covered by the [next] verse, to her hands; then at the time of going to bed, she should embrace her husband with her arms while reciting the verse concerning the pillow.

Having performed the scattering [of grain] and fasted, then on the following day she causes that *pāṭhā* plant to be raised; having dug it up with a spade, she extracts it with the subsequent verse, "This I dig" (*imāṃ khanāmi*, MP 1.15.1). Then she should consecrate it with the three subsequent verses beginning with "O you of upward-leaved [plant]" (*uttānaparṇe*, MP 1.15.2). Having cut its root into two pieces, she ties them to her hands with the subsequent verse, "I am... (*aham asmi*, MP 1.15.5); the meaning is that they are to be concealed so that her husband does not see them. In both cases there is a repetition of the mantra. Having tied them, she should then embrace her husband at bedtime during the night with the verse containing the word "pillow," "Upon thee I lie down" (*upa te adhām*, MP 1.15.6). Although one might simply say "with the subsequent verse," the specific mention of "the verse containing the word 'pillow'" is for the purpose of prescribing a particular method of embracing. The embracing should be performed in such a way that one of the two roots serves as a pillow beneath and the other as a cover above. 9.6.
He becomes submissive. || 9.7 ||

If the wife does not take pleasure in her husband, then this rite does not come to fruition; it is for the purpose of demonstrating that the husband becomes submissive to the wife, and not the wife to the husband. This is clear. Because of the masculine gender used in the word *vaśya*, the term *vadhū* here refers to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). (9.7)
He states its connection with another application:
"and the subduing of co-wives" (9.8).

This ritual act is not merely a means for the union of the hearts of both [the husband and wife]. What then? It is also a means of subduing a co-wife; the meaning is that even a co-wife can be subdued by this. Even in this view, the fire is indeed the *aupāsana* fire—that which was established for her through the marriage—which subdues the co-wife. For the fire is united according to the different types of marriage. And thus it is stated in the *Rājasūya*: "It is deposited in her *aupāsana* fire" (*ĀpŚr* 18.16.14). Likewise, the union with the fire is prescribed in the *Baudhāyanīya*; even after the union, it takes place in that very same fire, so that the co-wife being subdued does not know [of the ritual]. Some desire a second marriage in the very same fire; for them also, the ritual act takes place in that very same [fire].
Now he states another method for subduing rivals:
"With this very desire, one should constantly worship the Āditya with the following Anuvāka. (9.9)

With this very desire for the subduing of rivals, he should daily worship the Sun with the subsequent Anuvāka beginning with "ud asau sūryo agāt" (MP 1.16.1). The particle *eva* has the sense of "always" and serves to emphasize the repetition. 9.9.

For another woman seized by consumption, or for any other ailment, one who is observant of celibacy should touch her limbs according to their respective locations with the roots of the *puṣkara-saṃvarta* plant using the subsequent [mantras], and then cast them away toward the west.

*Yakṣma* refers to *rājayakṣma*, the disease of consumption (*kṣayaroga*). Having recognized that his wife or another woman under his care has been seized by this disease—such as a mother or other female relative—the following remedy should be performed. What is it? It is explained: one who is disciplined in celibacy (*brahmacarya*) should, with the roots of the *puṣkara* plant—which have a circular shape—or according to others, with *saṃvarta* roots; for the lexicographers state that *saṃvartikā* means "nine-petaled" [lotus]. With the subsequent mantras beginning with "From your eyes, from your nostrils" (*akṣībhyāṃ te nāsikābhyām*, MP 1.17.1), he should touch her limbs, such as the eyes and so forth, according to their respective characteristics, and then cast them out in a backward direction. Because of the use of words according to their specific characteristics, there is both touching and casting out for each mantra. There is touching with each individual root, because the plural number implies reference to all [the parts]. Since the intestines and other organs are internal, the wiping is performed on the external region of those parts. (9.10)
One who knows this should give [the gift] at the bride's residence with the following verses. 9.11.
Thus ends the third chapter, the section on the *namaḥ* [formula], in the *Gṛhyapraśna* of Āpastamba.

The garment that was put on at the time of the wedding should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who knows this [rite], specifically to one who knows the mantras recited in this section along with their meaning. Some consider this to be the remainder of the medical treatment because of its immediate sequence. For them, the qualification "the bride's garment" (*vadhūvāsaḥ*) is intended to preclude the giving of the garment of another woman afflicted by consumption (*yakṣman*). Furthermore, the phrase "who knows this" means one who has performed the medical rite. However, in the mantras such as *parādehi*, there is a censure of touching the bride’s garment worn at the time of the wedding, and the gift of it to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the *Sūryā* hymns is observed. Moreover, this is explicit in another ritual manual (*kalpa*): "Having completed his vow, he should give the bride’s garment to one who knows the *Sūryā* hymns" (ĀśGṛ 1.8.13). Therefore, its status as a remnant of medical treatment is untenable. As for what was said regarding "immediate sequence," the reason for that has already been stated: namely, so that the section on marriage (*vivāhaprakaraṇa*) may end in this manner. 9.11.
Thus ends the ninth section in the *Anākula*, a commentary on the *Āpastamba-Gṛhya-Sūtra* composed by Śrī Haradatta.
Now begins the fourth chapter.

Tenth Section. Now he announces the exposition of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), which follows according to the sequence of the traditional recitation of the mantras: "We shall explain the initiation ceremony. (10.1)

The rite by which the boy is led to the teacher’s family is called *upanayana*; it is a *śrauta* sacrament (*saṃskāra*) of the person. Although the qualification for *upanayana* is already established by the statement to be made later—“One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the sixth year after conception” (ĀpGṛ 10.2)—the explicit formulation of this promise is for the purpose of declaring its preeminence, as in the case of “We shall explain the *agnyādheya*” (ĀpŚr 5.1.1) and so forth. But how is *upanayana* preeminent? Because one who has not been initiated has no entitlement to any rites, whether *śrauta* or *smārta*. However, regarding *upanayana*, there is no entitlement for one who has not been consecrated by the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*. If the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*) were mentioned only in the context of the *sāmayācārika* (customary) rules, then even when they are stated here in connection with *upanayana*, they would apply to all schools (*caraṇa*). Yet it is desired that this ritual procedure (*kalpa*) belong to our own school alone; therefore, the instruction is given here. 10.1.
One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception.

The year in which one has been in the womb and lies there is designated by the word "garbha" (womb). Those years for whom that [year] is the eighth are these "garbhāṣṭamāni varṣāṇi" (years with the womb as the eighth). The plural number is used because the years differ according to the solar (*saura*) and other reckonings. Another says: from birth onwards, the seventh year is the eighth counting from the time in the womb; therefore, the initiation (*upanayana*) is enjoined even during the seven [lunar] years. Among those, because of unfitness during the first four years and because of the contradiction with other sacraments such as the tonsure (*caula*), the initiation takes place during the three [remaining] years beginning with the fifth. In this regard, there would be no distinction such that the initiation in the sixth and seventh years is optional (*kāmya*) while in the eighth it is obligatory (*nitya*); rather, it would be obligatory in all cases. Furthermore, when the fifth or sixth year is current, how can the year in the womb be the eighth? For the state of being a "filler" (*pūraṇatva*) is not possible unless there are things to be filled. Therefore, only when the seventh [lunar] year is current does the year in the womb become the eighth. Consequently, the plural number is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). Alternatively, the resolution is as stated previously. As for the optional initiation, it is obtained through another injunction. The reading *upanayīta* follows the Vedic revelation (*śruti*); however, the verbal root here is *śvi* (to swell/grow). Since the rule regarding the eighth year from conception is established as pertaining specifically to Brāhmaṇas due to the specific instruction for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, the rule for Brāhmaṇas is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the Vedic text. If the word *upanayīta* were not repeated, the previous mention of initiation would serve only as a general heading (*adhikāra*), and it would not accomplish the specific purpose that is to be accomplished therein. (10.2)
A Rājanya in the eleventh year from conception, and a Vaiśya in the twelfth year from conception. || 10.3 ||
Spring, summer, and autumn are the seasons in their sequential order. 10.4.

For a Brāhmaṇa, the rule is during the northern course of the sun and in spring; for a Kṣatriya, there is either an exception to that rule or a different rule; and for a Vaiśya, there is an exception [to the rule]. However, the beginning of the bright fortnight and so forth remain fixed. Here, as well as in the *Sāmayācārika* [duties], the rainy seasons and the [specific] times are prescribed. Among those, the prescription in the *Sāmayācārika* is for the sake of all Vedic schools (*caraṇa*). The prescription here is for the sake of restricting the specific caste (*varṇa*). By stating this—so that times seen in other scriptures might not be applied here—he makes known this: that even a time seen in another scripture may optionally apply in cases such as the tonsure ceremony (*caula*) and others. (10.3–4)

Having fed the Brahmins, having caused them to pronounce blessings, and having fed the boy, he mixes warm water with cold water with the first Yajus of the Anuvāka; then, with the following verse, he moistens his head. 10.5.

Now follows the procedure for the initiation (*upanayana*). On the previous day, the *nāndī-śrāddha* is performed. Then, on the following day, having fed the Brahmins, he causes them to pronounce blessings: "Auspicious day! Well-being! Prosperity! Thereafter, he should feed the boy. Thus far the ritual duties of the father and others. Then the teacher mixes warm and cold water with the first *yajus* of the subsequent section, namely, "With warmth, O Vāyu... (MP 2.1.1). While mixing, he pours the warm water into the cold, but not the cold into the warm. Then, with that water, he moistens the head of the boy—that is, wets it—with the subsequent verse, "May the waters moisten... (MP 2.1.2). Although the rule could have been established simply by saying "with the subsequent *yajus*," the statement "with the first *yajus* of the section" is made for the purpose of providing a specific designation. By this, the reference to the section is understood in the formula "with warmth, with water, O Vāyu..."; otherwise, there might be doubt as to whether "section" refers to the entire section or just the mantra. Although the act could have been established simply by saying "having poured the warm into the cold," the use of the word "mixing" (*saṃsṛjya*) is intended to show that it applies to all purposes; thus, he mixes the water intended for himself and the barber. This is made explicit for others: he should instruct the barber, "Perform the wetting with cold and warm water, making him free from pain and well. (10.5)
Having placed three blades of darbha grass between [the hair and the earth], he shaves the hair in each direction with the four subsequent verses, one mantra for each direction. || 10.6 ||

*Pravapati* means he first shaves; that is to say, he begins the shaving. By this it is stated that the teacher performs the shaving with the mantra first, and afterwards the barber. The procedure there is as follows: having placed three *darbha* blades upon the boy’s head in the eastern direction, he cuts them with the razor using the mantra, “With which [razor] they shaved... (MP 2.1.3). In place of the word *asau*, he takes the boy’s name in the nominative case—for example, “This one here, Yajñadattaśarman. In every instance where *asau* is used, the name must be substituted. Having cut [the hair], he throws a grain of barley onto a lump of cow-dung from an ox-hide. Then, having touched water, he does the same in the southern direction with the mantra, “With which Pūṣan...”; in the western direction with “With which [razor] more...”; and in the northern direction with “With which Pūṣan...”. Here, the name is taken in the vocative case: “With that I shave you, Yajñadattaśarman, for the sake of long life! (10.6)
While he is sowing, the mother or a student of sacred knowledge standing to the south addresses him with the next [verse]. 10.7.

When the teacher has thus performed the shaving in each direction, the barber shaves his hair while performing the preparatory rite with water that has been stirred together. While the barber is shaving him, the teacher consecrates him with the following verse, "That which [is done] with the razor" (MP 2.1.7). || 10.7 ||

To the south, the mother or a religious student, having placed barley grains on a lump of cow-dung from an ox, ties the hair onto that and places it at the root of an udumbara tree or upon a bunch of darbha grass with the following verse. 10.8.

Then the mother of the boy, or some celibate student, sits down to his right; having prepared a lump of bull-dung in a certain vessel and having placed barley-grains upon that lump, she gathers all the hair so as to hold it so that it does not fall on the ground. Having thus gathered it, she then places those hairs at the root of an *udumbara* tree or at a clump of *darbha* grass, with the following verse: “Having shaved the hair... (MP 2.1.8). If it is the mother, she causes her to recite the mantra to the end. 10.8.

After he has bathed, from the kindling of the fire until the end of the *yājyābhāga* offerings, [the teacher] causes him to place a fuel-stick of *pālāśa* wood with the following verse; then, to the north of the fire, he makes him step upon a stone with his right foot, saying, "Step upon it. (10.9)

“Having bathed the boy, dressed him in clean garments, and tied his topknot, he fastens the *yajñopavīta* upon him with the verse: ‘The *yajñopavīta* is the supreme purifier... Then, having invested him with the *yajñopavīta*, he leads him to the place of sacrifice,” so says Baudhāyana. The mention of the “bathed” boy is indicative of all those preceding rites. Thereafter, the teacher begins the ritual procedure (*tantra*) starting from the kindling of the fire. The production of the fire is as in the marriage ceremony. The *śamyā*-sticks serve the purpose of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). The vessels are set out only once. The garment, girdle, and other items are also placed down together. Then, at the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he causes the boy to place a fuel-stick (*samidh*) of *palāśa* wood upon the fire with the following verse: “O God, giver of life... (MP 2.2.1). The boy places the fuel-stick while reciting the mantra. The teacher directs him and makes him recite the mantra, causing him to place the fuel-stick. Since the deity is the object denoted, there is no contradiction regarding the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra. Others, however, maintain that the teacher alone performs the application of the mantra. Having caused him to place the fuel-stick, he establishes a stone firmly to the north of the fire with his right foot using the mantra: “Mount this... (MP 2.2.2). This mantra belongs to the teacher alone, because the boy is the object denoted. Thus, the teacher, having spoken the mantra, takes the boy’s right foot with both hands and causes it to be placed upon the stone. 10.9.

Having consecrated with the two following [verses] a garment freshly cut, and having caused him to put it on with the three following [verses], he consecrates the one who has put it on with the next [verse]. 10.10.

On the very same day, that whose weaving and sewing have been completed is called *sadyaḥkṛttotam*. Such a garment he should consecrate with the two subsequent *ṛg* verses beginning with “*revatīs tvā*” (MP 2.2.3). Then, he causes him to put it on with the three subsequent verses beginning with “*yā akṛntan*” (MP 2.2.5). These mantras belong to the teacher alone. Because of the specific statement “one [garment],” the putting on occurs at the end of the three verses. Then, the teacher consecrates the boy who has put it on with the subsequent verse, “*parīdaṃ vāsaḥ*” (MP 2.2.8). || 10.10 ||

Having girded him three times from left to right with a triple-stranded girdle of muñja grass using the next two [verses], he should place the deerskin over his left shoulder with the following [verse].

Then, with the two subsequent *ṛc*s, namely "This [girdle] from ill-spoken words" (*iyaṃ duruktāt*, MP 2.2.9), he thrice winds the girdle around the boy from left to right. Having himself uttered the mantra, the teacher causes him to recite it. Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, the girdle is threefold (*trivṛt*), made of *muñja* grass; that is, it consists of three strands. The long vowel in the reading "trivṛtām" is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) usage. Then, with the subsequent *ṛc*, "The eye of Mitra," he makes the deer-skin his upper garment; having himself uttered this mantra. Regarding the specific types of girdles distinguished by social class (*varṇa*), particular ones are prescribed in the *Sāmayācārika* rules. This statement, however, is intended to ensure that the *muñja* girdle is obtained for all classes. As for the specific types of deer-skins, those prescribed in the *Sāmayācārika* rules—such as "the black one for a Brāhmaṇa" (*kṛṣṇaṃ brāhmaṇasya*, ĀpDh 1.3.3)—are to be understood here as well. 10.11.

Having strewn darbha grass to the north of the fire, he places him upon it with the next [verse]. Having poured a handful of water into his joined palms, he sprinkles him three times with the next [verse]. Having taken hold of his right hand with the following [verses], having entrusted him to the deities with the next [verses], and having led him forward with the next *yajus*, he murmurs "Suprajāḥ" into his right ear. 10.12.
Thus ends the tenth section in the Gṛhyapraśna of Āpastamba.

Then the teacher, having strewn *darbha* grass to the north of the fire, makes the boy sit down upon it with the next [verse], “With the guest, we have come together” (*āgantrā samagan mahi*, MP 2.3.1). The teacher causes the boy to recite the mantra while he is seated. Having seated him, he himself stands behind him on the ground, fills his own joined palms (*añjali*) with water, and brings that handful of water toward the face of the boy who is seated on the *darbha* grass for the purpose of sprinkling; he pours it into the boy’s joined palms. Because of the use of the dative case in the word *asmai* (“to him”), this handful of water is for the sake of the boy. Thus, the boy becomes the agent of the sprinkling. Having brought the water, the teacher then performs the sprinkling with the next verse, “A wave from the ocean” (*samudrād ūrmiḥ*, MP 2.3.2). This is the boy’s mantra; the teacher causes him to recite it. (He sprinkles three times: once with the mantra and twice silently. He holds the water with his left hand and sprinkles with his right. One should understand that there is an elision of the causative suffix *ṇic* in the word *prokṣya*). Then he takes the boy’s hand with the ten subsequent mantras beginning with, “Agni has grasped your hand” (*agniṣṭe hastam agrabhīt*, MP 2.3.3). The taking of the hand is repeated with each mantra. Then, with the eleven subsequent mantras beginning with, “I entrust you to Agni” (*agnaye tvā paridadāmi*, MP 2.3.13), he entrusts him to the deities. In all instances where the word *asau* occurs, the boy’s name is to be inserted in the vocative case. Having entrusted him, the teacher initiates him (*upanayate*) with the subsequent *yajus*, “Of the god Savitṛ... (*devasya tvā savituḥ*, MP 2.3.24); the meaning is that he leads him into his own family for the purpose of practicing sacred knowledge (*vidyā*). His function there consists solely in the utterance of the *yajus*, nothing else. And the name is to be inserted in the vocative. Some hold that because the word *asau* is taught as having its final syllable accented, the teacher’s own name should be mentioned in the nominative case. Because of this connection, the entire rite is called the initiation (*upanayana*), just as the sacrifice of an animal is called *paśubandha*. Having initiated him, he mutters into the boy’s right ear the formula beginning with “May you be rich in offspring” (*suprajāḥ*) and ending with “rich in nourishment through nourishments” (*supoṣaḥ poṣaiḥ*). || 10.12 ||
Thus ends the tenth section in the Anākula commentary on the Gṛhyasūtra;
now begins the eleventh section.
“I have come to the holy life,” the youth said. || 11.1 ||
The mantra ends with "impelled by Savitṛ. The word "says" (āha) is for the purpose of indicating that it should be recited aloud. 11.1.
The reply of the prince to the question of the other. || 11.2 ||

The four mantras beginning with "What is your name? are for the purpose of answering questions. In this context, the action begins from where the question is asked; that is to say, it pertains to the ritual preceptor (*ācārya*). The form *praṣṭam* (instead of *praśnam*) lacks the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and is either a Vedic usage or a corruption. The response belongs to the youth (*kumāra*). In the case of the words beginning with "asau" (so-and-so), the youth indicates his name in the nominative case, while the preceptor uses the vocative case for the youth's name. Therein, the preceptor asks, "What is your name?"; the youth replies, "I am named Yajñaśarman. The preceptor asks, "Whose student (*brahmacārin*) are you, Śrī-Yajñaśarman?"; the youth replies, "I am the student of Prāṇa, Yajñaśarman. The word "āha" (he says) is supplied from the previous context and is used here in the loud register (*uccaiḥ*). || 11.2 ||
The other recites the remainder. || 11.3 ||
After the response to the question, the other teacher recites the remainder of the section, beginning with "This for you, O divine Sūrya. (11.3)
And he causes him to recite a benediction directed toward himself. || 11.4 ||
In that same remaining portion, he makes the boy recite the benediction directed inwardly, beginning with "O Lord of the paths, of the paths" (MP 2.3.32).
The portion ending with the *ājyabhāga* offerings has been explained. 11.5.
Having caused him to offer the subsequent oblations, he proceeds with the Jaya and following rites. || 11.6 ||

The ritual procedure (*tantra*) up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings has already been explained. Now, at this point, [the teacher] causes this boy to offer eleven principal oblations (*pradhānāhuti*) with the verses beginning with “yoge yoge” (MP 2.4.1). The boy offers with the subsequent mantras; the teacher employs him by making him recite the mantras. Regarding the second and fourth mantras as well, the boy alone is the speaker, because they are intended to name the deities. Another says: on account of the contradiction in the grammatical gender, the teacher is the speaker while the boy is the offerer (*hotṛ*). Because of the statement “having caused [him] to offer in the principal oblations,” the teacher alone is the performer in the subsidiary oblations (*upahoma*). 11.6.

Having performed the rites up to the final sprinkling, he places a bundle of grass (kūrca) with its tips pointing north behind the fire; upon it, the teacher makes the student sit down to his north with the following Yajus formula.

With the subsequent Yajus formula, "Thou art the sustainer of the kingdom," he does so by means of this one. The mention of the conclusion with the sprinkling of water is for the sake of indicating immediate sequence. Some perform the vow called Sāvitra at this time; others recite the Sāvitrī at the end of three nights. Both of these are undesirable to the Teacher. Because of the word "having placed," the Teacher alone is the agent of the placing, not the student. Although [the Teacher's agency] is established by the general context, the explicit statement "the initiator" (upanetā) is for the sake of what follows. In the rule "seated to the east, facing west," it is intended that he be to the east of the initiator (upanetṛ), not to the east of the fire. Likewise, in the rule "with his right hand [he takes] the right foot," it refers to the foot of the initiator, not the student's. 11.7.
Seated facing west in front [of the teacher], the boy, having grasped the teacher’s right foot with his right hand, says: "Sir, please recite the Sāvitrī to me. (11.8)

"He sits on *darbha* grass," according to another *Gṛhya* text. The mention of "with the right [hand]" is intended so that this alternative—namely, that both [hands] should be used for both [acts]—should not apply here. Consequently, the specific rule "he should clasp [the feet] including the ankles" comes into effect. 11.8.
Therefore he recites: "That [splendor] of Savitṛ... || 11.9 ||
Then [he recites] from the end, by hemistichs, and then the whole [verse]. || 11.10 ||

Because of the expression "after him" (*tasmāt*), there is a recitation for the purpose of assisting the boy. Therefore, in all three recitations, there is assistance provided to the boy. The prefix *anu* is intended to indicate assistance. One says "he recites after" (*anvāha*) because of this assistance. Consequently, if the boy is unable to speak at that time, he causes him to recite according to his capacity. Having first recited himself according to the rule—first by quarters (*pacchas*), with a pause at every foot; second by half-verses (*ardharcaśas*); and then the whole verse—he recites after him. Although one should have said "the next [verse]," the specific mention of "that [hymn] to Savitṛ" (*tat-savituḥ*) is so that, in the contexts concerning the Sāvitrī—such as "one should offer a thousand pieces of wood with the Sāvitrī" (ĀpDh 1.27.1)—only this [specific verse] may be understood. This is so that it does not apply to just any verse addressed to the god Savitṛ. Because of the word "then" (*tataḥ*), the recitation on this day consists of only this much. If, due to these statements, he is not grasped [at that time], the teaching occurs at another time. (11.9–10)
Now, he states a specific rule regarding that very recitation:
"The *vyāhṛtis* are to be inserted at the beginning or at the end of the quarters [of the verses]. (11.11)
Likewise, [he should recite] the last [verse] in the case of two half-verses, and the whole [hymn] in the case of a complete one. 11.12.

In this regard, there is a specific rule for the recitation (*anuvacana*): in the first recitation, the three *vyāhṛtis* should be uttered in sequence at the beginning or the end of the three quarters (*pādas*). In the second recitation, two *vyāhṛtis* should be uttered in sequence at the beginning or the end of the two half-verses (*ardharca*s). Thereafter, the last one remains, namely *suvar*. That last one should be recited in its entirety during the final recitation. The practical application (*prayoga*) therein is as follows: the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) must be uttered first, because of the scriptural statement: “The *oṃkāra* is the gate to heaven; therefore, one who is about to study the Veda... (*ĀpDh* 1.13.6). *Oṃ bhūḥ tat savitur vareṇyam.* *Oṃ bhuvaḥ bhargo devasya dhīmahi.* *Oṃ suvaḥ dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt.* *Oṃ bhūḥ tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi.* *Oṃ bhuvaḥ dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt.* *Oṃ suvaḥ tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt.* || 11.11–12 ||
With the subsequent mantra, the youth touches his upper lip. || 11.13 ||

Then, sitting right there, the youth touches his own upper lip with the northern mantra, "Vṛdham asau somya," and touches water. The word "upper" (uttaram) is used as a qualification because there are two lips. The inclusion of the word "mantra" is for the purpose of preventing the suspicion that the word "northern" (uttara) refers to a direction. In the mantra, by the word "asau" (so-and-so), the vital breath (prāṇa) is denoted, neither the teacher nor the student; therefore, no mention of a personal name should be made. 11.13.
With the following [mantra], the two ears. || 11.14 ||

With the subsequent mantra, "You two are the nooses of Brahmā" (MP 2.4.15), [he touches them]. The mantra is recited once; however, because of the dual number in the word "ears," the touching is performed sequentially. 11.14.
He takes up the staff with the subsequent [formula]. || 11.15 ||
With the following mantra, "O you of good fame, [bestow] good fame" (MP 2.5.1). || 11.15 ||
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa is made of Palāśa wood; that of a Rājanya is from the branch of a Nyagrodha tree and points downward; and that of a Vaiśya is made of Bādara or Udumbara wood. || 11.16 ||

Since this [rule] is already established by the specific injunctions for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, the mention of the Brāhmaṇa is intended so that this rule also becomes connected with his caste. Consequently, the option regarding the "staff made of wood" (ĀpDh 1.2.38) applies to the Brāhmaṇa as well; otherwise, it would apply only to the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, on the grounds that the injunction is connected with their respective castes. *Naiyyagrodha* is a derivative of *nyagrodha*. *Skandhaja* means grown from the trunk. *Avācīnāgra* means having its tip pointing downwards; the reading with the nasal *ṅ* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). *Bādara* is a derivative of *badarī*. Because the context concerns trees, *udumbara* refers to the tree, not copper. 11.16.
Some teachers instruct that the staff is made of wood, regardless of its specific color. 11.17.

*Vārkṣaḥ* means "made from a tree. According to another ritual manual (*kalpāntara*), it refers to "a tree fit for sacrifice. The previous rule was connected with specific social classes (*varṇa*), but this one is common to all and is not connected with any particular class. Furthermore, the rule regarding the staff (*daṇḍavidhi*) based on customary practice (*sāmayācārika*) is restated here for the sake of all schools (*caraṇa*), in order to ensure that the mantras apply to the staffs made of *nyagrodha* wood and others. Otherwise, the taking of the *pālāśa* staff alone would be accompanied by the mantra, while the others would be taken silently, because the mantra "O you of good fame" (*suśravaḥ*, MP 2.5.1) is a designation specifically for the *pālāśa*. The statement "The gods indeed spoke of the Brahman; the leaf (*parṇa*) heard it; its name is 'Suśravas'" (TS 3.5.7)—whereby the fact that the staff is made of wood (*vārkṣaḥ*) is established by this much alone—the inclusion of the phrase "not connected with a [specific] class" (*avarṇasaṃyogena*) is intended to show the non-confusion of the two ritual manuals (*kalpāntara*). That is to say, if a ritual manual connected with a specific class has been commenced, that very manual must be followed until the student's return home (*asamāvartana*). 11.17.

Having caused him to recite "And I have remembered," and having given a gift to the teacher, he raises him up with the words "O long-lived one! and worships the sun with the following verses. || 11.18 ||

Then, having taken up the staff and remaining seated right there, the boy recites this proclamation of his vow, "And I remember" (MP 2.5.2). Thereafter, he gives a gift to the teacher. Then he should rise with the mantra "O long-lived one" (udāyuṣā). With the subsequent mantras beginning with "That eye" (MP 2.5.12) and ending with "To see the sun" (MP 2.5.21), he worships the sun. The boy alone is the performer of these four ritual acts, beginning with the proclamation of the vow. However, the statement of the reason—"having made him recite" and "having made him rise"—is not intended to be significant in either case; for if that were intended, the teacher alone would be the performer of the giving of the gift and the worship. Therefore, this is a restatement of the operation of the reason which is already established by the sense of the matter. 11.18.
Now he states the optional rite: "If one should desire, 'May this man not be separated from me,' he should take him by the right hand with the following verse. (11.19)

If the teacher should desire to bring about some specific result for the initiate, asking "What? [the answer is]: "May he not be severed from me, may he not be separated from me, but remain entirely dependent on me until his formal return" (*samāvartana*). At that time, he should seize him by the right hand with the following verse, "In whom [is] the past... (*yasmin bhūtam*, MP 2.5.22). The mention of the name should be in the vocative case. This rule is optional (*kāmya*), not obligatory (*nitya*). This itself is the indicator that one need not remain in the presence of the teacher alone until the formal return. 11.19.
They maintain this fire for three days. || 11.20 ||
The father and others maintain this fire of initiation for three days, ensuring that it does not go out. || 11.20 ||
And there shall be the avoidance of alkaline salts and salt. 11.21.

The avoidance of alkaline substances and salt occurs for three days regarding food. For this student (brahmacārin), the prohibition based on conventional practice (sāmayācārika) is lifelong; however, this [present rule] is connected to a period of three days. There is an option between those two. But the prohibition concerning honey and so forth, being based on conventional practice, remains obligatory at all times. 11.21.
Having wiped [the fire] around it with the words "pari tvā," he should place fuel-sticks into it with the subsequent mantras. || 11.22 ||

Having wiped that *upanayana* fire all around with the mantra “*pari tvā*” (MP 2.6.1), and having performed a sprinkling of water on all sides, the religious student (*brahmacārī*) should daily place fuel-sticks (*samidh*) upon it, one by one, with each of the twelve subsequent mantras beginning with “*agnaye samidham*” (MP 2.6.2). The specific rule “in the evening and in the morning” (ĀpDh 1.4.16) is to be understood as pertaining to the conventional conduct (*sāmayācārika*). And there is also the statement: “Some say the worship of the fire is only in the evening” (ĀpDh 1.4.17). However, this instruction is for the purpose of initiating [the practice] at this time. Therefore, according to one view, the commencement of the fuel-stick offering is in the morning and its conclusion in the evening; according to the other view, the commencement is in the evening itself, and not at any other time. In that regard, one may proceed as one wishes at the start. Although that [fire] is already established by the context, the explicit mention of “upon that” is so that the placing of fuel-sticks may take place on that very *upanayana* fire even after three days have passed. By this, its constant maintenance is also established as an alternative. At the end, he places four fuel-sticks with the *vyāhṛtis*; this should be regarded as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), as seen in other ritual manuals (*kalpa*). The worship with the mantras beginning “*yat te agne tejaḥ*” is performed according to custom, as is the scattering of ashes. 11.22.

Having thus described the worship of the fire, including the ritual for placing the fuel-sticks along with its procedures, [the author] now states another quality related to the qualification for that very same [rite], and says:
"The same applies to other [rites] as well. (11.23)
Having brought fuel from the forest, [he should offer it]. 11.24.

Just as the taking of fuel is enjoined as a constant duty for this *upanayana* fire when it is to be maintained perpetually, so too, in the case of maintaining it for three days, the meaning is that after those three days, this ritual act must be performed even in another fire. By the mention of "wild" (*araṇya*), there is a prohibition against using fruit-bearing trees of the village. By the word "having brought" (*āhṛtya*), there is a prohibition against using wood brought by others. "Fuel" (*edhāḥ*) means pieces of wood. The inclusion of the term "fuel" is intended to prevent the suspicion that the fire itself is being brought. In the rules of customary conduct (*sāmayācārika*), the injunction prescribes that the student fetch fuel for the sake of his teacher; this [present rule], however, is for his own sake. (11.23–24)
He instructs with the following verse. 11.25.

Then, with the following verse, "O student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*), thou art" (MP 2.6.14), the teacher instructs him; the meaning is that he teaches him. According to the recitation, he instructs him by means of the verse and explains its meaning: "Thou art a *brahmacārin*; thou hast entered the stage of the *brahmacarya* life. Therefore, do not act, speak, or eat according to thy own will. [The student replies: "So be it. "Drink water, unless permitted by me."

"Drink water only, and nothing else. In every case, the response is as before. "Wear armor"—this refers to service to the teacher and the like. "Do not sleep"—this is a prohibition against sleeping during the day. Āśvalāyana says: "Do not sleep during the day" (ĀśGṛ 1.22.2). Another says: "Now, they say that he who rises early and goes to bed late does not sleep at all"; such is the absence of sleep intended here. "Go on the alms-round"—this is the rule for begging according to the prescribed discipline. "Be dependent upon the teacher"—the meaning is that you must remain under the authority of the teacher, having relinquished even the control of your mother and father. The practice of begging for alms follows immediately after the instruction. On this point, Bodhāyana says: "Then, handing him an unfilled bowl, he says: 'Beg from your mother first'" (BauGṛ 2.7). Āśvalāyana, however, says: "He should beg first from one who will not refuse, or from a woman who will not refuse" (ĀśGṛ 1.22.7). || 11.25 ||
On the fourth day, he takes up a garment with the following verse; having caused him to put on another, [he performs the rite]. 11.26.
Thus ends the eleventh section of the *Gṛhyapraśna* of Āpastamba;
the fourth chapter is completed.

Now, when the three nights have passed, on the fourth night—the accusative case being used in the sense of the locative—the meaning is "on the fourth [day]. What happens there? The teacher takes away that garment which was worn by the boy, which was newly cut and woven, and put on him, with the following verse: "O you whose first garment... (MP 2.6.14). Having caused him to put on another garment—though during those three days it must necessarily be one that is newly cut and woven—the word "fourth" here does not intend to refer merely to a night. What then? It refers to a complete period of day and night. In that regard, the taking away of the garment occurs during the day, because of the rule: "The day of the northern solstice and the bright fortnight" (ĀpGṛ 1.2).

Having cast away into the water a girdle, a deerskin, a staff, a sacrificial thread, and a water-pot that have become worn out, he should take up others while reciting the appropriate mantras. (11.26)
Thus ends the eleventh section (khaṇḍa) in the Anākulā commentary on the Gṛhyasūtra;
this is the fourth chapter (paṭala). [The following chapter does not have a section number; it is not included in Winternitz’s edition.]
Now begins the chapter on the commencement and conclusion [of Vedic study].
Now, therefore, we shall explain the commencement and conclusion.

The word *atha* at the beginning is for the sake of auspiciousness, as it marks the commencement of a new treatise. The two words *ataḥ* [in the compound *athātaḥ*] signify a reason. Since it is impossible to employ these two terms without providing an explanation of them, we shall therefore explain them. || 1 ||
When the herbs have grown during the fortnight of Śravaṇā, on the full moon day of the month of Hasta, the commencement of Vedic study (upākarma) shall take place.

"In the fortnight of Śravaṇa" means in the first (waxing) fortnight of the month of Śravaṇa. "When the herbs have grown" means when they have sprouted due to the rains; the meaning is that the commencement of the term (*adhyāyopākaraṇa*)—that is, the beginning of the ritual for opening the term (*adhyāyopākarma*)—should be performed on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa under the asterism Hasta. Because of the expression "when the herbs have grown," [the rite] takes place on the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada if the herbs have not yet grown. And so there is another ritual manual (*kalpa*): "On the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, or of Prauṣṭhapada, or of Āṣāḍha. ||2||

From the kindling of the fire until the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, while the [disciples] maintain contact [with him], he offers oblations to the *kāṇḍa*-ṛṣis: having offered to Sadasaspati, to Savitṛ, to the Ṛgveda, to the Yajurveda, to the Sāmaveda, and to the Atharvaṇaveda, he performs the secondary offerings (*upahoma*) after the Veda-oblations; according to some, [he offers] with the verse beginning "sadasaspatim."

Thus the time for the *upākaraṇa* has been stated. Now follows the ritual procedure (*prayoga*). One undertakes the ritual framework (*tantra*) beginning with the kindling of the fire. The fire is to be brought from the house of a *śrotriya* or produced by friction (*manthya*), but not the domestic fire (*aupāsana*), because here there is no co-presence of multiple fires. Furthermore, because there is no co-presence of the wife, the specific mention [of the fire] is made here in the procedure. This rite, connected with the Veda, is for the purpose of refining one's knowledge. There, at the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, while the students hold on to him, he offers the principal oblations. The five *kāṇḍa*-seers are Prajāpati, Soma, Agni, Viśvadevas, and Brahmā Svayaṃbhū. Among these, the oblation is offered with "To Prajāpati, svāhā. Others say: "To Prajāpati, the *kāṇḍa*-seer, svāhā. With the verse "The wonderful Lord of the Assembly" (*sadasaspatim adbhutam*, MP 1.9.8), he offers to Sadasaspati. With the verse "That of Savitṛ" (*tat savituḥ*), he offers to Sāvitrī, as that is seen in another *kalpa*. Then there are four oblations for the Vedas: "To the Ṛgveda," "To the Yajurveda," "To the Sāmaveda," and "To the Atharvaṇaveda. After that come the subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*). The meaning is that one proceeds with the *jaya* and subsequent rites. Some teachers maintain that Sadasaspati should be offered to after the oblations to the Vedas.
Having performed everything up to the final sprinkling, they should recite the first three sections (anuvākas).

Having completed the remainder of the *tantra*, they should study the first three *anuvākas* of the Veda: “*iṣe tvorje tvā*,” “*āpa undantu*,” (MP 2.1.2), and “*uddhanyānam*. [Then: “For Anumati, he offers a cake on eight potsherds; a cow is the sacrificial fee. These are the first four *anuvākas* of the sections dedicated to Prajāpati, Soma, Agni, and the Viśvedevas. [The fifth is] “*Saha vai devānāṃ cāsurāṇāṃ ca*,” which belongs to Svayambhū. This is the study of these five *anuvākas*. 4.
Or rather, it is the first and the last recitations (anuvākas).
Or alternatively, they may recite the first and last sections of the Veda: "For food, thee! and "Bhṛgu, indeed, was the son of Varuṇa. || 5 ||
They may study after having waited for three days or one day.

Starting from the day on which the *upākaraṇa* (commencement) has been performed, they should study after having waited for three days or one day. The meaning is that there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) for three days or one day once the commencement has taken place. In that regard, there is one day’s suspension for the commencement of a *kāṇḍa*, and three days for the commencement of the *pārāyaṇa*. The statement "they should study" is intended so that study may proceed as a rule after the three days have passed following the commencement.
The lesson follows the introductory rite. || 7 ||

The study should be conducted in the same manner as the formal commencement (*upākaraṇa*) was performed. If, after making offerings to all the *kāṇḍa*-ṛṣis, the commencement of the first three sections at the beginning of the Veda—or of the first and last sections—has been made, then the study should be carried out according to the chapters (*adhyāya*). However, if the commencement of all the *kāṇḍa* sections has been made, then it should be studied according to the *kāṇḍas*. For one who is unable to study the entire Veda in the forest—excluding the *anuvākyās*—prior to the ritual of suspension (*utsarjana*), there is a separate commencement for each *kāṇḍa*. In that case, for that specific *kāṇḍa*, there is only one ṛṣi; Sadasaspati is the deity; the *Sāvitrī* and the oblations to the Vedas are the secondary offerings (*upahoma*); at the end of the *pariṣecana*, there is a day of non-study (*anadhyāya*) for one section of that same *kāṇḍa*; and the study consists of that very *kāṇḍa*. (7)
The ritual of release (utsarga) takes place under the asterism Rohiṇī in the month of Taiṣa, or on the full moon day.

Having thus performed the opening ceremony (*upākaraṇa*), except during periods when study is forbidden, one who is reciting the Veda or a section (*kāṇḍa*) in the forest—omitting the *anuvākyā* verses—should perform the formal conclusion (*utsarga*). This may be done on the full moon day of the month of Taiṣya, or indeed at any time during that fortnight. In this rite, there is also an oblation (*homa*). How is it performed? It is performed like the opening ceremony, because the procedure is identical; having offered the oblation in the house just as at the opening, one proceeds with the rite while seeking forgiveness. However, according to the followers of Hiraṇyakeśin, the oblation takes place at the edge of the water after the libation (*tarpaṇa*). || 8 ||

Having gone out toward the eastern or northern direction together with his retinue, and having reached the edge of waters that are pleasant, easy to enter, shallow, and abounding in shells, he performs ablutions; then, having purified himself with the *surabhimatī*, *ābliṅga*, *vāruṇī*, *hiraṇyavarṇā*, and *pāvamānī* verses, he enters the water and performs three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting the *aghamarṣaṇa*. Having emerged, sipped water, and stood up, they hand darbha grass to one another and prepare their seats upon pure ground with darbha grass blades pointing eastward. || 9 ||

"Accompanied by his retinue and disciples, where there is water in front"—that is to say, in whatever place one sees water in the eastern direction; "pleasant," meaning pleasant to the touch; "easy to enter," with good landing places; those in which there are *avaka* plants are called *avakinyaḥ*, and likewise those with *śaṅkha* plants; having gone near their edge (*anta*), having performed ablutions (*abhiṣeka*) with jars, then with the *surabhimatī* verse, "O Dadhikrāvan... (*RV* 4.39.6), with the *ābliṅga* verses beginning with "O Waters, you are the source of happiness" (*RV* 10.9.1–3), with the three *vāruṇī* verses beginning with "Take away our sin" (*RV* 1.24.14), "Release us from every bond" (*RV* 1.24.15), and "Do thou, O Varuṇa, let go of us" (*RV* 1.24.11), with the four *hiraṇyavarṇīya* verses beginning with "Golden-colored, pure, and purifying" (*RV* 9.1.6–9), and with the *pāvamānī* verses beginning with "Pavamāna, who dwells in light" (*RV* 9.67.21–22)—having purified himself with these, and having sprinkled himself, there is a repetition of the action for each mantra, or according to others, for each quarter-verse (*pratipāda*). Then, having entered within the water, submerged in the water, he performs three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *aghamarṣaṇa* triplet seen by Aghamarṣaṇa, beginning with "Righteousness and Truth" (*RV* 10.190.1). In all cases, he remains accompanied by his retinue. Having immersed himself in the water, he mutters this section (*anuvāka*) once; that constitutes one breath-restraint. Having thus performed them three times, having emerged, and having put on unwashed, unsoiled garments after washing his feet—according to the observation of other *Gṛhya* texts—and having sipped water and stood up, two of them together hand darbha grass to one another. Then, in a clean place at the very edge of the water, having prepared separate altars (*sthaṇḍila*), they arrange seats with darbha grass pointing eastward. || 9 ||
To whom? To the gods, the ancestors, and the seers;

to Brahmā, Prajāpati, Bṛhaspati, Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, Candramas, the constellations, the seasons, the year, Indra the king, Soma the king, Yama the king, Vaiśravaṇa the king, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, the Maruts, the Ṛbhus, the Bhṛgus, and the Aṅgirases—thus for the hosts of gods. (10)

"Devagaṇa" means both the gods and their hosts. Here, the ten deities beginning with Brahmā; the five kings beginning with Indra; and the ten divine hosts beginning with the Vasus [are intended]. Because of the statement "they arrange them at the very end," the phrase "I arrange" (*kalpayāmi*) is to be connected everywhere. Thus: "I arrange for Brahmā, I arrange for Prajāpati," and so forth. These twenty-five seats are arranged with their ends toward the north. And their libation (*tarpaṇa*) is performed with the *daiva* (divine) *tīrtha*. 10.

Then the ṛṣis—Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, Gautama, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Kaśyapa; these are the seven ṛṣis. Having made the offering for the seven ṛṣis, they make the offering to Agastya from the south.
To the north of the gods are the seats of the Seven Sages; to the south is that of Agastya; and above Kaśyapa is that of Arundhatī, according to the observation of other Gṛhya texts. 12.11.
Then they arrange them as far as those with a single tooth. || 12 ||

Immediately after that, they assign [the portions] to as many as there are who share the same *vedyanta* (end of the Veda) with the Seven Seers (*saptarṣi*). Who, then, are these? They are the seers beginning with Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana. This is what is meant: [to] Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, Jātūkarṇya, Tarukṣa, Tṛṇībindu, Somaśuṣmin, Somaśuṣka, Varmin, Sanadvāja, Bṛhaduktha, Vāmadeva, Vācaratna, Haritayajvan, Udamegha, Gautama, Ṛṇañjaya, Kṛtñjaya, Babhru, Tryaruṇa, Tridhātu, Trivarṣa, Śibindu, Parāśara, Vasiṣṭha, Indra, Mṛtyu, Karta, Tvaṣṭṛ, Dhātṛ, Savitṛ, Bhṛtaśravas, Sāvitrī, and the Vedas—each separately. These thirty-four seers beginning with Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, together with the four Vedas, constitute the thirty-eight who share the same *vedyanta* as the Seven Seers. Some, however, maintain that the Atharvāṅgirasas, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, all the divine beings, and all living creatures are also included by the mention of the "Vedas," because such is seen in another ritual manual (*kalpa*). 12.

Having arranged their sacred threads over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), [he says]: "I offer to Vaiśampāyana, to Paiṅgi, to Tittiri, to Ukha, to Ātreya, to Padakāra, to Kauṇḍinya, to Vṛttikāra, to Baudhāyana the author of the *Pravacana*, to Āpastamba the author of the *Sūtra*, to Bharadvāja the author of the *Sūtra*, to Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin, to the teachers, to those who have sublimated their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*), to those whose husbands are living (*ekapatnī*), and to the forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*). || 13 ||

Then, having all arranged their sacred threads over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), they prepared seats for the twelve beginning with Vaiśampāyana to the south of the gods and of Agastya. In that regard, there is another ritual rule stating that on ground sloping toward the south, the seats should have their tips pointing southward and be completed toward the west.
Then they arrange the offerings for their respective ancestors and for their maternal grandfathers separately.

The meaning is that they prepare [the offerings] for all those on both sides, each according to their own respective ancestors—namely, the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, as well as the maternal grandfather and the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather of the mother. The instructions "having arranged the sacred thread over the right shoulder" (*prācīnāvītāni kṛtvā*) and "to the south" (*dakṣiṇataḥ*) continue to apply here. In that regard, the preparation is performed by uttering the names of the ancestors and so forth, each according to their own [lineage], such as "for Rudraśarman," "for Viṣṇuśarman. Others, however, prepare the offering simply by saying "to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ*). Why, then, is it specified "each according to their own"? It is for the purpose of making known a specific procedure even in this case for those whose fathers are still living, just as there is a specific procedure regarding the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*). || 14 ||

Having placed the sacrificial threads over their left shoulders, they satisfy the gods and the sages in those very places and in that same sequence, using those very names; however, wearing the threads over their right shoulders (prācīnāvītin), they satisfy those beginning with Vaiśampāyana down to their maternal great-grandfather, saying: "I satisfy so-and-so; I satisfy so-and-so; I satisfy so-and-so. || 15 ||

Now, a distinction is observed in another ritual manual: "Homage to such-and-such, homage to such-and-such" with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps; "Svāhā to such-and-such, svāhā to such-and-such" with food; and "I satiate such-and-such, I satiate such-and-such" with fruits and water.
Or they are mutually moistened. || 16 ||

They obtain this form. *Abhiṣyā* means longing. Here, in the rite of *utsarjana*, the simultaneous engagement of the disciples and the teacher in acts such as bathing and so forth is enjoined, because the plural number is used throughout—[as in the phrase] "having performed the consecrations (*abhiṣeka*), they prepare the seats. In that regard, this optional distinction is taught: either they long for one another, or two by two, having come together, they long for one another for the sake of proceeding with the rite, rather than all together. In the reading *adhīṣanta*, this is the form of the root *ṛdh*. And due to the influence of the prefix, the meaning remains the same. However, for those who read only the letter *t* after the word *adhi* and not even the letter *r*, their verbal root has the sense of "to prosper" (*mṛgī-artha*). || 16 ||
Having performed the preliminary rites of the sacrifice, they should study the first three sections (anuvākas). || 17 ||
The method of study has been explained by [the description of] the opening ceremony (upākaraṇa). || 17 ||
The first and last [verses] of each section (kāṇḍa) may optionally [be recited].
This conceptual construction has also been explained in the section on the requisites. || 18 ||
With the two verses beginning, “From joint to joint they sprout,” they plant *dūrvā* grass in a place near water. || 19 ||

Then, having brought a clump of *dūrvā* grass together with its roots, he plants it near water. They bury it so that the *dūrvā* may sprout, using the two verses beginning with "From joint to joint they sprout. Since the word *dūrvā* is heard in the singular there, only one person—the principal officiant—buries it, while the others hold on to him from behind; others, however, maintain that this should be done for each individual person.
Having plunged into the waters, they make the ocean their place of immersion. || 20 ||
Then, having entered the waters, they turn them into an ocean; the meaning is that they agitate it like the great ocean (udadhi).
To the question "How is that so?", he says:
"Surrounding it on all sides, they create a wave within. (21)
The meaning is that, having surrounded him on all sides and hemmed him in with many [waves], they act so that waves arise there; thus they do it three times. 12.21.
Having been lifted up, they run the race until they have reached the end. || 22 ||

Having emerged and crossed [the water] until they are exhausted, they run a race starting from the hermitage. They run toward either the eastern or the northern direction; such is the completion [of the rite]. 22.
Having returned and offered the [gifts] such as the flour-meal and the cooked rice, he feeds the Brāhmaṇas and causes them to pronounce blessings. || 23 ||

"Having returned" means having entered the house; "blessings" refers to the *puṇyāha* and others, meaning having caused [the guests] to recite, "May it be a meritorious day! May there be well-being! May there be success! || 23 ||
Likewise, at the conclusion of the *pārāyaṇa*, the rites beginning with the *kāṇḍa* [of the Veda] are performed, excluding the planting of *dūrvā* grass and the running with curds.

Just as the ritual of *utsarga* (the formal conclusion) is enjoined upon the completion of this rainy-season term (*vārṣika*), so too must it be performed upon the completion of the *pārāyaṇa* (the complete recitation). In that regard, the following are to be avoided: the study of the beginnings of the *kāṇḍas*, the planting of *dūrvā* grass, the performance of water-libations (*udadhi-karaṇa*), and the running of a race (*ājidhāvana*). || 24 ||
Having returned, he undertakes the ritual acts such as feeding the Brahmins. || 25 ||

Some maintain that because of the mention of "sections" (*kāṇḍa*) and so forth, during the study of the *pārāyaṇa* the recitation must follow the sequence of the sections exactly, and not a conflated reading. Others, however, say that since the mention of "sections" and so forth is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), there is a prohibition against studying the *anuvākas* in any form whatsoever; furthermore, they state that in the *pārāyaṇa*, the recitation may be according to one's preference. 25.
In this very manner, one should daily satiate the gods, the seers, and the ancestors with water.

Because of the statement "with waters," the daily libation (tarpaṇa) is performed with water alone. Consequently, in the rite of renunciation (utsarga), there is also the application of the previously mentioned items such as perfumes (gandha) and so forth. The daily libation occurs after the knowledge of Brahman, as seen in another Kalpa. || 26 ||
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, the section on the commencement and conclusion of Vedic study (*upākarma-utsarjana*), in the *Anakulā* commentary on the *Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the fifth chapter.

Now begins the twelfth section. In the preceding [section], the initiation (*upanayana*) has been explained. For one who has been initiated, the duties (*dharma*) have been taught in the *Dharmaśāstra*, beginning with the words, "Now follows the rule for studentship" (*atha brahmacaryavidhiḥ*; ĀpDh 1.2.18). Furthermore, the rule for the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) and conclusion (*samāpana*) of the *adhyāya-kāṇḍa* vows has been fully explained in the passage: "In the commencement and the conclusion, whichever seer (*ṛṣi*) is known [to be the author]" (ĀpGṛ 8.10). Now, therefore: "Having mastered the Veda, or the vows, or indeed both... (YDh 1.51)

Having explained the rite known as *snāna*—also called *samāvartana*—which is to be performed by one who has completed his duties through the practice of the meaning of such injunctions and has returned from the teacher’s house, some [authorities] state that since these two [rites] are not well-known in this ritual manual (*kalpa*) according to the rule “at the commencement and at the conclusion” (*upākaraṇe samāpane ca*, ĀpGṛ 8.1), one must necessarily rely on what is well-known elsewhere; thus, they explain the section on vows (*vratapaṭala*) beginning with “Now, therefore, we shall explain the commencement and the conclusion” (*athāta upākaraṇotsarjane vyākhyāsyāmaḥ*), immediately after the initiation (*upanayana*).

This is not so, because the commentator has already fully explained these two injunctions in the very passage, "At the commencement and at the completion" (ĀpGṛ 8.1), and because the study of the Vrata-paṭala is subject to dispute, and because there is no occasion for such a discussion in the Bhāṣya.

Having studied the Veda and being about to perform the ceremonial bath (snāna), he should enter the cow-pen before sunrise, remain there behind a curtain made of a hide with the hair side inward, and wait. 12.1.

When one who has been thus initiated, having lived the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*), studied the Vedas along with their six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and desires to seek another stage of life (*āśrama*) than that of the teacher’s family, for him the rite called "bathing" (*snāna*) is prescribed. That rite in which a distinguished bath is performed according to rule is termed "the bath"; the meaning is that he shall perform that "bath," which is the "return home" (*samāvartana*). The phrase "before the rising of the sun" implies sunrise is intended, as seen in the passage: "The sun does not rise over this man on this day. "Vraja" means a cow-pen. "With a hide whose hair is inside" means with the hide of any wild animal with its fur turned inward. The mention of "seating" is for the purpose of prohibiting departure. The singular number in "the Veda" (*veda*) is not intended to be restrictive; the meaning is: having studied one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas, both in terms of recitation and in terms of understanding the meaning. The statement "intending to bathe" is so that the subsequent duties of a lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) do not apply. 12.1.
On this day, the sun shall not scorch him. 12.2.

While he is performing this rite on this day—on this very day—the sun shall never heat him. Therefore, even urine, excrement, and so forth, should be discharged right there in the cow-pen, even in the shade. Because of the specific mention of the "sun," there is no prohibition against the heat of fire. 12.2.

At midday, from the kindling of the fire until the end of the *yājyābhāga* offerings, having placed a fuel-stick of *palāśa* wood with the following [verse], he sits down to the west of the fire on a mat of *kaṭa* grass or *erakā* grass; having consecrated the razor with the following [verse] and handed it to the barber with the following *yajus*, the procedure is the same from the mixing of the waters until the disposal of the hair. 12.3.

Then, on that day at midday, the ritual action is commenced, beginning with the kindling of the fire. [He offers] *śamyā*-sticks. He prepares the vessels once, together with the razor and other implements. The performer himself acts; the teacher does not. The mention of the conclusion at the *ājyabhāga* offerings is for the purpose of indicating the time for the subsequent rites, beginning with the placing of the fuel-sticks (*samid*). Even though the general procedure (*tantra*) is already established by this very rule, the specific mention of "kindling the fire" and so forth serves to restrict the commencement of the *tantra* itself to midday, rather than the entire ritual action. With the following verse, "This hymn... (MP 2.7.1), he performs the offering. There is no utterance of *svāhā*, because there is no injunction to use the root *hu* (to sacrifice). A *kaṭa* is well known; *erakā* is the grass that serves as its material. Others say it is *kaśipu*. With the following verse, "The threefold life-span... (MP 2.7.2), having consecrated the razor, he addresses it with the following *yajus*: "Auspicious by name you are... (MP 2.7.3). The shaver is the barber, not the teacher. Having handed the razor to him, then the ritual actions beginning with "Bring warm water into the cold... and ending with the depositing of the hair are the same as those in the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). What is the meaning? The word *kārayati* ("he causes to do") is supplied. By whom does he cause it to be done? By the teacher. Although he has returned from the teacher's house, nevertheless the teacher comes together at the time of the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) and at the time of marriage, by the force of the common expression, and because of the observation in the rule: "Whomever he honors, him [the teacher] does otherwise" (ĀpGṛ 3.9). This is also clear in the *Āśvalāyana-gṛhya-sūtra*: "Now, one returning [from study] prepares these things... (ĀśGṛ 3.7.1), etc. Others, however, desire the return to take place right at the teacher's house. There, the teacher, having performed the mixing of the waters and the kindling of the fire, takes the razor from the barber, distributes it in each direction, gives it back to him, and while he is shaving, the teacher consecrates him with the following verse. Thus ends the ritual action of the teacher. 12.3.
Having sat down on the ground at the rear half of the cow-pen and loosened her girdle, she gives it to a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin). || 12.4 ||

Then, having had his hair, beard, and nails clipped, he sits down on the hindquarters or the rear half of a cow-pen; having loosened and untied his girdle, he gives it to some student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*). 12.4.
With the following Yajus formula, he hides it at the root of an Udumbara tree or in a clump of Darbha grass. || 12.5 ||

He covers [the head] with the subsequent *yajus* formula, beginning with “Here I conceal the evil of such-and-such...,” (MP 2.7.12). In this context, the name is to be inserted in place of the word *adaḥ*: “Here I conceal the evil of Yajñaśarman Gārgya; may Yajñaśarman be superior to his enemies. Or, if the name should be Yajñaśarman Gārgyāyaṇa, [it should be used accordingly]. At this time, there is also the renunciation of the staff and the deerskin. 12.5.
Having bathed with these six subsequent waters prepared in this manner, he cleanses his teeth with a stick made of udumbara wood using the next [verse].

"Prepared in this manner" means as before, mixed together—that is, with both cold and warm water. In that mixing, there is an omission of the mantra; [the mixing is done] with the *ṛc*s beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and those beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ. Among these, the inclusion of the verse "yāsu jātaḥ" is intended. And the sprinkling is performed with each mantra individually. He cleans his teeth, removing the impurity from the teeth, with the following verse: "Spread yourselves out for the sake of food" (MP 2.7.19). || 12.6 ||
