Having bathed, he was anointed with bathing unguents. || 12.7 ||

Having put on an inner garment with the next *yajus* verse, having offered *sarvasurabhi* sandalwood paste to the deities with the following verses, and having anointed himself with it using the next verse, he should—using the next verse—three times circulate clockwise a golden amulet together with its case and tied with a cord over a vessel of water; then, having fastened it around his neck with the next verse, he should likewise fasten a jujube-wood amulet on his left hand, omitting the mantra, and put on a new upper garment with the verse, "O wealthy ones, [protect] you," which is the same as before. 12.8.

Then, having been rubbed with bathing substances suitable for bathing, such as *klītaka* and others, so that his impurities are removed, he bathes again with those same waters while reciting the subsequent *yajus*: "Thou art the body of Soma" (*MP* 2.7.20). He puts on two garments: the inner one (*antaram*) is that by which the waist is covered; the upper one (*uttaram*) is that by which the outer fold (*nīvi*) or the sacred thread (*upavīta*) is formed. Having put on the inner garment, he applies anointment with sandalwood paste. Of what kind? With "all-fragrant" (*sarvasurabhiṇā*), meaning that which contains all fragrant substances. [Note: If the reading is *sārvasurabhiṇā*, the grammatical derivation must be sought elsewhere. Therein, first he offers [the anointment] to the deities with the three subsequent mantras beginning with "Homage to Graha" (*MP* 2.7.21). Then he anoints himself with the subsequent verse: "The fragrance which is among the Apsarases" (*MP* 2.7.24). Āśvalāyana says: "A Brāhmaṇa should anoint the face first, a Kṣatriya the arms, and a Vaiśya the belly" (*ĀśGṛ* 3.7.10–12). Then he fastens a gem; he puts it on his neck. That gem is made of gold and set with lapis lazuli and other stones. It is "strung on a thread" (*sūtrotaḥ*), meaning it is threaded through with a cord; this is the sense of "with its loop. He causes that gem to float three times in a water-vessel with the subsequent verse: "This, O herb... (*MP* 2.7.25). The mantra is recited only once. Then he fastens it on his neck with the subsequent verse: "Free from the noose art thou, O hero... (*MP* 2.7.26). This word *grīvā* denotes the veins (*dhamani*); being plural, it is used here for the throat because of its connection with them. In this *ṛc*, the Earth is praised; therefore, this herb must be "Trāyamāṇā" (the Protector). The elision of the *sakāra* is Vedic. Then, having caused a bead made of jujube seeds (*bādara*)—strung on a thread—to float three times clockwise in the water-vessel, he fastens it on his left hand. There is a prohibition of mantras for both the floating and the fastening; they are done silently. Because of the repetition of the word "gem," there is no setting [of this bead] into a vessel. But it is strung on a thread. Having fastened the gem, he then puts on the upper garment, which is indeed new. In that regard, the ritual procedure beginning with "O wealthy ones... (*revatīs tvā*) should be understood as identical to that of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). Although the result would have been established simply by saying "with these [verses]" or "with the subsequent [verses]," the statement "identical" is for the purpose of indicating the application is like that of the initiation. Therefore, the teacher's duty begins with the consecration by the two subsequent verses and ends with the consecration of the garment already worn. 12.8.

Having tied two blades of grass from its stalks, placed them in a ladle, and poured clarified butter over them while reciting the subsequent oblations, he offers the *uttarā āhutayaḥ* and proceeds with the *jaya* and following rites. || 12.9 ||

Having fastened two golden ear-ornaments (*pravarta*) onto the fringe of that upper garment and placed them upon a ladle, he offers the eight principal oblations (*pradhānāhuti*) with clarified butter (*ājya*), while causing [the ornaments] to be moved back and forth over them—meaning, having caused the clarified butter to be poured over the two *pravarta* ornaments. Or rather, the reading may be *abhyānayan*; in this case, the moving back and forth is performed with the left hand. The form *abhyānāyam* is appropriate as a gerund (*ṇamul*). The meaning is: "having moved them back and forth" (*abyānīya-abhyānīya*). In any case, the principal oblation is performed with the clarified butter sprinkled over the two *pravarta* ornaments. The mention of the *jaya* and subsequent formulas is for the purpose of removing the two *pravarta* ornaments and returning to the ordinary course of action as established. (12.9)
Having performed the rites up to the final sprinkling, he should fasten [the amulet] upon the right ear with these same verses, and upon the left ear with these same verses.

The statement ending with "the sprinkling" (*pariṣecana*) is for the purpose of indicating immediacy (*ānantarya*). By that, there is no eating on this day. The meaning is: "with these very oblations," that is, with the mantras intended for the oblations. Because of the specific wording, a single ritual act (*karman*) may employ many mantras, and the mantra must be used together with the *svāhā* exclamation. If it were merely said "and with the left hand," there would be a separate application (*viniyoga*) of the mantras; therefore, it is stated again, "with these. (12.10)

In the same way, with the subsequent [mantras], he should place a garland on the head according to its specific mark, as well as collyrium, the looking into a mirror, sandals, an umbrella, and a staff. || 12.11 ||

In this manner, with the subsequent mantras as well, one should apply the six substances—garlands and so forth—to the appropriate parts according to their indicative marks (*liṅga*) as is fitting. Among these, the binding of the garland on the head is performed with two verses beginning, “O auspicious one, [place] the head” (MP 2.8.9), because of the wording of the indicative marks. With the two verses beginning, “Having fastened this [garland] upon her” (MP 2.8.10), it is likewise; for the word *srajaḥ* is a genitive singular, not a plural in either the nominative or accusative case, due to the singular form in “this [garland] here” (*imāṃ tām*). Because of the mention of the word *śirasi* (“on the head”), it does not apply to the other [limbs]. Āśvalāyana states: “One should not say ‘mālā’ [garland]; if they should say ‘mālā’, one should cause them to call it ‘sraj’ [wreath]” (ĀśGṛ 3.8.12).

Then, with the two verses beginning, “The collyrium from Mount Trikakud” (MP 2.8.11), he should apply collyrium to his eyes. There, using both mantras, he first applies the collyrium to the right eye, and then to the left eye with those same two mantras. Although the dual number occurs in the mantra, “With that I anoint you two,” nevertheless, by the force of the extension (*atideśa*) indicated by the word “thus,” there is a repetition of the action and a repetition of the mantras, just as in the case of binding the two forelegs. In this regard, the dual number is used as in the case of the *sānnāyya* pot, for example: “I place the two hearth-stones of the *ukhya* sacrifice, which do not leak.”

Then follows the looking into a mirror with the verse, "Whatever luster is mine... (MP 2.9.2). If "looking" were not explicitly stated, there would be only the taking [of the mirror] at this time, because of the indicative mark [in the mantra], "Take that back again" (MP 2.9.2); therefore, the mention of "looking" is made. Then he puts on his two shoes with the *yajus* formula, "You two are the supports" (MP 2.9.3). As in the case of applying collyrium, there is a repetition of the action and a repetition of the mantra. Then, having taken an umbrella, he covers himself with it with the *yajus* formula, "Thou art the refuge of Prajāpati" (MP 2.9.3). With the *yajus* formula, "Thee, by the impulse of the god... (MP 2.9.5), he takes a staff. According to Āśvalāyana, it should be made of bamboo (ĀśGṛ 3.7.15). 12.11.
He restrains his speech until the appearance of the stars. || 12.12 ||

When the stars have risen, having gone out toward the eastern or northern direction, he should worship the directions with the second half-verse, and the stars and the moon with the following verse. 12.13.

Then, with the subsequent half-verse beginning “O divine six wide ones” (*devīḥ ṣaḍ urvīḥ*, MP 2.9.6), facing eastward with palms joined in reverence, he brings all the directions to mind; having turned clockwise at the end of the mantra, he gazes upon them. There are indeed six directions, as indicated by the word “six wide ones” (*ṣaḍurvīr*): the four starting with the east, plus the zenith and the nadir. Then, with the following half-verse beginning “May we not abandon [you]” (*mā hāsmahi*, MP 2.9.6), he worships the lunar mansions together with the moon. 12.12–13.
Having conversed with the giver according to the facts, he departs. || 12.14 ||

Thus ends the twelfth section in the Āpastamba Gṛhyapraśna. Having conversed with a benefactor (*rātin*) who is a kinsman, asking, "What should I do? Which stage of life (*āśrama*) should I enter?", he goes forth together with that benefactor; the meaning is that he departs once the stage of life has been determined. Although this is already established by the rule, "Having understood his duties, he should undertake whatever he desires" (ĀpDh 2.21.5), the repetition is so that for one going forth (*pravrajat*), the ritual of the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) shall likewise conclude with the conversation. 12.14.
Thus ends the twelfth section in the *Anākulā*, a commentary on the *Gṛhyasūtra*.
Now begins the thirteenth section: having thus prescribed the primary ritual procedure for the bath (*snāna*), he now prescribes the secondary procedure (*anukalpa*).
Now, furthermore, having silently bathed at the sacred ford, he silently places a fuel-stick upon the fire. || 13.1 ||

The primary and most important rite of bathing has been explained. Now, this other, secondary, and lighter procedure for bathing is being explained. What is it? One bathes silently in water that reaches the ground at a *tīrtha*, not with water drawn out or cold. One also places a fuel-stick silently, not with a mantra; the fuel-stick is made of *palāśa* wood. Only this much is to be done in this rite; nothing else, such as the rule "before sunrise [one enters] the fold," and so forth. However, acts such as shaving the hair are worldly and devoid of religious merit (*adharmaka*). The performance there is as follows: having had the hair of the head, the beard, the nails, and the body hair shaved; having removed the girdle, staff, and deerskin; having silently bathed at a *tīrtha*; having cleansed the teeth with a stick of *udumbara* wood; having bathed again while covered by bathing garments; having put on two unwashed (*ahata*) garments; having sipped water (*ācamya*); having kindled the fire and strewn grass around it; having placed a *palāśa* fuel-stick into the fire while meditating upon Agni in the mind; and having taken up ornaments such as jewels as they become available—all this is done silently. (13.1)
Wherever they offer him honor, there he sits upon a grass mat (kūrca) as was done previously. 13.2.

By either of the two [vows] mentioned above, one becomes a *snātaka*. At this time, his relatives must pay him honor, because of the statement: "One who has mastered the Veda is worthy of the cow and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*). According to another ritual manual (*kalpa*), "Having announced him, one should offer the guest-water (*arghya*)" (Baudhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.2.1). The followers of Kauṣītaki prescribe the announcement with the formal formula: "We shall honor you, sir, who have well completed your vows. Āśvalāyana states: "A seat (*viṣṭara*), water for the feet (*pādya*), guest-water (*arghya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and a cow—these they announce three times each" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.21.6). In that place where his relatives perform the honoring for him, he sits upon a grass mat (*kūrca*) offered by them, just as the teacher sat previously at the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). Having taken the mat offered to him and placed it with its tips pointing north, he sits upon it with the mantra: "Thou art the sustainer of the kingdom" (Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā 2.9.7); such is the meaning. || 13.2 ||
In the same way, according to their respective genders, the king and the chief artisan [are addressed] by the following two verses. 13.3.

In this manner, the king and the *sthapati* sit upon the *kūrca* just as the *brāhmaṇa* *snātaka* does; they sit according to their respective characteristics (*yathāliṅga*) on the teacher’s seat (*ācāryāsandī*). In this way, the king and the *sthapati*, being honored, sit down according to their respective characteristics with the two subsequent *yajus* formulas. In that context, the *kṣatriya* who has been consecrated (*abhiṣikta*) as the sovereign of the realm for the sake of kingship—sovereignty (*sāmrājya*) is his characteristic mark. He alone is the lord of people (*janādhipati*). The *sthapati* is one who has been consecrated for the office of *sthapati*; lordship (*ādhipatya*) is his characteristic mark. Since the rule "the king and the *sthapati*" by means of the two subsequent [formulas] would have already established this, the words "in this manner" (*evaṃ*) and "according to their respective characteristics" (*yathāliṅga*) are stated for the purpose of indicating that just as there is an application (*viniyoga*) of the first mantra based on its characteristic mark, so too there is for the two subsequent ones. Consequently, the first mantra belongs to the *brāhmaṇa* alone, because of the characteristic mark "the teacher’s seat" (*ācāryāsandī*), and because it has been stated that the *brāhmaṇa* is remembered as the teacher (*ācārya*). Therefore, the sitting of the *kṣatriya* and the *vaiśya* is performed silently (*tūṣṇīm*). In that regard, the honor shown to the king is expressed by the formula "to the teacher, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the father-in-law, and the king"; however, the honor shown to the sovereign (*adhipati*) is through his status as a father-in-law. (13.3)
"Water for the feet," he said. || 13.4 ||
Then the giver of the honey-mixture, having brought forward water for the washing of the feet, says: "The waters are for the feet. (13.4)
Having consecrated it with the *uttarā* [verse], he should offer his right foot to a Brāhmaṇa and his left foot to a Śūdra. 13.5.

Then, while being honored, he consecrates those waters with the following verse, "The waters for washing the feet" (*āpaḥ pādāvanejanī*), and causes the one who is washing them to extend his right foot first to a Brāhmaṇa; his left foot to a Śūdra; there is no fixed rule regarding Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, because the masculine gender is not intended to be restrictive. It is the same among women. Regarding this, there is another ritual manual which states: "A woman washes [the feet] and a man sprinkles [the water]; some say the reverse. In the sacrifice, the specific rule is that the wife and the sacrificer wash each other's calves. Although it would have been established by the context alone that these are "waters for the feet" (*pādyā āpaḥ*), the explicit mention of "feet" (*pāda*) is for the purpose of ensuring that the term "foot" (*pāda*) does not recur in subsequent sections; therefore, the touching of the feet by the one who is washing them does not take place. 13.5.
Having touched the one who has washed him, he should touch himself with the following Yajus formula. || 13.6 ||

Likewise, there is another ritual rule: "He should touch the hands of the one who has washed with his own hand" (Baudhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.2). With the subsequent Yajus formula, "May greatness [reside] in me" (Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā 2.9.11), he performs the touching toward the west; and that takes place at the region of the heart, for that is the seat of the self. 13.6.
Holding [the vessel] with two bunches of kuśa grass, he spoke with an earthenware vessel: "Waters worthy of honor. || 13.7 ||

Then the donor, having taken up water brought in an earthen vessel with two *kūrca* grass-bunches from below and above, says and offers it, "These are the waters for honoring. According to another ritual manual (*kalpāntara*), they should be joined with flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). || 13.7 ||
Having consecrated [the water] with the following verse, while it is being brought in part into his joined palms, he should mutter the subsequent Yajus formula. 13.8.

The water fit for honoring has been presented; with the following verse, "Come to me" (MP 2.9.12), the giver consecrates it. Then the recipient, having formed the añjali gesture, the giver takes a portion of that water from his hand and pours it into the recipient's añjali. While it is being poured, the recipient should mutter the subsequent Yajus formula: "Thou art the milking of Virāj" (MP 2.9.13). || 13.8 ||
He consecrates with the following [verse] the remainder being poured forward in front.

Then the giver leads the remainder of that water toward the eastern direction. While it is being led, he, being honored, consecrates it with the following verse: "samudraṃ vaḥ" (MP 2.9.14). At this time, he should give a pair of garments, a pair of earrings, a cow, a garland, and whatever else is for the purpose of adornment—all of that. Others say [it should be given] at the end of the meal. All of that is to be understood as being enjoined by the term *apaciti* (honor/return-gift). || 13.9 ||
Having mixed curd and honey, covered it with a large bronze vessel, and grasped it with two bundles of grass, he announces, "The honey-mixture (madhuparka).

He announces the *madhuparka* with a large, wide bronze vessel; or rather, the connection is that he covers it with a large bronze [lid]. By this, the rule that both vessels must be of bronze is established. The word "iti" indicates a manner—namely, either "curd and honey" or "milk and honey. (13.10)
Some [offer] the threefold [oblation] and ghee. 13.11.
The collection of three substances is called *trivṛt*. It consists of the two previously mentioned—either curd and honey, or milk and honey—with clarified butter as the third. 13.11.
Some say that parched grains and groats constitute the *pāṅkta* offering. 13.12.
A collection of five substances is called *pāṅkta*: curds, honey, clarified butter, parched grain, and flour. 13.12.

Having consecrated water with the two subsequent *yajus* verses, he sips it; having sipped it three times with the following verse, both before and after [the meal], he should give it to one who is worthy of compassion.

Then, having consecrated that *madhuparka* with the two subsequent verses, namely "To the triple knowledge... (*trayyai vidyāyai*) and "May [the gods] come to me... (*ā mā gan*; MP 2.10.1–2), the one being honored receives it. Since the consecration and reception of the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other items is observed, the *madhuparka* is received after being consecrated, not consecrated after being received. Then he consumes it three times with the verse "That which of the honey... (*yan madhunaḥ*; MP 2.10.5): once with the mantra and twice silently. Then, before and after the consumption, he sips water with the two *yajus* formulas read immediately following, namely "Thou art the under-layer of immortality" (*amṛtopastaraṇam asi*) and "Thou art the covering of immortality" (*amṛtāpidhānam asi*; MP 2.10.3–4), respectively. The procedure there is as follows: having sipped the water to be used as an under-layer with the words "Thou art the under-layer of immortality," he consumes the *madhuparka* with the mantra; then, having sipped water, he likewise consumes it twice silently and sips the water to be used as a covering. Afterwards, there is a sip of water for the sake of purification. He should give the remainder of the *madhuparka* consumption to a son, a brother, or a returned student (*samāvṛtta*) who is worthy of compassion and favor. He too consumes it. The learned remember that there is no state of being "impure from remnants" (*ucchiṣṭa*) during the consumption of Soma, the consumption of *madhuparka*, or while eating. 13.13.
Having accepted it, the king or the architect shall give it to the domestic priest.

By the use of the word "only," it is meant that he should give [the remainder] to the domestic priest without having first consumed it himself; he [the priest], in turn, consumes it according to the prescribed rule. 13.14.
"Ox" (gaur) refers to a cow. 13.15.

Then, having sipped water and sat down, he presents a cow, saying, "A cow. And the cow may be female, because of the observation that "the cow is to be offered" (*gauḥ prasthāpyā*); or it may also be male, for it is heard in scripture: "Just as here, when a king of men or another worthy guest has arrived, they slaughter a bull or a pregnant cow" (*Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* 1.3.4). It is for this very purpose that the word "cow" (*gām*) is used here, so that there may be an offering of the cow-species in general. Otherwise, by merely saying "having presented a cow" (*gaur iti prahā*), the matter would be established just as it is in the case of the water for the feet and other offerings. 13.15.

Having consecrated it with the following [verse], he cooks its omentum; then, having spread an underlayer of ghee and poured ghee over it, he offers it with the next [verse] using either a middle or the smallest leaf of a *palāśa* tree.

The word "he should permit" (*anujānīyāt*) is to be supplied [as the verb], because it is seen so in another ritual manual (*kalpa*). [The rule states: "One who intends to cause [the animal] to utter *oṃ* should permit it. When the cow has been addressed, he should consecrate her with the following verse while she is being honored: "The cow art thou, whose sin has been struck away" (*gaur asy apahatapāpmā*, MP 2.10.6). Whatever animal one desires to sacrifice, he should permit it. Although only a single half-verse (*ardharca*) is traditionally recited, nevertheless, because of the feminine gender designation, this is indeed a *gāyatrī* verse. In that context, in place of the word "of him" (*amuṣya*), the name of the giver is to be inserted—namely, "and of me, Yajñaśarman."

Then, when the giver has been permitted by him [the host] and the cow has been seized according to the worldly procedure (*laukikyāvṛt*), he extracts the omentum (*vapā*), takes hold of it with the two omentum-roasting spits (*vapāśrapaṇī*), and cooks it either on the *aupāsana* fire or on a cooking fire. Having spread a base-layer of ghee (*upastīrṇa*) and poured a libation over it (*abhighārita*), he offers it into that very same fire with the middle or the last leaf of a *palāśa* branch, using the verse, “May Agni eat it” (*agniḥ prāśnātu*, MP 2.10.7). The phrase “having spread a base-layer and poured a libation over it” means that one performs the spreading of the base-layer and the pouring of the libation. After the offering, they prepare the meat and present it to him along with food. This is because of the statement, “The hospitality (*ātithya*) is unmodified” (ĀpGṛ 7.26); this statement serves to preclude the possibility of [spontaneous] spreading and pouring. Although it would have been sufficient simply to say “with a *palāśa* leaf,” the specification “with the middle or the last” is so that the offering might not be made with a leaf from a two-leaved *palāśa* stalk. Alternatively, it is for the purpose of providing an option in case of absence: first with the middle leaf, and in its absence, with the last. 13.16.
If he should release it, he should mutter the following verse in a whisper, and then say aloud, "Om, release! (13.17).

Now, if he releases the cow, when it is said, "This cow is being honored," he mutters the next four mantras, beginning with "May the sacrifice increase" (MP 2.10.8), in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). Having muttered them, he gives the command loudly: "Om, release her! And the giver, having released her, prepares another portion of meat; for according to another ritual manual (*kalpāntara*), "The *madhuparka* is not without meat" (ĀśGṛ 19.28). In that case, regarding the immolation of a bull, the cow is one fit to be a milch-cow, the mother of the Rudras; there is an omission of these two [mantras] because of a contradiction in gender, so say some. Others say no. Since the result is already established by the fact of the muttering itself, the mention of "in a low voice" is for the sake of restriction: only the next four mantras are to be spoken in a low voice, not the *praṇava*. This is because we see other scriptures where there is a possibility [of the *praṇava* being included], such as "like the *praṇava*" or "above the *praṇava*. By this, this option is established specifically for the *brahmán*. Although there is no explicit rule for the command here, the command (*prasavavidhi*) is to be understood from the very statement "loudly. 13.17.
Having consecrated the food with the following mantras in a low voice, he should recite "Oṃ kalpayata" loudly. || 13.18 ||

Then, having brought food containing meat, he announces to him: "It is ready" (*bhūtam*). According to another ritual manual (*kalpa*), one says "it is ready" when the food is prepared: "When the food is ready, he says 'it is ready'" (BauGṛ 1.2.55). And this is also our rule for the *vaiśvadeva* offering. Therefore, the announcement is simply "it is ready. Having consecrated that food silently with the five subsequent mantras beginning with "it is ready," he gives the command aloud: "Om, prepare it! Once commanded, the servers serve the food. He should say: "Feed four Brahmins of different lineages. When they have eaten, they bring food to him; such is another ritual manual (BauGṛ 1.2.58–59). 13.18.
This [offering] should be made to an Ācārya, a sacrificial priest (ṛtvij), a father-in-law, and a king, when they have come to visit within the course of a year. 13.19.

The *ācārya* and the others are well known. When these four have returned from their travels for a full year and come to the house as guests, this act of hospitality—beginning with the *kūrca* (seat of grass) and ending with the meal—must be performed by the householder. For it is stated that once the establishment of the household has occurred, the obligatory duties (*naiyamikāni*) are prescribed, according to the scriptural injunction: "The *agnihotra* and guests [are one's duties]. Regarding this, some say:

This duty is to be performed for the teacher, the officiating priest, the father-in-law, and the king; this constitutes one rule. Furthermore, it should also be performed for those who visit after a year has passed. By this, it is meant that immediately following the wedding, hospitality must be shown by inviting the teacher and the father-in-law; likewise for the officiating priest upon the completion of the ritual, and for the king after his consecration. Then, it should also be performed for those very same persons when they have arrived after being away for a year. (13.19)
To Citra, who spoke [this] once. || 13.20 ||

In the Kali age, because the immolation of a cow is forbidden, one should not perform this [rite] every year; rather, having said "Raur" (Obeisance), one should mutter "May the sacrifice increase," and so forth. This is because there is an omission of the intermediate mantra. It is for the sake of the teacher of the Veda and its meaning, who is "citrāya"—meaning well-known and whose doubts have been dispelled. For such a person who has approached, this act of propitiation (*apaciti*) should be performed once, and not annually. || 13.20 ||
Now begins the sixth chapter, the fourteenth section.

The sacraments beginning with marriage have been explained according to the sequence of the transmission of the mantras. Hereafter, the sacraments beginning with the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) are explained in that same sequence.
The parting of the hair is performed during the first pregnancy in the fourth month. || 14.1 ||

The *sīmanta* is a particular line in the middle of the hair. That rite in which it is raised (*unnīyate*) is called *sīmantonnayana*; it is a sacrament for the fetus. It should be performed in the fourth month. Because it is the first rule [for the fetus], this is a preparatory sacrament (*ādhārasaṃskāra*). And when the substratum has been prepared, all the fetuses placed therein become consecrated. (14.1)

Having fed the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce blessings, he performs the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire and ending with the *ājyabhāga* offerings; while she maintains contact with him, he offers the subsequent oblations and proceeds with the *jaya* and following rites.

On that occasion, on the preceding day, the *nāndī-śrāddha* is performed. Then, on that very day, having fed the Brahmins and having had them pronounce blessings while they are eating, he proceeds with the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire. The vessels and the *śalalī*-grass and other items are used only once, together with the *śamyā*-sticks. There are eight principal oblations: four with the verse "May Dhātṛ grant us wealth" (*MP* 2.11.1) and four with the verse "He whom [I worship] with a lowly heart" (*MP* 2.11.5). 14.2.

Having performed the rites ending with the sprinkling of water, he seats her to the west of the fire facing eastward; then, with a three-spotted porcupine quill, three bunches of *darbha* grass, and a bunch of *śalālu* fruit, he parts her hair upward with the *vyāhṛtis* and the two following verses. 14.3.

[The father] himself, facing west, [performs the ceremony] for the woman who faces east. A *treṇī* is a white [line] in three places; the elision of the vowel *i* and the substitution of *ṇ* are Vedic. A *śalalī* is the hair-needle of a porcupine. A stalk with branches is called a *puñjīla*. There are three *puñjīlas* of *darbha* grass. A young cluster of *udumbara* fruit is called a *śalāluglapsa*; others say it is a *piśācodumbara*. Having taken these substances together, he parts the hair (*sīmanta*) upwards with them, using the [three] *vyāhṛtis*, "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ," and the two following verses, "rākām aham" (MP 2.11.10) and "yās te rāka" (MP 2.11.11). At the end of the three [verses], there is a single parting. Here, the recitation of the *vyāhṛtis* in the collection of mantras (*mantrasamāmnāya*) need not be performed; the understanding [of their use] is already established by the word "with the *vyāhṛtis*" alone, as in such cases as "having muttered the *vyāhṛtis*" or "the *vyāhṛtis* distributed. Since this is already established, the recitation of the *vyāhṛtis* here is for the sake of the collection [of mantras]. Furthermore, if they were not recited, when it was said "with the *vyāhṛtis* and the two following [verses]," the inclusion would result from the *Yājamāna-samāmnāya*—namely, with the two mantras "ucchuṣmo agne" and so on—because that recitation is well-known there. Also, the status of being the primary offerings (*pradhānāhuti*) might be understood for "rākām aham" and "yās te rāka" due to the absence of distinction [otherwise]. Therefore, the *vyāhṛtis* are recited here so that the inclusion may be from this very collection. 14.3.
"Sing!"—with these words he instructs the two lute-players. || 14.4 ||

He who sings a verse with a lute is a *vīṇagāthī*. Both of them have already been brought forward. He instructs and sends them forth, saying, "Sing! They sing. In this regard, there is a restriction concerning the *ṛc* verses. 14.4.
Of the two northern [regions], the former belongs to the Sālvas and the latter to the Brāhmaṇas. 14.5.

Of the two subsequent verses, that which is first, “Yaugandhari” (MP 2.11.12), is a *gāthā* for the parting of the hair (*sīmantakarma*) among the Sālvas; the meaning is that this verse is to be sung by those residing in the Sālva country. That region lies on the bank of the Yamunā, and Vaiśyas predominate there. Yaugandhari is the king of them alone. The other, “Soma eva no rājā” (MP 2.11.13), belongs not to all Brāhmaṇas, but specifically to the Sālvas. 14.5.
And there is the description of the river in which they dwell. 14.6.

In the second mantra, in place of the word *asau*, the name of the river should be indicated in the vocative case; the meaning is "in which [river] they dwell" and "upon which they depend. For example: *tīreṇa kāveri tava* ("O Kāverī, by your bank"). However, for all Kṣatriyas, the singing takes place upon the *Sārvavarṇikī* verse seen in another ritual manual (*kalpa*), namely: "Soma alone, say the human subjects, is our king, sitting with his wheel turned back" (MP 2.11.13). Here too, the indication of the river is in the vocative case. (14.6)
Having tied up germinating barley grains, he restrains his speech until the stars appear.

She ties sprouted and germinated barley grains, bound with threads, upon the head of the bride; she alone restrains her speech. Thus they prescribe this instruction and this meal for her on this day. And the barley must be sown even earlier, so that it has sprouted by this time. 14.7.
When the stars have risen, having gone out toward the eastern or northern direction, having touched a calf and having murmured the *vyāhṛtis*, he should release his speech. 14.8.
The calf is both male and female. The *vyāhṛtis* in their entirety are to be understood from the *Yājamāna-samāmnāya*. 14.8.
The rite for ensuring the birth of a male child is performed when the fetus has become manifest, under the asterism Tiṣya.

The rite by which a male child is produced is called *puṃsavana*. The substitution of *uvaṅ* is Vedic; it is based on the observation of the mantra: "Thou art the producer of a male. Āśvalāyana, however, employed the word with its secondary derivative suffix (*guṇa*). That rite is to be performed when the embryo has become manifest. The manifestation of the embryo occurs in the third or fourth month. Even if it is in the fourth month, the *puṃsavana* must be performed before the *sīmantonnayana*, because the occasion for the former arises first. We shall explain later the purpose of the instruction that it follows [the *sīmantonnayana*]. It is performed under the asterism Tiṣya; the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locus according to Pāṇini 2.3.45: "And [the instrumental is used] for an asterism when the suffix *lup* is elided. (14.9)

Having brought a shoot with testicles from an eastern or northern branch of a banyan tree, [the ritual] beginning with the kindling of the fire is performed as at the parting of the hair (*sīmanta*). 14.10.

One should take a shoot (*śuṅgā*)—that is, a terminal sprout—from a *nyagrodha* tree, either from its eastern or northern branch; it is designated as "testicle" (*vṛṣaṇa*) because of its resemblance to one. Having brought that shoot which possesses [the fruit], one performs the ritual beginning with the kindling of the fire and ending with the sprinkling around (*pariṣecana*), just as in the *sīmantonnayana* ceremony. Because of the specific mention of "kindling the fire" and so forth, there is no feeding of Brahmins or the pronouncing of blessings prior to that point. However, they do occur at the conclusion, according to the rule: "In all rites, one should feed pure men who know the mantras" (ĀpDh 2.15.11). Likewise, those acts such as the instruction (*saṃśāsana*) that follow the sprinkling around also do not take place here, because of the repeated instruction here that [the wife] should sit to the west of the fire facing east.

The procedure for this is as follows: on the previous day, the *nāndī-śrāddha* is performed. On the following day, beginning with the kindling of the fire and so forth, the vessels are prepared once. Only the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are used together with the *śuṅgā* branch, not the *śamyā* pegs. At the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, while she [the wife] maintains contact [with him], he recites the four verses beginning with “May Dhātṛ grant us wealth” (MP 2.11.4) and the four verses beginning with “He who [loves] thee with a longing heart” (MP 2.11.5). He proceeds with the *jaya* offerings and the rest. After the final sprinkling of water (*pariṣecana*), the ritual act to be described hereafter is performed. 14.10.

Now, at the conclusion of the remainder of the ritual manual (*tantraśeṣa*), he states what is to be performed: Having had a maiden who has not yet bathed for her menses grind [the substance] with a stone on a stone, and having sprinkled it, she causes it to enter through the right nostril with her thumb by means of the *aperaṇa* formula, while the patient is lying on her back facing eastward, after she has been placed to the north of the fire with the *yajuḥ* formula. 14.11.

She whose menses have appeared is *avasnātā*; the opposite of that is *anavasnātā*. A maiden of such a description is the agent of the grinding; the husband is the prompter (*prayojaka*). The *upala* is the son of the grinding-stone (*dṛṣatputra*); even when referring to the stone itself, it is called *dṛṣatputra*. Having ground the *śuṅgā* there and having moistened it with a cloth, he causes her—standing behind the fire, facing east (*prācīm*), with her face turned toward the east (*prāṅmukhīm*), and lying supine (*uttānām*, i.e., with her face upward)—to lie down. With the following Yajus formula, "Thou art the production of a male" (*puṃsuvanam asi*, MP 1.11.14), he introduces (*apinayati*) that juice into her right nostril with his thumb. He himself faces eastward as well. (Having closed [her] eye, he himself also faces eastward.)
It produces a male. || 14.12 ||

In this way, a woman consecrated by this rite gives birth to a male child. Some consider this to be a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), because if it were an injunction regarding a result (*phalavidhi*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the rite being non-obligatory due to its connection with a specific desire. If it were an *arthavāda*, there would be the consequence of it having to be repeated for every conception. In that case, the phrase "in the first conception" (*prathame garbhe*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. It is for this very purpose that it is taught later. This is clearly stated by the Chandogas: "In the first conception, in the third month, the *puṃsavana* [rite] is performed. Others, however, consider it an injunction regarding a result. And in that regard, because of the statement, "He indeed is free from debt who has a son" (*TS* 6.3.10), the production of a son is obligatory; thus, as long as one son has not been produced, the rite must be performed during the conceptions. But after that, it is performed when there is a desire for more sons, and it is not performed when there is a desire for a daughter. Furthermore, the mention of "first" does not carry over here, because "conception" (*garbha*) is mentioned again. As for the teaching of the *puṃsavana* later [in the sequence], it is so that it may be performed in the fourth month, for the purpose of its subsequent application. 14.12.
Swiftly giving birth. || 14.13 ||
That action by which one is quickly delivered is called the action known as *kṣiprasuvana*. || 14.13 ||

Having fetched water with a vessel that has not been rinsed, following the current, and having placed a cooking pot upon it while it is steaming, he should touch it with the head while it is still steaming with the subsequent Yajus formula, and then sprinkle it with these waters using the following verses. || 14.14 ||

[The patient] is not touched with water that has not been consecrated, nor [is she touched] while following the flow of water as it streams out, nor against the current. From the feet—that is, from below the feet—there is a plant whose leaves are like white [lotuses] and whose flowers are like yellow; it blooms at midday and grows in the forests, known as *tūryantī*. There is another whose leaves are like bamboo leaves and whose flowers are like red [lotuses], which they call *agniśikhā*. This is *śoṣyantī*. Having taken these two plants together with their roots and leaves, she places them very firmly upon the head—the meaning being "on the head. Others, having ground them, smear [her with the paste]. Then she touches her with the subsequent *yajus*: "With these ten I touch you" (*ābhiṣṭvāhaṃ daśabhir abhi mṛśāmi*, MP 2.11.15). Because of the mention of "ten," the touching is done with both hands. [She touches] in the natural direction, beginning from the face. Then she should sprinkle her with the very same waters brought there, using the three subsequent *ṛc*s: "Just as Soma purifies himself" (*yathaiva somaḥ pavate*, MP 2.11.16), sprinkling her with each mantra. 14.14.
Now he states another remedy:
"If the placenta does not fall, one should sprinkle it with water prepared in this manner using the following two [verses].
Thus ends the fourteenth section in the Āpastamba Gṛhyapraśna.

The *jarāyu* is the fetal membrane; if that does not fall away, then the subsequent rite must be performed. What, then, is this? It is the rite prescribed for a swift delivery, beginning with the words, "With an unbaked earthen bowl... and so forth. With water prepared in this manner, one should sprinkle [the woman] while reciting each of the two subsequent mantras: "O drop, fall down like sesame" (MP 2.11.19) and "Let the speckled Śevala come out" (MP 2.11.20). These two rites concern one's own wife, as indicated by the effort made in another ritual text regarding a woman seized by consumption (*yakṣman*) or another [woman]. Others, however, maintain that they apply without distinction. 14.15.
Thus ends the fourteenth section in the *Anākula*, a commentary on the *Gṛhyasūtra* composed by Śrī Haradatta.
Now begins the fifteenth section.

Having touched the newborn with the Vātsapra hymn and placed him on his lap with the following Yajus formula, he performs the consecration with the next two verses, smells [the child] on the head, and mutters [the mantra] into the right ear. 15.1.

Because the masculine gender is intended in the word *jātam*, this sacrament called *jātakarma* belongs to the male alone, not to the female. *Vatsaprī* is the name of a seer; the hymn seen by him, beginning with *divas pari*, is the *vātsapram*. There is a touching [of the child] at each verse. Others say that the entire section beginning with *sarvān te* [is used].

With the subsequent *yajus* formula, "In this [I place you]" (MP 2.11.32), he places [the child] upon his own lap; for the qualification "of the mother" follows later, whereas here it is his own lap. The reading is "with the subsequent ones" (*uttarābhiḥ*). With the three subsequent *ṛc*s, the three acts beginning with the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) are to be performed. "From limb by limb" (MP 2.11.33) is the consecration. "Become a stone" is the smelling on the head. "May wisdom [be yours]" (MP 2.12.2) is the muttering (*jāpa*) into the right ear; the meaning is "muttering. However, some, relying on the dual ending in the reading "with the two subsequent ones" (*uttarābhyām*), maintain that both mantras are to be employed in all three rites. For them, the act of smelling would follow from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the [first] mantra, and the muttering into the ears would follow from the [second]. And Āśvalāyana says: "Having placed [the child] near the two ears, he mutters the production of wisdom: 'May the god Savitṛ [bestow] wisdom upon you'" (ĀśŚr 1.13.2). || 15.1 ||

And he points out the name of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). In the formula "I smell upon you, O [Name]," the word "O [Name]" (*asau*) is replaced by the designation of the lunar mansion's name. One should point this out using its vocative case—for example: "I smell upon you with the *hiṃkāra* of cattle, O Āśvayujī," and so forth. Regarding the words for lunar mansions, there is a verse for determining their grammatical form (*rūpa*) in the sense of being born under them (*jātārtha*): "In the case of *rohiṇī*, *mṛgaśiras*, *ārdrā*, *puṣya*, *viśākhā*, *anurādhā*, *jyeṣṭhā*, *mūla*, *pūrva-phalgunī*, *uttara-phalgunī*, *hasta*, *citrā*, *svāti*, *viśākhā*, and *aśvinī*, there is a vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) at the beginning [of the suffix]."

In the remaining cases, when there is no *m* or *v*, the final vowel followed by *k* or *p* is desired; likewise, for words ending in *svāp* or *su*, a short vowel followed by an *i* and a visarga is desired.

The names beginning with *rohiṇī* are indicated here by their initial syllables; the meaning is that the vowel increment (*vṛddhi*) must be applied to the beginning of these. Thus: *rauhiṇaḥ*, *revataḥ*, *māghaḥ*, *mārgaśīrṣaḥ*, *jyeṣṭhaḥ*, *caitraḥ*. Where the word *paśabda* follows a *ṭha*-suffix, there is vowel increment: one born under the *proṣṭhapadā* stars is *proṣṭhapādaḥ*. By the rule “*je proṣṭhapadānām*” (Pāṇini 7.3.18), there is vowel increment in the second member of the compound. In these cases, the suffix *luṅ* does not occur because of the word “*bahulam*” (variously) in the rule “*nakṣatrebhyo bahulam*” (Pāṇini 4.3.37). Among the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the last is called *apabharaṇī*; regarding it, there is an option: *āpabharaṇiḥ* or *āpabharaṇaḥ*. Similarly, *śroṇaḥ* or *śrāvaṇaḥ*. In these two cases, the option for *luṅ* occurs precisely because of the word “*bahulam*. One born under *śatabhiṣaj* is *śatabhiṣak* or *śātabhiṣajaḥ*; here, in one alternative, there is also the elision of the *ṭi* suffix, resulting in *śatabhiṣa*. Similarly, *āśvayuk* or *āśvayujaḥ*; in these two, the option for *luṅ* occurs by the rule “*vatsaśālābhijidaśvayukchatabhiṣajo vā*” (Pāṇini 4.3.36). Regarding the remaining lunar mansions—those other than those mentioned—the vowel increment at the beginning does not occur. Here, by the rules “*śraviṣṭhāphalgunyanurādhāsvātitiṣyapunarvasuhastaviśākhāṣāḍhābahulāḷ luk*” (Pāṇini 4.3.34) and “*nakṣatrebhyo bahulam*” (Pāṇini 4.3.37), only *luṅ* occurs: *śraviṣṭhaḥ*, *phalgunaḥ*, *anūrādhaḥ*, *svātiḥ*, *tiṣyaḥ*, *punarvasuḥ*, *āṣāḍhaḥ*, *bahulaḥ* (i.e., *kṛttikaḥ*). In the case of *āmbu*—namely *ārdrā* and *mūla*—the final vowel becomes *kaśamba* (i.e., *ka*); thus: *ārdrakaḥ*, *mūlakaḥ*. The suffix *vun* is added according to the rule “*pūrvāhṇāparāhṇārdramūla-*” (Pāṇini 4.3.28), and the vowel is lengthened. In the case of *svāpv*—namely *svātī* and *punarvasū*—the final vowel is desired to be short and accompanied by a visarga: *svātiḥ*, *punarvasuḥ*. The elision [of the suffix] occurs by the rule “*śraviṣṭhāphalgunī-*” etc. The presence of the visarga occurs when the lunar mansion is indicated in the nominative case in formulas such as the *sūktavāka*; however, here the indication is by the vocative: *svāte*, *punarvaso*. Prior to the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), and during rites such as the worship of the fire (*agnyupasthāna*), this very name of the lunar mansion should be used. And where there is an indication of two names, even then the lunar mansion name is of this kind, while the other is that which was made on the tenth day. 15.2.
That is the secret. || 15.3 ||
The name of the lunar mansion is secret; the meaning is that it should be spoken in such a way that others do not know it. This is likewise the case in the *sūktavāka* and other such formulas. 15.3.

Having mixed honey and ghee, and having tied a piece of gold with a knot (*niṣṭarkya*) on a blade of *darbha* grass and taken it up, he should feed the boy with the subsequent mantras; then, having bathed him with the five subsequent [verses], and having mixed curd and ghee, he should feed the boy the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) from a bronze vessel with the *vyāhṛtis* followed by the syllable *oṃ* as the fourth; then, having mixed the remainder with water, he should pour it out in a cow-pen. 15.4.

Having mixed honey and ghee in unequal proportions in a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*), he places a piece of gold therein, tied with a blade of *darbha* grass using the *niṣṭarkya* knot—a specific method of tying well known in common practice. Having taken those two liquids with the gold thus bound, he should have the boy eat them, administering the food with each of the three subsequent mantras beginning with "In thee, wisdom" (*tvayi medhām*, MP 2.12.35). Then, he bathes him with the five subsequent *ṛc*s beginning with "For the field-disease thee" (*kṣetriyai tvā*, MP 2.12.6), administering the bath with each mantra. Then, having mixed curds and ghee in another bronze vessel—that is, *pṛṣadājya*—he has him eat it from that same bronze vessel with the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, namely "Bhūḥ svāhā," and so forth, with each mantra. Then, having mixed the remaining two substances with water, he should pour them out in a cow-pen. The mention of the "boy" (*kumāra*) is intended so that even for a boy who is incapable [of eating], the act of eating may still take place by means of this method. Therefore, in cases such as "They feed roasted grains to the boys" (*dhānāḥ kumārān prāśayanti*) or "They feed the *kṣaitrapatya* [offering]," the feeding does not apply to those who are incapable. 15.4.

Having placed [the child] on his mother’s lap with the first [verse], having caused her to suckle the right breast with the second, having touched the earth with the next two [verses], he places him who has lain down with the final Yajus-verse. 15.5.

Then, with the verse, "Do not [fear] the boy" (MP 2.13.1), he places that boy upon his mother's lap; for this duration of time, [the child remains] on her own lap. Therefore, even the pouring out of the remnants must be caused to be performed by another. Then, having caused him to take hold of the right breast with the following verse, "This is the boy" (MP 2.13.2), he touches the earth with each of the two subsequent verses, "That which is the heart of the earth" (MP 2.13.3). Then the mother causes the boy to lie down on the ground she has touched. When he is lying there, she touches him with the following Yajus formula, "He does not bend, he does not cry" (MP 2.13.5).

Having placed a water-pot at the head [of the bed] with the following Yajus formula, and having offered mustard seeds mixed with husks three times each with his joined palms while reciting the subsequent formulas accompanied by the utterance of "svāhā," he instructs [the assistant]: "Whenever [the spirit] has entered, silently cast [the mixture] into the fire. (15.6)

Then, to the north of his head, he places a water-pot with the Yajus formula, "The waters [are] among those who sleep" (MP 2.13.6). Then he offers mustard seeds mixed with *phalīkaraṇa* husks with his joined palms (*añjali*) using the eight subsequent mantras beginning with "This Kali... (MP 2.13.7). In this case, there is an oblation three times for each *svāhā* utterance: once with the mantra and twice silently. The material must be taken up again and again; however, some offer three times with the material taken up only once. In the two subsequent oblations, they repeat only the *svāhā* utterance. This oblation is *apūrva* (unprecedented), because no ritual framework (*tantra*) is prescribed; nevertheless, the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*) does take place, as does the sprinkling of water all around on both sides. Having offered the oblation, he then gives instructions. To whom? To those who enter the lying-in chamber. In that instruction, the particle *eva* is used in the sense of "thus. This is what is meant: whenever you enter this lying-in chamber, then and there you must silently throw mustard seeds mixed with *phalīkaraṇa* into this very fire three times each, just as I have thrown them with my joined palms. In this context, the word "silently" prohibits the use of the mantra which would otherwise be obtained by extension. They perform it according to the instruction. And this oblation is a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the protection of the child, not for the mother, because of the context. Therefore, although protection for the mother is also implied by the words "whose mind [was troubled] when she had given birth" (MP 2.14.2), the oblation is nonetheless not for her sake. Consequently, it does not take place during the ten-day period following a woman's delivery, nor in the event of the death of a son. 15.6.
In this manner, day after day, until the tenth day has passed.

The meaning is that the *homa* and the *saṃśāsana* must be performed for exactly as long as they do not go out, from the time of their being recognized until the tenth day. And the *homās* are to be performed only once, not every evening. Although the *saṃśāsana* follows immediately after, this extension (*atideśa*) does not apply to it alone; for it is a subordinate part of the *homa*. Nor does it apply to the *Vātsapra* and so forth, because the entirety of those is not established in all other ritual manuals (*kalpas*). || 15.7 ||
Having thus described the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), he states the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), which follows in due order:
"On the tenth day, when she has risen and bathed, the father and mother give a name to the son. (15.8)

"Rising" (*utthāna*) means the removal of the signs of childbirth, such as the fire and the water-jar, and the barbering of the husband. Whatever else women know, that also takes place on the tenth day for all social classes (*varṇas*). By the word "tenth," the night is not meant; rather, it refers to a collection of days and nights, as in the expression, "therefore, of similar nights. Therein, by virtue of the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*), the ritual act and the bath occur specifically on the day, and if possible, they must take place on that very day as a rule. Although the status of being a son is already established from the context, the explicit mention of "the son" is so that the specific characteristics of the name—which will be described later—should apply to him alone. Consequently, for a girl, only this much applies: "The name of a girl has an odd number of syllables" (*ĀpGṛ* 15.11); it does not include rules such as "the noun first, followed by the verb. The mention of "the father and the mother" is for the purpose of ensuring that those two should pronounce the name first. This is known from the *Taittirīya Saṃhitā*: "The father and the mother gave [the name] first" (*TS* 1.5.10). The practical application is as follows: having fed Brahmins who are pure and learned in the mantras at all rites, according to the rule, "One should feed pure men learned in the mantras at all ceremonies" (*ĀpDh* 2.15.11), the father and mother, having pronounced the name first, should cause the Brahmins to pronounce the benediction. This is because we see in another ritual manual (*Kalpa*) the formula, "May there be well-being for such-and-such a person. Some, however, desire a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), saying, "We shall perform the naming ceremony. (15.8)
A name consisting of two or four syllables, with the noun preceding and the verb following, ending in a long vowel or a visarga, beginning and containing voiced consonants and semivowels. || 15.9 ||

Now, the specific characteristics of a name (*nāman*): A vowel, whether accompanied by a consonant (*savyañjana*) or without a consonant (*nirvyañjana*), is a syllable (*akṣara*). A name is a substance (*dravya*) as its primary element; that which has such a [substantive] word as its prior member is "name-prior" (*nāmapūrva*). A verb (*ākhyāta*) is the cause of action; that which has such a [verbal] word as its subsequent member is "verb-posterior" (*ākhyātottara*). That which has a *visarjanīya* following a long vowel and a sibilant (*abhiniṣṭhāna*) at its end is "ending in a long vowel and a sibilant" (*dīrghābhiniṣṭhānānta*). Likewise, that which has a sonant consonant (*ghoṣavat-vyañjana*) as its initial element is "sonant-initial" (*ghoṣavad-ādi*). That which has a semivowel (*antastha*) in its middle is "semivowel-middle" (*antarantastha*). Among the classes of consonants, the third and fourth letters and the letter *ha* are sonants (*ghoṣavat*). *Ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* are the semivowels (*antastha*). Examples include: *dyutiḥ* ("he leads to heaven"), *gośriḥ* ("he rests upon cows"), *goprīḥ* ("he pleases the cow"), *hiraṇyadāḥ* ("he gives gold"), *bhūridāḥ* ("he gives much"), and *haradattaḥ* ("given by Hara"). Baudhāyana says: "The name should be after the likeness of a seer (*ṛṣyaṇūka*) or after the likeness of a deity (*devātāṇūka*), according to how the names of their ancestors were. "After the likeness of a seer" means denoting a seer, such as Vasiṣṭha or Jamadagni. "After the likeness of a deity" means denoting a deity, such as Rudra or Viṣṇu. "Ancestors" refers to the father and others. (Baudhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 2.2.28, 29) 15.9.
Or rather, that upon which the prefix *su-* occurs is indeed firmly established; for so says the Brāhmaṇa. 15.10.

Alternatively, there is this other view: in whatever name the prefix *su-* occurs, that alone is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) in that case; not other [features] such as having two syllables and so forth. For that [name with *su-*, even if it lacks two syllables,] is firmly established (*pratiṣṭhita*). The word *hi* indicates excellence. It is more firmly established than even the former [view]; therefore, by that [criterion], the former [names] such as those with two syllables are also considered firmly established. And thus, remaining within that very same former definition, Bharadvāja said: "A name of two or four syllables, beginning and containing a voiced consonant (*ghoṣavat*), ending in a semi-vowel (*antastha*), and terminating in a long vowel or a visarga (*abhiniṣṭhāna*), is known to be 'well-known' (*prasiddha*). [The term used here is] *pratiṣṭhita*. The meaning is: stable, indestructible, and conducive to longevity. Examples include *Subhadra* and *Sumukha*. Because of the mention of the prefix (*upasarga*), names such as *Somasut* do not become firmly established. (15.10)
The uneven-numbered syllables belong to the maiden. || 15.11 ||

That number which cannot be measured by [even] a single unit is an odd number (*ayuk-saṃkhyā*). Where there are an odd number of syllables, that is "odd-syllabled" (*ayuj-akṣara*)—such as one syllable, three syllables, and so forth. This alone is the defining characteristic of a maiden's name: for example, Gauḥ, Vāk, Pṛthivī, and Pārvatī. (15.11)

Having returned from his journey, he should perform the consecration over his son with the two following verses, smell him on the head, and mutter the subsequent mantras into his right ear. || 15.12 ||

Having returned from his journey, he should perform the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) and the smelling (*avaghrāṇa*) in sequence with the two following [mantras]: the consecration with “From limb to limb” (MP 2.14.3), and the smelling with “Become a stone” (MP 2.14.4). The naming should be done thus: “I smell you, Yajñaśarman. Although the mention of a son is established both by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra and by the instruction for a different consecration in the case of a girl, the explicit inclusion of the word “son” is intended to prevent the smelling on the head and the whispering in the right ear from applying to a girl; otherwise, since there would be no contradiction of the indicative mark, both rites might apply to a girl as well, given that she too is the subject under discussion. Furthermore, the rule “the girl with the following [mantras]” (MP 2.14.10) should be understood as a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) specifically for the consecration, and not for the other two acts. The five mantras beginning with “Agni is long-lived” (MP 2.14.4–9) are prescribed as the subsequent ones. He should whisper these into the right ear of the son. The separate mention of the mantras is made to indicate that the word “five” in the phrase “the five beginning with ‘Agni is long-lived’” refers to the mantras themselves. 15.12.
He consecrates the maiden with the following Yajus formula. || 15.13 ||

Thus ends the fifteenth section in the *Gṛhyapraśna* of Āpastamba. Having returned from a journey, [the father] addresses a daughter who has borne female offspring with the following *yajus*: “O thou who hast arisen from my entire self” (*sarvasmād ātmanaḥ sambhūtāsī*, MP 2.14.10). Although one might have said "daughter" (*duhitaram*), the use of the term "maiden" (*kumārīm*) is intended so that this rite does not apply after she has been given away in marriage. As for a son, however, [this applies] as long as he lives; for even when a son returns from a journey, the triad beginning with the addressing [of him] takes place, since the underlying principle is the same. 15.13.
Thus ends the fifteenth section in the Ākula commentary on the Gṛhyasūtra composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the sixteenth section.
Now the first feeding with solid food is taught.

In the sixth month after birth, having fed the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce blessings, he should mix together curds, honey, ghee, and boiled rice, and have the boy eat it with the following mantras. 16.1.

Now follows the *annaprāśana* (the first feeding with solid food) for the boy. This should be performed in the sixth month from the day of birth, beginning from the day of the *jātakarma*. The months referred to here may be solar, lunar, or others. Intending to perform this rite, he should feed an even number of Brāhmaṇas and have them pronounce blessings: "An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity! There is no *abhyudaya-śrāddha* on the preceding day here, because there is no worship of the gods (*devejyā*). Where the worship of the gods occurs on the following day, the offering to the ancestors (*pitṛ*) is performed on the preceding day, according to the scriptural statement: "Therefore, the offering is made to the ancestors on the preceding day; on the following day, one sacrifices to the gods. Having had the blessings pronounced, he should mix together the four substances beginning with curd and have the boy eat from that mixture with the four subsequent mantras beginning with "Bhūr apāṃ tvā" (MP 2.14.11). He appends the phrase "tvauṣadhīnām" to the two middle mantras. The reading of the word "apām," however, is intended to indicate that there are four mantras. In the place of "asau," the name is inserted in the vocative case, such as: "May herbs be [beneficial], O Yajñaśarman. The feeding takes place with each mantra. Others say that the phrase "sarvān te" applies to all. Because of the mention of "the boy" (*kumāra*), the *annaprāśana* for a girl is not performed according to these rules, based on the statement of Āśvalāyana: "The rite for a girl is performed silently" (ĀśGṛ 1.14.7). 16.1.
Some say [it should be done] with the meat of a Taittirya bird. 16.2.

Some teachers maintain that this first feeding of solid food should be performed with the meat of a partridge (*tittiri*). Is the meat a condiment for the rice? Others, however, maintain that the meat itself is to be eaten while reciting the mantra. The mention of "meat" is for the purpose of excluding blood and other such substances. (16.2)
The tonsure ceremony (caula) should take place in the third year from birth, under the two Punarvasu constellations.

Now follows the rule for the *caula* ceremony: that rite in which the hair is first cut is called *caula*, because the *cūḍā* (the tuft of hair) is its purpose; there is no distinction between the letters *ḍa* and *la*. This should be performed in the third year from birth under the *nakṣatra* of Punarvasu. Since it is prescribed that "one should cause the boy (*kumāram*) to eat [the food]," this formal *caula* is intended only for a male; for a girl, however, it is merely a ritual procedure (*āvṛt*). If this were the case, the masculine gender in the phrase "having done so, [he places the boy] to the west of the fire, facing east" would be appropriate. The mention of "birth" is to ensure that the third year is counted from the time of delivery, and not from the beginning of the pregnancy. 16.3.
The feeding of Brahmins is like a formal gift. 16.4.

Since there is no distinction regarding the feeding of Brahmins at the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), the elision of the initial word (*ādi-pada-lopa*) should be understood here. Thus, "brāhmaṇabhojanādi" (beginning with the feeding of Brahmins) is to be understood here as meaning: having fed the Brahmins, having caused them to pronounce blessings, and having fed the boy. The phrase "with the first [verse] of the section" (*anuvākasya prathamena*) and so forth will be extended [to this case] later on. (16.4)
The kindling of the fire and the subsequent rites are performed as at the *sīmantonnayana* ceremony. || 16.5 ||

The rites beginning with the kindling of the fire and ending with the sprinkling of water around it are to be performed as in the *sīmanta* ceremony. On the preceding day, the *nāndī-śrāddha* is performed; the vessels are used only once; and *śamyā*-sticks are provided along with the porcupine quills and other items. In the instruction "when she has taken hold [of him]," it is the boy who takes hold of her. There is also an extension (*atideśa*) of the rites ending with the sprinkling of water. However, there is no extension here of the rule "the lute-player and the singer sing 'Sing! (ĀpGṛ 14.4), because of the injunction that he should sit facing east behind the fire. 16.5.

Having seated him facing eastward by the fire, he silently shaves off his hair with a three-spotted porcupine quill, three tufts of *darbha* grass, and a bunch of *śalālu* stalks; then he arranges the topknot according to the specific *ṛṣi* [of the boy's lineage]. || 16.6 ||

*Vinayana* means the separating out of those hairs that are to be shaved for the sake of the topknots. The term *tūṣṇīm* (silently) is intended to prescribe silence, not to prohibit the use of mantras, because there is no [prior] rule establishing their use. "According to the seers" (*yathārṣi*) means he makes as many topknots as there are seers in his *pravara*—three for one with three seers, five for one with five seers. (16.6)
Just as it may be their family custom. || 16.7 ||

Alternatively, he makes the topknot (*śikhā*) in such a way that the family custom (*kuladharma*) of these [people]—the sons of noble lineage—is observed. The use of the plural "of these" is intended to ensure that the family custom does not belong to the performer alone; therefore, there is no fixed rule that the father himself must be the performer of this rite. However, in other rites pertaining to the son, the rule applies to him (the father) provided it is possible. || 16.7 ||
From the pouring out of water until the placing of the hair, it is the same [as previously described]. 16.8.

The meaning is that everything from "warm [water] is to be brought for the cold" and so forth, up to "or he places [it] on a clump of *darbha* grass" (ĀpGṛ 10.8), is to be performed just like the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). || 16.8 ||
Having washed the razor, he sets it down. || 16.9 ||
The washing of the razor is prescribed; its setting aside follows from the sense of the context. When he sets it aside, then he should wash it.
Therefore, there is a cessation of ritual activity for three days. || 16.10 ||
For three days and nights, one must not perform the work of a barber with that razor. || 16.10 ||
He grants a boon. || 16.11 ||
When this rite was completed, the prince’s father bestowed a boon upon Brahmā; it is said, "A cow is indeed the boon. (16.11)
In this same manner, the gift of a cow may also be performed under another lunar mansion in the sixteenth year. || 16.12 ||

Just as the *caula* ceremony is performed, so too should the rite called *godāna* be performed for him. In that case, there is an exception to the third year, namely that it may be done in the sixteenth year. It may also be performed under another lunar mansion, provided it is an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*). This is an exception to the rule regarding the *punarvasu* asterism. (16.12)
Or he may be one who has performed the Agni-godāna ceremony. || 16.13 ||

Where Agni is the deity at the *godāna* ceremony, that is the *agnigodāna*. He whose [ceremony] is the *agnigodāna* is one for whom Agni is the deity of the *godāna*. (By the word "Agni," the *godāna* rite dedicated to that deity is indicated; the analysis of the compound is: "he whose *godāna* is Agni"). There is the elision of one of the two words *godāna*, as in the case of *uṣṭramukha* ("camel-faced"). Regarding this, Baudhāyana says: "The *godāna* takes place in the sixteenth year. Its performance and conclusion are silent, like the *caula*. ... Or he becomes an *agnigodāna*. Its performance and conclusion are according to the *kāṇḍopākaraṇa* and *kāṇḍasamāpana* rites" (BauGṛ 3.2.52–58). What is meant by this? Whatever ritual procedure (*kalpa*) applies to the commencement and completion of the *kāṇḍas* dedicated to Agni, the rules of the *caula* are extended to them. It occurs in the sixteenth year. The vessels are used only once; they are not to be cleaned. Since this is not taught in this *Gṛhyasūtra*, the rule regarding the *śamyā* (wooden pin) applies only where the *godāna* is specifically taught. The practical application (*prayoga*) is as follows: having fed the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce blessings, having shaved the hair and beard silently, and having performed the rites from the kindling of the fire up to the sprinkling around the altar according to the *kāṇḍopākaraṇa* of the Agni-section, the worship of the deities is performed like the *Śukriya*: "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall observe the vow. Others say the observance of the vow lasts for a year, and its release is at the end. The modification is "Thus indeed have I observed," etc., as in the *Śukriya*; the deity is the same. There is the shaving of hair and beard. At the end, there is the feeding of Brahmins. In both cases, some perform the *nāndīmukha-śrāddha*, others do not. 16.13.
Some teachers instruct that the vow of giving a cow lasts for one year.

Some teachers instruct that even for one who has performed the *godāna* ceremony, there is the observance of a vow (*vrata*) for one year as a supplement to it. This option applies to the *caula* and *godāna*; however, in the case of the *agnigodāna*, because of the extension (*atideśa*) of the rules from the *kāṇḍopākaraṇa*, the vow-observance is mandatory. When the vow-observance takes place, then after the granting of the boon (*varadāna*), the worship of the deity (*devatopasthāna*) occurs at the end as before, and the dismissal (*visarga*) is likewise just as before. (16.14)
This much is the difference: he has all his hair shaved off. || 16.15 ||

In this *caula-godāna*, however, there is this much difference from the *caula*: here one has all the hair shaved, including the topknot (*śikhā*). In the *caula*, however, one leaves the topknot according to the number of one's *ṛṣis*. Others explain that the inclusion of the word "all" is for the purpose of including the beard and so forth; for them, the word "hair" (*keśa*) is intended as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). Thus says Āśvalāyana: "He issues the command [to the barber] regarding the hair, beard, body hair, and nails, [directing them] toward the north" (ĀśGṛ 1.18.6). || 16.15 ||
"The Chāndogas say that it is touching water. 16.16.
Thus ends the sixteenth section and the sixth chapter in the Gṛhyapraśna of Āpastamba.

Regarding this Godāna vow, the Chandogas teach that one should perform the ritual touching of water (ablution) day after day; some, however, say it should be performed at the three times of day (triṣavaṇam). 16.16.
Thus ends the sixteenth section in the *Anākula*, a commentary on the *Gṛhyasūtra* composed by Śrī Haradatta.
Now begins the seventh chapter.

The seventeenth section: The bodily consecrations (*dehasaṃskāra*) for a person who is about to be qualified for sacrifices have been explained. And these [consecrations] must be performed in the very house, provided there is no statement to the effect that "having moved out from the *śālīna* [stage of life]. Furthermore, they must be performed in a house constructed according to the rules. Through entry into the house in accordance with the rules, the attainment of desired results—such as longevity, sacrificial merit, and wealth—is secured. Therefore, the rule concerning the construction and entry into the house, which follows the sequence of the recitation of the mantras, is now being explained.

Having leveled a space outside the village that slopes toward the south-west, he sweeps it toward that same direction with a broom made of *pālāśa* or *śamī* wood, reciting the following verse. || 17.1 ||

Now follows the procedure for the consecration of the house (*gṛhasaṃmāna*). This consecration of the house is neither obligatory like all other sacrifices and the like, nor is it occasional like rites for portents or expiations. What then? It is optional (*kāmya*). Therefore, there is no fault in its non-performance; and if it is performed, there is the restriction regarding the northern solstice (*udagayana*) and so forth. In this regard, the site where one intends to build a house is the "house-site" (*agārāvakāśa*); it should slope toward the south and west. That is to say, it should be lower in the direction between the south and the west. The meaning is that the house should be built on such a location. One digs that house-site with a spade, excavating until earth is brought up. Having dug it, one sweeps away that earth toward that same direction with a broom made of *palāśa* or *śamī* wood, using the following verse: "Whatever of the earth is cruel... (MP 2.15.1). By this, one sweeps it from the elevated place down to the lower ground. It is called a "sweeper" (*udūha*) because by means of it, [the earth] is swept away (*udūhyate*). 17.1.
Thus three times. 17.2.
Having thus raised it three times, he fans it upward. 17.2.

Having touched the prepared site with the next verse and having dug the post-holes while circumambulating from left to right, he pours earth inside them with the following two verses and sets up the southern door-post.

Having thus removed the earth from that spot, they prepare it so that it becomes level on all sides. Then he touches the prepared ground with the following verse, "O Earth, be pleasant" (*syonā pṛthivi*, MP 2.15.2). Thereafter, he causes the holes for the pillars to be dug clockwise; the absence of the *na*-suffix is an archaic Vedic usage. The meaning is that starting from the outside and moving inward, they are dug until they meet in the middle. In that regard, since the specifications "clockwise" and "inward" are impossible in the case of the central pillars which support the beams, they apply only to the peripheral ones. Thus, in a house with an eastern door, having dug starting from the hole for the southern door-pillar and proceeding clockwise until the hole for the northern door-pillar, he then places as many middle pillars as there are, beginning from the south and ending toward the north. In the same way, even in a house with a different orientation, one must ensure the clockwise direction and the inward progression as far as possible. Having dug in this manner and having thrown out the loose soil from the holes, he then places a pillar into the hole for the southern door using the two subsequent verses, "Stay right here" (*ihaiva tiṣṭha*, MP 2.15.3).
In the same way, [he should address] the other [wife]. || 17.4 ||

The meaning is that with these very two verses he fixes the other and the northern door-post. Here, "the southern" and "the other" are to be understood as the left and right [posts] for one exiting, not for one entering. 17.4.
Having placed the other [bricks] according to the way they were dug out, he consecrates the bamboo pole being set up with the *utteraṇa-yajus* formula. || 17.5 ||

The two door-posts are set in their holes with the recitation of the mantra; for the others, however, they are set in their holes silently, in the same order as the pits were dug. When all the middle posts have been thus set, the workmen place the beam (vaṃśa) upon them. While the beam is being placed by them, he consecrates it with the following Yajus formula: "By Truth, [O] two posts... By the term *vaṃśa*, the backbone (pṛṣṭhavaṃśa) is understood, because of its primary importance. This is explicit in the Bhāradvāja-śrautasūtra: "With 'By Truth, [O] two posts,' he places the backbone. In that mantra, the dual form *sthūṇau* is a Vedic alteration of gender; the dual number should be understood according to the requirements of the context. 17.5.
It is measured by the subsequent [verses] according to their respective gender. 17.6.

Then, that house, having been measured and prepared, he consecrates with the six subsequent mantras beginning with "Brahma ca te kṣatram" (MP 2.15.6). What does he do? He consecrates; this is the meaning. "According to the characteristic mark" (*yathā-liṅgam*) means that whichever part of the house is indicated by a particular mantra, he consecrates that part while facing toward it. Even when the front pillar is already fixed, the consecration is performed with reference to two [pillars] alone, because the word for the house is in the dual number. In this way, everywhere: the central pillar in the middle of the house is the *sthūpā* (stūpa); it is the backbone. Here, some desire an ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) in the four mantras containing the word "pillar" (*sthūṇā*), such as "May the two pillars protect [you]" (*sthūṇe abhirakṣatu*). [They argue that] on the right side, where it says "Sacrifice and sacrificial fees," one should supply "may the two pillars protect [you]. Others say that even the word "those" (*te*) should be supplied, as in "Sacrifice and those sacrificial fees [protect you]. We say no, because the mantras are not deficient in sense (*sākāṅkṣatva*). For it is impossible to connect the plural endings of "sacrificial fees," "strengths," and "powers" with the singular ending of "may [it] protect. Furthermore, there is no rule for modification (*ūha*), nor is there a recitation like that of the *abhyātāna* formulas, and because there is no repetition at the end—which is seen in all cases of ellipsis. As for the claim of deficiency, that too is not a cause for ellipsis, since deficiency is satisfied by mere proximity (*saṃnidhi*). Or rather, in the case of "Dharma is yours, O King Pillar" and "Prosperity is yours," there is no need for the phrase "may [it] protect," because both are in the nominative case. Thus, "sacrificial fees" and so forth should be understood as being in the nominative. Therefore, there is no deficiency at all. And the understanding of the "pillars" arises from their proximity. 17.6.
Now he states the ritual for entering the house:

Having kindled a fuel-stick made of *pālāśa* or *śamī* wood with the following [verse], having carried the fire forward with the next [verse], and having led it into the house with the next *yajus*, he establishes the fire in the northeastern part of the house with the next [verse]. 17.7.

Now follows the rule for entering [the house]. Even for a house that has been constructed in another manner, this same rule applies to the entry.
