Some say it depends on the northern solstice (*udagayana*) and so forth; others say no. Āśvalāyana says: "He enters the houses containing seed. The mention of "seed" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all household implements. There, about to enter, he kindles a fuel-stick (*idhma*) made of *palāśa*, *śamī*, or *aya* wood in the fire. And here the fuel-stick is defined by its purpose, not by a fixed measure. Having kindled it, he carries that fire-vessel out with the following verse, the five-footed one beginning with "Being carried out" (*uddhriyamāṇa*, MP 2.15.12). If the entry takes place during the day, a verse containing nocturnal characteristics should be used without dispute; likewise, if at night, a verse containing diurnal characteristics should be used without dispute, because there is no division of application [of the verses]. However, those who require the northern solstice do not desire entry at night; the meaning is that the removal of sin committed by day and by night is thereby effected. Nor is there any contradiction, as in the text: "Whatever evil we have done at night, O Waters... He brings that carried-out fire into the house with the following *yajus*: "The houses of Indra, wealthy and protective" (MP 2.15.13). Having brought it in, he establishes that fire in the north-eastern part of the house with the following verse: "The immortal oblation" (MP 2.15.14). Here, the words "of the house" (*agārasya*) and "fire" (*agnim*) need not be stated. Why? Because both are heard in this very sentence. If that is so, then this word "house" is not for the purpose of qualifying a location. What then? It is for the purpose of qualifying the fire—namely, "he establishes the fire of the house. But what is the fire of the house? It is the cooking fire (*pacanāgni*). Therefore, the carrying out of this fire does not come from the *aupāsana* fire. Some say it comes only from a common (*laukika*) fire. Others, however, maintain that because of its connection with the *homa*, this fire is indeed the *aupāsana*. For them, the two words "of the house" and "fire" would be redundant. Furthermore, *homas* are seen even in the cooking fire, as in the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice. Therefore, this is simply the cooking fire. Even if this is so, there is nevertheless a consecration of the location because of the connection with the *homa*. Now, the bringing in and establishment of the *aupāsana* fire and the sacrificial fires (*vaihārika*) occurs at that very time in their respective places. And the wife and others enter at that very time. (17.7)
Therefore, the southern side is the location for the water-vessel. || 17.8 ||
For the fire thus established, the southern site for the water-vessel (udadhāna) should be prepared; that in which water is placed is the *udadhāna*, known as the *maṇika*. || 17.8 ||

Having spread out Darbha grass with its tips pointing in various directions upon that [spot], and having poured rice and barley grains over them with the following verse, he establishes the water-pot there. || 17.9 ||

In that place, having spread out *darbha* grass with its tips pointing in all directions—toward every quarter—he pours rice and barley grains mixed together upon those *darbha* blades while reciting the following verse, "O Lord of Food" (*annapate*) (MP 2.15.15). Then, he establishes a water-vessel in that place, setting it down so that it remains steady. 17.9.
Over that, with the following Yajus formula, he pours four water-pitchers. || 17.10 ||

With the following Yajus mantra, "May we be unharmed" (MP 2.15.16), there is a repetition of the mantra for each jar. In that regard, one may either bring [the water] separately using four jars, or else fill a single jar again, as in the case of the injunction: "having poured out the three ladles.
He consecrates the torn cloth with the following verse. || 17.11 ||

Now, if that water-vessel breaks, he consecrates it with the following verse, "The earth, the earth" (MP 2.15.17). This applies even at a later time when it has cracked, or when another vessel has taken its place. || 17.11 ||

Having performed the rites from the kindling of the fire up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, and having offered the subsequent oblations, he proceeds with the *jaya* and following rites. || 17.12 ||

The four subsequent principal oblations are: “O Vāstoṣpati, recognize us; O Vāstoṣpati, with auspicious [favor]; O Vāstoṣpati, be our protector; O Vāstoṣpati, the dispeller of disease” (MP 2.15.18–21). In this case, the establishment of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is already established by the mention of the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, as in the rule: “As at the *Pārvaṇa*, until the end of the *ājyabhāgas*. What, then, is the purpose of the specific mention of the kindling of the fire and so forth? It is for the sake of restricting the fire—that is, so that the kindling may apply specifically to the fire installed in the house for the purpose of cooking, and not to any other. Otherwise, the oblation would have to be performed only in the *aupāsana* fire for the sake of all *pākayajñas*. The mention of the *jayādi* oblations is for the purpose of prohibiting the *sthālīpāka*. But what is the basis for the application of the *sthālīpāka* here? It is because it is seen in another ritual manual (*kalpa*). How, then, does the mention of the *jayādi* oblations result in the prohibition of the *sthālīpāka*? It is said: first, the prohibition of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is understood, since the text says, “Having offered the subsequent oblations, one proceeds to the *jayādi* and so forth, but not to the *sviṣṭakṛt*. And that [prohibition] applies to *sthālīpākas*. Therefore, by means of the prohibition of the *sviṣṭakṛt*, this results in the very prohibition of the *sthālīpāka*. (17.12)

Having performed the rites up to the final sprinkling, he should sprinkle water three times clockwise around the interior of the house or the dwelling with a water-pot while reciting the following Yajus formula; then he should feed the Brāhmaṇas with cakes, barley meal, and boiled rice. || 17.13 ||
Thus ends the seventeenth section in the Gṛhyapraśna of Āpastamba.

The statement ending with the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*) is for the sake of immediate sequence. Having completed the remainder of the ritual procedure (*tantraśeṣa*), only the sprinkling of the house must be performed; nothing else, such as the *vaiśvadeva* offering and so forth. This is done with the following *yajus*: "Auspicious, auspicious... (MP 2.15.22). It is to be done with a water-pot, not with the hand. Although this is already established by the general rule (*paribhāṣā*), the specific mention of "clockwise" (*pradakṣiṇam*) indicates that this single act of sprinkling is to be performed clockwise three times, continuously and without interruption, using the same water-pot taken up once. By this, it is established that there are three acts of sprinkling, like the threefold winding around with a girdle (*mekhalā*). The mention of "inside" (*antarataḥ*) is so that the sprinkling does not take place outside the house; rather, it should be strictly internal. "House" (*agāra*) means the dwelling; "residence" (*niveśana*) means the sleeping quarters. He should feed an even number of Brahmins with cakes and other foods. The word "iti" has the sense of inclusion (*samuccaya*). (17.13)
Thus ends the seventeenth section in the Anākula commentary on the Gṛhyasūtra composed by Haradatta.
Now begins the eighteenth section.
Now he states the application (*viniyoga*) of the subsequent mantras:

A boy seized by *śvagraha* (the dog-seizure demon), being joined with ascetic fervor (*tapas*), should be covered with a net; while sounding a bronze gong (*kaṃsa*) or a small bell (*kiṅkiṇī*), he should be led into the assembly hall (*sabhā*) by a way other than the door. Having leveled the gaming ground (*adhidevana*) in the middle of the assembly hall and sprinkled it, he should set down the dice, lay the boy down supine upon the dice, and sprinkle him with his joined palms (*añjali*) using curds mixed with salt, reciting the subsequent [mantras] at morning, midday, and evening. 18.1.

There are many child-seizing spirits (*bālagraha*) associated with days, months, years, and so forth. Among them, that by which one seized is made to behave like a dog is the "dog-spirit" (*śvagraha*). Some say that when a boy is seized by this spirit, it does not affect a girl because of the masculine gender used in the reference. The performer of the rite must be endowed with ascetic power (*tapas*); some say he should be the father, others say anyone at all. "Ascetic power" refers to celibacy and the like; the meaning is that he should perform as much as he considers sufficient for success. Having covered [the area] with a net used for catching fish, he takes a bell-metal vessel (*kaṃsa*), which is well known, and a small bell (*kiṅkiṇī*), a specific type of bell; making one of these two resound—that is, causing the sound of one to be heard—by means of another person, he himself takes the boy and leads him into the assembly hall (*sabhā*). This means he enters by a way other than the door, having removed the roof-covering to make a path. What is that place? It is the assembly hall. In its center is the gambling ground where gamblers play; having raised up that spot and sprinkled it with water, he casts the dice (*akṣa*) there. "Dice" refers to the gaming pieces (*śāra*); others say they are *vibhītaka* nuts. Having spread them out widely, he lays the boy down on his back—that is, makes him lie there. Then he should sprinkle him with curds mixed with salt using his joined palms, reciting the subsequent mantras beginning with "Kūrkuraḥ sukūrkuraḥ" and ending with "śvānam icchvād anna puruṣaṃ chat" (MP 2.16.1–11). The sprinkling is done with each mantra. Among those, the first three are *ṛc*s, then two *yajus* formulas: "tat satyam" (MP 2.16.7) and "vigṛhya bāhū" (MP 2.16.5); then five *ṛc*s beginning with "vibhranniṣkanṃ ca" (MP 2.16.6); then one *yajus*, "śvānam" (MP 2.16.11). Thus, there are eleven mantras in total. As long as the ritual action is being completed, the sounding of either the bell-metal vessel or the small bell continues. In this manner, this ritual—from the covering with the net to the final sprinkling—must be performed at the three junctions of the day. || 18.1 ||
It becomes a remedy. || 18.2 ||

“Agada” means free from disease; the meaning is that the cessation of disease is its purpose. What is established by this? It is that if the boy becomes free from disease through medicine alone, then this [rite] need not be performed there. Otherwise, it would be understood that when the boy has this disease, this occasional rite (*naimittika*) must necessarily be performed by the father, just like the *gṛhadāheṣṭi* (the sacrifice for a house fire) and so forth. For those who argue thus, the fault would be that even when the disease is pacified by other means—such as [the rite prescribed for] another woman seized by consumption—this [rite] would still have to be performed. Therefore, this has a different purpose. Thus, when this ritual action has been performed during the three coughs, the boy becomes free from disease. If he does not become so, it must be performed again, joined with ascetic toil (*tapas*). || 18.2 ||

Having consecrated the boy Śaṅkhin with the two [verses] beginning with *uttarābhyām* while engaged in austerity, he should pour water from a water-pot over his head with the following [verse], in the morning, at midday, and in the evening. 18.3.

There is a spirit named Śaṅkha who causes terror among children; one seized by him cries out like a conch shell. Having consecrated the child seized by that spirit with these two subsequent verses, "These two are your adversaries" (*ete te pratidvaśyete*), one should then pour water from a water-pot over his head, sprinkling him with the following verse, "The seer Bodha is awakening" (*ṛṣir bodhaḥ prabodhaḥ*, MP 2.16.14). This consecration and so forth should be performed at the three times of day. 18.3.
It becomes a medicine. || 18.4 ||
Its purpose is as before. 18.4.
Now he explains at what time and by what ritual procedure the undertaking of the snake-offering (sarpabali) is to be performed.
On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, when the sun has set, there is an offering of cooked food (sthālīpāka).

Now, the ritual known as the *sarpabali* (serpent-offering), which is to be performed annually, is taught. Its commencement is on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, and its conclusion is on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa. At its beginning, on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, when the sun has set, there is an offering of cooked rice (*sthālīpāka*). Even in the absence of the conjunction with the [specific] lunar mansion, the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa is called "Śrāvaṇī" by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Regarding this, there are two verses: [Verse 1] [Verse 2]
Whichever new moon (darśa) occurs while the sun is situated in Aries and the subsequent signs,
those ending with it are recorded as the twelve lunar months beginning with Caitra.

Among those, whichever day is the full moon is traditionally designated as Caitrī and so forth; the determination [of its specific name] is based on its occasional conjunction with a particular lunar mansion (nakṣatra). Thus it is said.

Having offered the evening oblation there, one undertakes the *sthālīpāka* rite; it has been stated that other [rites] follow the *pārvaṇa* model, and specifically the full-moon sacrifice on the full moon day. Having set aside rice or barley intended for the full moon of the month of Śrāvaṇa, and having performed the rites up to the final sprinkling of clarified butter (*abhighāraṇa*), one proceeds with the kindling of the fire and so forth, using pairs of implements, placing the vessels face down, together with *kiṃśuka* flowers and fuel-sticks made of *āragvadha* wood. (18.5)

As at the Pārvaṇa [śrāddha], after the offering of the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), he makes an oblation from the cooked mess of rice (sthālīpāka) and then offers kiṃśuka flowers with his joined palms (añjali), reciting each of the subsequent mantras one by one. || 18.6 ||

It is said that "everything is like the *pārvaṇa*": one offers from the *sthālīpāka* itself according to the *pārvaṇa* rite, but not with *kiṃśuka* flowers. Therefore, the rule for cutting portions (*avadāna*) does not apply to them. Nor is there a cutting of portions for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering from them. The *samidhs* are explained by means of the *kiṃśukas*. The mention of the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings is for the purpose of establishing the ritual framework (*tantra*). The oblation from the *sthālīpāka* is performed with the words, "To the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, svāhā! Then, with the three subsequent mantras beginning with "The mosquito has been eaten" (MP 2.16.15). *Kiṃśukas* are the flowers of the *palāśa* tree; others say they are the flowers of thorny *palāśas*. It is stated "with each mantra" so that there may be a multiplicity of *kiṃśuka* flowers for each mantra. Otherwise, an oblation of only a single *kiṃśuka* would follow, as is the case with the *samidhs*. (18.6)
With the following three verses, he offers fuel-sticks made of *āragvadha* wood. || 18.7 ||

The *āragvadha* is the *rājavṛkṣa*, which has golden-colored flowers and fruits the size of a cubit (*aratni*). With the three subsequent *ṛc*s beginning with “O Indra, slay the biting one” (*indra jahi dandaśūkam*), he places fuel sticks upon the fire or offers oblations; in every case, the mantras end with the utterance of *svāhā*. (18.7)
The subsequent oblations of clarified butter. || 18.8 ||

He offers four subsequent oblations of clarified butter: [the verse] "That is the truth which [is yours] on the new moon," (MP 2.17.4), and three [verses] beginning with "Homage be to the serpents" (MP 2.17.5). || 18.8 ||
One undertakes [the rites] beginning with victory. || 18.9 ||

Having thus offered these eleven principal oblations (*pradhānāhuti*) and having offered the *sauviṣṭakṛta* oblation from the very *sthālīpāka*, one then proceeds with the *jaya* and subsequent rites. This statement is intended to make known the primacy (*prādhānya*) of the oblations beginning with the *kiṃśuka* flowers; otherwise, because it is prescribed that "on the full moon day, when the sun has set, [one offers] the *sthālīpāka*" (ĀśGṛ 2.1.1), and because the name of its deity is given as "the Full Moon" (*paurṇamāsī*), and because it is a primary ritual act (*arthakarmaka*), the primacy of the *kiṃśuka* flowers would not be understood. Consequently, having performed everything up to the secondary offerings (*upahoma*) as in the case of the *Pārvaṇa* rite, the offering of the *kiṃśuka* flowers and so forth would follow thereafter. 18.9.

Having performed the rites up to the final sprinkling, remaining silent and taking the ritual materials, he goes out toward the east or the north; having prepared a sacrificial mound there and drawn three lines each toward the east and the north, and having poured water over them, he scatters groats upon them with the following verse.

The statement ending with the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*) is for the purpose of indicating immediate sequence (*ānantarya*). What is established by this? It is that the departure (*upaniṣkramaṇa*) occurs only at the end of the sprinkling and nothing else. By this, the displacement (*utkarṣa*) of such rules as "one should feed a Brāhmaṇa with ghee" (ĀpGṛ 7.15) is established. Restrained in speech (*vāgyataḥ*), meaning not making noise, [he prepares] the following materials: parched grains (*dhānāḥ*), fried grains (*lājāḥ*), collyrium and ointment, *sthagara* and *uśīra*, and a vessel of water. A smeared portion of ground is the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). Because of the word "having prepared" (*kalpayitvā*), the preparation is to be done by himself; there is no acceptance of what has been prepared by others. Because of the word "there" (*tatra*), the place for the offering (*bali*) is in the middle of the mound. And there is a verse:
One should first draw the eastward lines, ending toward the north and beginning from the south;
then one should draw the northward lines, ending toward the east and beginning from the west.

Others, however, desire that the commencement [of the lines] be from the south of the eastern ones. (The eastern ones are those extending eastward; likewise, the northern ones are those extending northward, because the sequence is intended to be significant. First the eastern ones, then the northern ones. This act called "drawing the lines" is one, as it is stated: "The commencement is either in the east or in the north, and the conclusion is likewise" (ĀpGṛ 1.5–6). In this case, since a commencement in the east is impossible, there is a commencement in the north and a conclusion in the east. By this, the drawing of the lines mentioned in the rule "wherever the fire may be" (ĀpDh 2.1.13) is explained. Having thus drawn the lines, he pours water near them; he pours water near them for all the divine hosts, just as one gives the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) to the ancestors. Then, upon those lines, with the following verse, "Homage be to the serpents who are terrestrial... (MP 2.17.8), he scatters groats (*saktu*) with his hand or with a ladle, as seen in the *Āśvalāyana* school. The use of the plural "upon those" (*tāsu*) is for the purpose that the offering (*bali*) may pervade all those lines. 18.10.
Silently [he offers] sampuṣka, parched grains, fried grain, collyrium, ointment, sthagara, and uśīra. || 18.11 ||

He pours into them these six substances: *saṃpuṣkā*, unbroken and undivided rice grains (*akṣata*), *sthagara*, and *uśīra*—these being the fragrant materials. The word "iti" has the sense of a conjunction (meaning "and"). Since this implies that the pouring in [of the substances] everywhere would otherwise be performed with the preceding mantra alone, the phrase "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*) serves as a prohibition of the mantra. 18.11.

Having worshipped with the following [verses] and having sprinkled water around, he should go back silently without looking behind him; then, having sprinkled water three times clockwise—internally—around the house or the dwelling with a water-pot while reciting the two verses beginning with "O white-footed one," he should feed the Brāhmaṇas. 18.12.
Thus ends the eighteenth section in the Gṛhyapraśna of Āpastamba.

In this very manner, having offered this *bali* with seven substances, he then worships that *bali*-deity with the eighteen subsequent mantras beginning with “*takṣaka veśāleya*” (MP 2.17.9). The phrase “I have brought this *bali* for them” (*tebhya imaṃ balim ahārṣam*) is a modification of the final quarter-verse of the preceding mantra, not a separate mantra. As [the author] will state: “The modification of the *bali*-mantra” (ĀpGṛ 19.4). Having thus worshipped, he sprinkles water all around; since the *bali* that was scattered is the subject under discussion. Then, without looking back—that is, not looking behind him—he returns silently and with speech restrained. Having returned, and having sprinkled water inside the house or the dwelling with a water-pot while reciting these two verses beginning with “*apaśveta padā*” (MP 2.17.26), he should feed Brahmins to the number of a *yuga* (four) with the remains of the *sthālīpāka* and other offerings. 18.12.
Thus ends the eighteenth section in the *Anākula*, a commentary on the *Gṛhya-sūtra* composed by Śrī Haradatta.
Now begins the nineteenth section.
They feed parched grains to the boys. 19.1.
They feed the grains remaining from the *bali* offering to those boys who are capable of eating; the girls also partake of the food, as indicated by the use of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*). 19.1.
Thus, from this point forward, until the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, he should offer this oblation of whatever food is available or of barley meal.

Regarding this *baliharaṇa* (food offering), beginning with "the one who has restrained his speech, having taken the materials... and ending with "...silently" (ĀpGṛ 18.10–12): after this rite, until the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, every four months, one must perform [this] daily for as much food as is fit to eat, or specifically for groats (*saktu*). Whatever food is prepared in the house for the purpose of eating is what is meant by "fit to eat. However, the sprinkling around the house and so forth belongs only to the remainder of the *sthālīpāka* (cooked sacrificial rice), not to the *bali*. Therefore, this [daily offering] is prescribed here. Even though items such as collyrium, intended for adornment, are not edible, nevertheless, because there is an identical injunction for all of them—such as "he pours out the groats with the following verse; silently, the roasted grains (*dhānā*) with husks"—and because they are mentioned equally in the mantra, "I shall offer this *bali* to them," all seven substances of the *bali* are included. This substitution applies to all of them, and not merely to the first three. But it does not apply to water, because the injunction is different. Regarding the words "having poured down and having sprinkled": the word "thus" (*evam*) is for the purpose of prescribing the time; just as the *baliharaṇa* takes place at sunset here, so too from now on it must be performed at sunset. The word "this" (*etam*), however, is for the purpose of prescribing the ritual characteristics; that is, "this *bali* has these same characteristics. Nor is the accomplishment of both purposes achieved by either one alone. For if the word "thus" were to serve both purposes, it would follow that the *pārvaṇa* (full-moon sacrifice) would take place at night. How? Because the *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Agni arises at night, and likewise, by the rule "from now on" (ĀpGṛ 7.19), the *pārvaṇa* [would apply]. Similarly, if the word "this" were to serve both purposes, then the honoring (*apaciti*) would take place at night, according to the rule "this should be done for those who have been present for a year"; for the honoring arises at night during the *samāvartana* (return home). Therefore, both words must be stated for both purposes. Thus, for the time being, the *baliharaṇa* occurs once at night.
Another says: "The offering of the bali is for both times. How so? Because of the statement, "whatever is fit to be eaten," [it applies] to whatever [is offered].

The meaning of this is indeed that whenever food is prepared for the purpose of eating, [the Vaiśvadeva] must be performed for each such instance, because eating occurs at two times, according to the statement "eating at the two times. Consequently, just as the Vaiśvadeva—which consists of oblations and offerings (*balis*) of whatever is to be eaten by the householder—is performed at both times, so too is this [rite]. This is clear from the *Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra*: "He should offer the *bali* with the words 'Svāhā to the serpents and the divine folk' in the evening and in the morning, until the *pratyavarohaṇa*" (ĀśGṛ 2.1.14). In this view, the word *evam* (so) is for the sake of what follows: so that it may not be understood that there is an option regarding the materials for this first *baliharaṇa*, as indicated by the statement "from here onwards" (ĀpGṛ 7.19). The phrase "until the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa" is an instruction regarding the time of conclusion for the *baliharaṇa*. If this is so, then this [present rule] is unnecessary, since he will state later, "At this point he discontinues it" (ĀpGṛ 19.5). We shall explain its purpose in that very place. 19.2.
On the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, after sunset, there is an offering of cooked food (sthālīpāka).

This has been explained by the statement, "on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa. The word *evam* (thus) also carries over here. Just as this rite was performed on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, so too [is it performed] on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa. Consequently, the entire ritual procedure (*kalpa*), beginning with "like the *Pārvaṇa*, up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings" (ĀpGṛ 22.1) and ending with "they cause the boys to eat the parched grains" (ĀpGṛ 19.1), applies here. The only difference is that for the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, there is an oblation of the *sthālīpāka* with the mantra: "To the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, svāhā! The mention of "full moon day" again, even though "on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa" was already established, is for the purpose of making known that the term "full moon day" does not carry over into this particular section. Therefore, in the preceding sūtra, the phrase "up to the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa" is not taken as a limit for the rite itself. What was raised there—that time is not prescribed by this sūtra—is thus resolved. If the particle *ā* were used in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*), then the offering of the *bali* of whatever is fit for eating would not apply to the day of the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa. If, however, it were used in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*), then the offering would apply only to whatever is fit for eating after sunset. Yet, it is desired that the *bali* offering of seven substances be made at sunset when the *sthālīpāka* rite is completed, and also the offering of whatever is fit for eating during the day. Therefore, the specific qualification "on the full moon day" is added so that there may be a designation of the rite in the previous case, and not merely a designation of time. Thus, what was stated—that the offering of the *bali* occurs at both times because of the mention of "whatever is fit for eating"—remains established. By saying "at sunset," it is meant that it should not be restricted to the daytime alone. It has been stated that the word *evam* lacks the capacity to effect both the transfer of ritual details (*dharma*) and the prescription of time simultaneously. (19.3)
"I have taken" is the modification of the *bali* mantra. || 19.4 ||

The modification (*sannāma*) is the substitution of "I shall take" (*hariṣyāmi*) with "I have taken" (*ahārṣam*). Although this modification is recited within that very mantra, if this instruction did not exist, there would be no separate application for the fourth quarter of the *baliharaṇa* mantra; consequently, it would be understood as consisting of four quarters. Therefore, the rule for modification is commenced. That [mantra] consists of only three quarters; this final quarter is recited as the modification of its third quarter, and its time of application is not prior to that.

Furthermore, this entire rite up to the eating of the grains is designated by the term *sthālīpāka*; this is what is being shown here. The purpose for the offering of the *bali* will be explained in the subsequent sūtra. 19.4.
He releases it from him. || 19.5 ||

In this rite designated as *mārgaśīrṣa*, he offers this oblation (*bali*). By the word "thus" (*evam*), the entire procedure prescribed for the *śrāvaṇī* is extended [to this rite]; consequently, the offering of the oblation (*baliharaṇa*) is obtained as a subsidiary part of this *sthālīpāka* as well. In that case, one might assume "on the *śrāvaṇī*" to be the limit. Therefore, the rule is simply "I have taken [the remainder] of the *mārgaśīrṣa*. This [statement] is for the purpose of prohibiting the remainder of the oblation. However, the phrase "until the *mārgaśīrṣī*" is for the purpose of prescribing the disposal of the remainder of the oblation from the *śrāvaṇa*. (19.5)
He states the application of the subsequent Yajus formula for that ritual act: "The Āgrayaṇa sacrifice for one who has not established the sacred fires. (19.6)

The root *eti* here has the sense of "eating. That in which there is first (*agre*) an eating (*ayana*) is the *āgrayaṇa*. Although the form would have been *agrāyaṇa*, the lengthening of the vowel is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). That ritual will now be described. In this context, the mention of one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) is for the purpose of prohibiting the combination of the *āgrayaṇa* with the Śrauta *āgrayaṇa* for one who has established the fires and maintains the domestic fire (*aupāsana*). Consequently, a combination does take place in the case of the *Pārvaṇa* and other rites. In that regard, if the Smārta rite is performed, there is prosperity; if it is not performed, there is no transgression. By the name *āgrayaṇa*, the characteristics of the Śrauta *āgrayaṇa* are extended [to this rite], according to the rule: "One who has established the fires shall not eat of the new grain until he has performed the *āgrayaṇa*" (ĀpŚr 6.29.2). Furthermore, it is stated: "In the rainy season, one should sacrifice with *śyāmāka* grains; in autumn, with rice (*vrīhi*); in spring, with barley (*yava*); and according to the season, with bamboo-grains (*veṇuyava*)."

Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* of new grain and offered oblations to the deities of the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, with *Sviṣṭakṛt* as the fourth, he should fill his mouth with rice grains, swallow them, sip water for purification, form a ball of the cooked rice, and fix it upon the roof-peak of the house with the following *Yajus* formula. (19.7)

Having cooked new rice or barley on the *aupāsana* fire, and once it is established, having sprinkled it with clarified butter, having added fuel to the fire, having strewn grass around it, and having silently sprinkled water all around, he cleans the *durvī* (the ladle-handle). He offers four oblations from the *sthālīpāka*, taking portions as required, to the deities of the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, with the *Sviṣṭakṛt* as the fourth: "To Indra and Agni, Svāhā! or "To Agni and Indra"; then to the Viśvedevas; then to Heaven and Earth; and to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. The sprinkling of water is as before. This much only is the ritual, and nothing else, because there is no [other] *parvan*. Some perform everything. Then he fills his mouth with rice grains. Here the word "rice" (*taṇḍula*) refers to the grains or fragments of the boiled rice, as in the expression "rice grains on the stirring-spoon. Therefore, the filling is done by taking a portion from the remainder of the sacrificial offering. Others, however, desire plain rice grains. Having chewed them and swallowed them, and having sipped water, he then rolls the ball of boiled rice, preparing it with effort. Having rolled it so that it does not crumble when being thrust into the *stūpa*, he should thrust it into the *agāra-stūpa* (the roof-beam of the house) with the *yajus* formula "Thou art the Supreme," so that it falls into the *stūpa*. The *stūpa* is the backbone (the ridge-pole). "Viddhet" is a corruption, or it is a Vedic form. Since the term *āgrayaṇa* itself establishes this, the mention of "new" is so that for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), there may be only the *sthālīpāka* of new grain. This is so that other rituals seen in the *Śrauta* texts do not apply here. The mention of the *Sviṣṭakṛt* as the fourth is for the purpose of excluding *Soma*; therefore, the *āgrayaṇa* of *śyāmāka* millet and bamboo-barley is also performed by one who has not maintained the sacred fires. 19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.7.19.
The descent [from the high bed] at the beginning of the winter season. || 19.8 ||

The ritual known as *hemantapratyavarohaṇa* (the descent for winter) is an obligatory rite to be performed every year; that is now taught: when winter has arrived, one abandons the bed and sleeps on a layer of straw. The "descent for winter" (*hemantapratyavarohaṇa*) is the act of descending from the bed toward the winter season; this is to be performed with the following Yajus formula: “Winter has descended upon us” (MP 2.18.2). What, then, is its time? That night on which winter begins and autumn ceases is its time.

Another says: "The Pratyavarohaṇa takes place on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, after the sun has set and following the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice, because this is well-known for all [rites]. Others maintain that the phrase "on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa" should be carried over [from the previous rule].

Having descended from that [chariot], they lie down—that is, they sleep—on a bed prepared with nine fresh *palāśa* leaves spread out, using the five subsequent mantras beginning with "In the dominion" (*prati kṣatre*, MP 2.18.3), with their right sides downward, placing their right sides underneath. This includes the householder, his dependents such as sons and others, and unmarried maidens. This is a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) for sleeping, which is otherwise constant: that the act of lying down intended for sleep must be performed on this very night. The mantra for descending [from the chariot] is also to be recited at that same time. 19.8.
Having descended with the subsequent Yajus formula, they lie down on new straw mats on their right sides with the following [verses]. 19.9.

Among those lying down, he who is the father lies on the right side, and she who is the mother lies on the left. Their relative positions as right and left are mutually dependent; Āśvalāyana states: "Together with his attendants, [the deceased] should lie with his head to the east and facing north" (ĀśGṛ 2.3.6), and also: "Those who know the mantras should mutter the mantras" (ĀśGṛ 2.3.9). || 19.9 ||
Furthermore, by means of two verses, he specifies the very manner of lying down:
"The father on the right, the mother on the left; in this way for the remaining [sons], each elder is immediately after the next elder. (19.10)

Of the remaining ministers, whichever prince or princess is the eldest sits to the right of the father; the next in order sits to the left of the mother. The third sits to the right of the first, the fourth to the left of the second, and so forth. Others maintain that they should sit only to the left of the mother, according to seniority. All should have their heads toward the east and face the north, and those who know the mantras should mutter them. The mention of "immediately following" is for the purpose of indicating close proximity. (19.10)
Having recited the two [verses] beginning with "saṃhāya," they touch the earth. || 19.11 ||

Having thus entered [the hut], having slept for a short while, and having risen from the bed, he is seen by them as they sit down. For it is said: "He who lies down is Kali; but he who rises is Dvāpara" (AitBr 7.15). Having risen and sipped water, they should touch the earth with the two subsequent verses, namely "O Earth, be pleasant... (MP 2.18.8) and "Thus indeed... (MP 2.18.9). || 19.11 ||
In this manner, the laying down [of the child] and so forth is performed three times. || 19.12 ||

The meaning is that the entering [of the fire], the gathering [of the embers], and the touching [of the fire] should be performed three times with the recitation of mantras; however, the descent [of the fire] is done only once. Āśvalāyana states: "When the sun has risen, having murmured the hymns to Sūrya and the *svastyayana* prayers, having prepared food, having fed the Brāhmaṇas, and having caused them to pronounce a *svastyayana* blessing" (ĀśGṛ 4.6.18). 19.12.

Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* for Īśāna and one for Kṣetrapati, and having gone out toward the east or the north and prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), he performs the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire. (19.13)

Now the *pākayajña* known as the *Īśānabali*, which is commonly called the *Śūlagava*, will be described. Although the immolation of a cow is enjoined in other scriptures, for us there is only the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice-offering), because of the rule that "this much constitutes the place of the cow's immolation. Furthermore, this is a permanent (*nitya*) refinement of the person, not optional (*kāmya*) or occasional (*naimittika*), since no desire or specific occasion is mentioned. It is to be performed only once, because there is no connection with a [recurring] time; for repetition occurs only when there is a connection with a recurring time, due to the repeated association with that time. What, then, is its time? Other scriptures state it is either in autumn or spring, and it should be performed under the constellation Ārdrā. For us, there is also the rule of the northern solstice (*udagayana*). Among these, the primary time for it is when the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Phālguna coincides with the constellation Ārdrā. Being about to sacrifice with that, he cooks a *sthālīpāka* in the domestic fire (*aupāsana*): one portion intended for the god Īśāna, and another for Kṣetrapati. Having gone out from the village toward the east or the north together with those [portions], and having reached the place where he intends to sacrifice, he prepares a single sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) sufficient for the place of sacrifice and the two shrines. In the eastern half of that, having scraped out the hearth for the fire and established the fire, he proceeds with the ritual procedure beginning with the kindling. The vessels are in pairs, as are the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). 19.13.
Having constructed two huts to the west of the fire. || 19.14 ||
Thus ends the nineteenth section in the *Gṛhyapraśna* of Āpastamba.

Then, to the west of the fire, he constructs two huts, one for the god and one for the goddess, with doors facing either west or east. They are situated south and north, ending toward the north. Having fashioned images of the god and the goddess within them— 19.14.
Thus ends the nineteenth section in the Anākula, a commentary on the Gṛhyasūtra composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
Now begins the twentieth section:
With the following [verse], he invokes Īśāna in the southern [direction]. 20.1.

Having fashioned an image of Jayanta in the very sky in the center, he invokes Īśāna in the south with the subsequent ṛc, namely, "ā tvā vahantu" (MP 2.18.10). Since the laying of the fire and so forth has already been mentioned, and since the principal oblations will be described later, only the construction of the hut takes place at the conclusion of the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga). || 20.1 ||
With worldly speech, [he worships] Mīḍhuṣī in the northern [direction]. || 20.2 ||
Jayanta in the center. || 20.3 ||

With worldly speech, he invokes the goddess Mīḍhuṣī in the north. In the center, he invokes Jayanta. With worldly speech—either saying "Come, Jayanta" or "I invoke Jayanta. Jayanta is Skanda. If the phrase "with worldly speech" were not stated, the invocation would result in being performed with the preceding mantra. 20.2–3.

Having offered water as it was brought, having prepared three portions of cooked rice, having brought fire near, and having sprinkled [the guest] with water using the subsequent [mantras], he should offer oblations from the portions of rice according to their respective [mantras] using the subsequent [mantras]; then, having taken portions from all [the portions], he should offer to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the subsequent Yajus formula. 20.4.

With whatever sound, in whatever places, and in whatever order the invocation has been prescribed, he offers the *arghya* (water for honor) belonging to those respective deities. These are prepared in separate vessels and, because they are *arghya*, are joined with flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). He says: "O Īśāna, this is your *arghya*; O Jayanta, this is your *arghya*. Then, having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, he takes portions from the *sthālīpāka* (cooked sacrificial rice) and prepares three portions of boiled rice in three vessels: for the Goddess, for Skanda, and for the God, both for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*) and for the offering (*upahāra*). In the pot itself, he leaves a large remainder of rice for the feeding of the Brahmins. Then, having brought those portions of rice near the fire, he establishes the fires upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) to the west, to the north, and in the middle, following the direction of the water (*apaga*). Here, the sprinkling of clarified butter (*abhighāraṇa*) is performed over the established fires. Then, with the three subsequent mantras, he causes the three portions of rice to be touched according to the order of invocation; he effects the relationship between each deity and its portion. He touches them with the subsequent mantras beginning with "Let the Bountiful One touch" (*upaspṛśatu mīḍhvān*). He touches them according to the respective deity, just as one would say, "This is for Agni," in the case of the portion belonging to Agni. Having thus caused them to be touched, he then performs the principal oblations (*pradhānāhuti*) with seventeen subsequent mantras, offering from each respective portion of rice according to the deity whose ownership was indicated by the touching. The meaning is that he offers from whichever rice was marked by the touching as belonging to whichever deity. Among these, he offers from the rice for the God with the eight [mantras] beginning with "To the God Bhava" (MP 2.18.14); from the rice for Mīḍhuṣī with the eight [mantras] beginning with "To the wife of the God Bhava, Svāhā" (MP 2.18.22); and from [the rice] for Jayanta with "To Jayanta, Svāhā" (M 2.18.30). Having thus offered the principal oblations, he then takes portions from all [the portions] together and worships Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the subsequent Yajus formula: "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, well-offered" (MP 2.18.31). It is said "taking portions from all together" so that there may not be a separate Sviṣṭakṛt offering from each individual portion of rice.

Although this [rite] beginning with the *upasthāna* (reverential salutation) is stated immediately after the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, nevertheless, because of the instruction heard in the text, "He offers the *jaya* oblations and so forth," the *jaya* and subsequent offerings take place immediately after the principal oblations (*pradhānahoma*), while the *upasthāna* and following rites occur at the end of the *pariṣecana* (sprinkling). 20.4.
Having worshipped with the subsequent *yajus* formula, he gives two leaves each for the cooked rice portions using the following [mantras], ten to the divine armies and ten to the higher ones. 20.5.

With the subsequent *yajus* verse, “*svasti naḥ pūrṇamukhaḥ*,” he performs the worship (*upasthāna*) of Mahādeva, because that deity is the primary focus of the rite. The term “*pūrṇamukhaḥ*” is also a designation for him alone; he is “full-faced” (*pūrṇamukhaḥ*) because he is filled (*pūrṇa*) with oblations (*āhutibhiḥ*). Having performed the worship, he then offers the cooked rice (*odana*) upon leaves (*parṇa*) to the deities indicated by the mantras, using the eighteen subsequent mantras beginning with “*gṛhapyupa spṛśa*. Among these, he first gives two leaves for each mantra during the first seven verses. By saying “to the ten divine armies” (*daśadevasenābhyaḥ*) in the eighth verse, he indicates the deities perceived in the mantra. In this context, “*gṛhapa*” is considered a name for Mahādeva, meaning “the protector of the house. There is also another mantra: “*namo rudrāya vāstoṣpataye*. Therefore, with this [mantra], two leaves are given to the god from his very rice. *Gṛhapī* is the goddess; therefore, with this mantra, it should be given to the goddess from her own rice. “*Ghoṣiṇī*” and the others are all the hosts who are the attendants of the god; to them also, near the temple (*devakuṭī*), two leaves each are given from his very rice. The “divine armies” (*devasenāḥ*) are the hosts of spirits (*bhūtagaṇāḥ*); to them also, as in the case of the serpent-hosts, ten leaves are given with the subsequent mantra, “*yā ākhyātā*,” which refers to the subsequent deities. To those, ten leaves are given with that same mantra from the god’s very rice. 20.5.

As before, with the subsequent [mantras]. (20.6) With the four subsequent mantras beginning with “O Dvārāpa, touch! (MP 2.18.42), leaves are to be offered as before—meaning two for each individual mantra. Here, Dvārāpa is the male gatekeeper; Dvārāpī is the female gatekeeper. The Abhyāsariṇas are also the attendants of the goddess. “O thou who carriest a quiver” (niṣaṅgin) is the name of Jayanta. To them, offerings of cooked rice are to be given there, each according to their respective share. (20.6)
Having formed a ball of rice and placed it in a leaf-cup, he hangs it on a tree with the subsequent Yajus formula. || 20.7 ||

Then, having taken a ball of that same boiled rice, having rolled it firmly with both hands, and having placed it in a fold made of sewn leaves, he puts it in a sling and hangs it upon a tree with the following Yajus formula: "Homage to the one who bears a quiver, to the one who possesses a bow-case" (MP 2.18.46). || 20.7 ||
In this case, one should recite the Rudra hymns. || 20.8 ||

At this time, one should mutter the eleven sections beginning with "Homage to you, O Rudra, to your wrath" (*namas te rudra manyave*). The meaning is that one should worship the deity with these very [sections]. (In that regard, the phrase "of them, [the range is] a thousand yojanas" (*teṣāṃ sahasrayojanam*) is to be supplied to the first ten verses of the final section; at the end, the three mantras—"Homage to the Rudras who are on earth, whose arrows are food," "Homage to the Rudras who are in the intermediate space, whose arrows are the wind," and "Homage to the Rudras who are in heaven, whose arrows are rain"—are to be supplied everywhere. || 20.8 ||
Or rather, the first and the last [of the two].
Alternatively, the worship should be performed with only the first and the last sections (anuvākas). 20.9.
Now, he states what is to be done at the very time of the principal oblation: he stations the cows on both sides of this fire so that the smoke may reach them. 20.10.

He stations his own cows around this Agni while it is being offered; in stationing them thus, the smoke may reach those cows. "In the direction of the wind" means nearby. And at the time of the principal oblation, it is said, "this very one," referring to "this Agni while it is being offered. 20.10.
He sprinkles them with perfumes and a handful of darbha grass, beginning first with the bull.

He sprinkles it with fragrant substances such as sandalwood and the like, using a handful of *darbha* grass, not with his hand. "A handful of the teacher" (*gurumuṣṭi*) is the same as "*grumuṣṭi*"; the elision of the vowel *u* is a Vedic archaism. The meaning is: with a handful of *darbha* grass whose tips are intact. Regarding that, the statement concerning the time of the *homa* indicates that the sprinkling takes place at that same time. He sprinkles first that very bull (*vṛṣāṇam*). Even if it does not stand there at the beginning, nevertheless, because it is a subordinate element (*aṅga*), the sprinkling belongs to it alone; the time for that purpose is indeed at the beginning. 20.11.
On a path used by cattle, where there is no fire, one should sacrifice to the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati).

Now follows the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Kṣetrapati: "In every path (*marge mārge*)," [where] the short vowel is used according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). It is performed on the ground itself, not in the fire; for since the sacrifice is prescribed to be performed on the path when some cow among those departing [from the herd] has gone there, this [rule] serves as a prohibition against using the fire. (20.12)
The invocation is like that of Īśāna. 20.13.

The invocation of that Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati) should be performed as with Īśāna; the meaning is that it is done with this verse: "ā tvā vahantu" (MP 2.18.10). Furthermore, the word *śarva* should also be understood as a synonym for him. || 20.13 ||
He places the naming formula upon four or seven leaves. 20.14.

Having invoked [the deity] and offered the *arghya* water, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, and having set down the *sthālīpāka* (cooked sacrificial rice) and poured clarified butter over it, he places four or seven leaves near the deity. Having assigned the name [of the deceased] by means of the formula "namādeśam," he offers a ball of cooked rice from the *sthālīpāka* upon those leaves. Since there is a rule that the mantras for offering the leaves in the preceding [rites] must end with the word *svāhā*, here too the offering of the leaf is made with the formula: "To the Lord of the Field, svāhā! This indeed constitutes his sacrifice. 20.14.
One should quickly sacrifice to the god Pāka. || 20.15 ||
The meaning is: just as a child is subject to digestion, so too this deity is prone to moving away; therefore, one should sacrifice quickly. || 20.15 ||
He worships with the two following [verses]. || 20.16 ||
With the next two [verses], namely the two beginning with "By the Lord of the Field, we... (RV 2.18.47). || 20.16 ||

By the passage beginning with “having formed a ball of boiled rice,” the disposal of the remnants of the oblation and the sacrificial offering has been stated. Now he describes the disposal of the remnant of the *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Īśāna:
“He should feed the Brāhmaṇas with the *sthālīpāka*. (20.17)
The statement "with that [oblation] mixed with ghee" is made for the purpose of prescribing plurality, since it is already established by the extension of the rules from the *pārvaṇa* rite. 20.17.
He states the ritual procedure for the offering to Kṣetrapati:
"Those who are blood relations consume the portion belonging to Kṣetrapati. (20.18)

"Sons and brothers" refers to those who share the same navel and the same womb; although the term "sanābhayaḥ" (those sharing the same navel) would have sufficed, the explicit statement "ye bhavanti" (who are) is intended to include other relatives such as daughters' sons and the like for the purpose of receiving gifts. 20.18.
Just as may be their family custom. || 20.19 ||
Thus ends the twentieth section and the seventh chapter in the *Gṛhyapraśna* of Āpastamba.

Regarding these [ceremonies], the consumption [of the food] may be according to the family custom of those born into the sacrificer’s lineage—whether it be the consumption by the sons alone, or the consumption by all those born into one's own lineage, or even the consumption by maternal cousins and others. 20.19.
Thus ends the twentieth section and the seventh chapter in the *Anākula* commentary on the *Gṛhyasūtra* composed by Haradatta Miśra.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
The twenty-first section:

Furthermore, another *pākayajña* is taught—a rite for the ancestors known as the *māsi-śrāddha*, which is to be offered to three persons and serves as the archetype for the *aṣṭakā* and other such rites.
The times for the *māsi-śrāddha* are those occurring in the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*), according to the traditional instruction. 21.1.

The ancestral rite called *māsi-śrāddha* is to be performed month after month. Regarding this, those specific times within the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) that are established in the rules of customary practice (*sāmayācārika*), such as "when performed on the first day" (ĀpDh 2.16.8) and so forth, and "the afternoon of the dark fortnight is better" (ĀpŚr 2.16.4), all these are to be understood month after month exactly as they were taught there, according to the instruction. Even though those specific details are already established by that very statement, this declaration is made for the purpose of indicating that the procedural injunction (*prayoga-vidhāna*) for this rite is set forth hereafter. Otherwise, one might wonder in which rite the rule regarding "pure persons who know the mantras" and so forth is prescribed. If that were the case, then let this very [statement] serve as the introductory heading (*adhikāra*) for the *māsi-śrāddha*. Therefore, its purpose is this: so that the festival times (*parva-kāla*) may occur according to the instruction by virtue of the dark fortnight, regardless of the measurement of the month; thus, for one who has not performed the *śrāddha* on the fifteenth day of the first fortnight, the performance takes place on all dates, beginning with the first, of the subsequent fortnight for one who desires the respective results. 21.1.
He should feed those who are pure, learned in the mantras, unrelated by birth, lineage, or mantra, an odd number, at least three, without regard for material gain. 21.2.

"Pure, clean, possessing the sacred mantras, and perfected in learning and study"—since this is already established by the rule, "One should feed those who are pure and possess the mantras at all rites" (ĀpDh 2.15.11), the repetition here is for the sake of emphasis. "Brāhmaṇas" refers to those related by birth, such as fathers-in-law and maternal uncles; those related by lineage, namely those of the same *gotra*; and those related by the mantras, such as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), teachers (*ācārya*), and pupils (*antevāsin*). He will state later that one may feed others when there is a deficiency in these qualities. The term "uneven numbers" is intended to prohibit even numbers. "At least three" is intended to prohibit a single person. Āśvalāyana says: "But never one for all; however, one may at will [feed one] in the case of no food being available" (ĀśGṛ 4.7.3). This means that in the case of an *āmaśrāddha* (a rite with raw food) or during a famine, one may feed even a single person in the family. Although the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) is seen to be performed for women as well, nevertheless, the feeding of Brāhmaṇas here does not extend to them, because the *homa* (oblation) and the touching of the food are not prescribed for them, and because it would contradict the rule regarding the use of uneven numbers. Therefore, the feeding of Brāhmaṇas is for the three ancestors—father, grandfather, and great-grandfather alone. For each one, there should be three or five, as is seen in other ritual manuals (*kalpa*) and law-books (*dharmaśāstra*). The feeding of Brāhmaṇas for the Viśvedevas (the All-Gods) is by an even number. Yājñavalkya says: "The same applies to the maternal grandfathers; or the rite for the Viśvedevas may be performed as a common procedure" (YDh 1.228). 21.2.
He offers of the food with the following verses. || 21.3 ||

With the seven *ṛc*s beginning with “*yan me mātā*” (MP 2.19.1), which contain feminine designations, he offers a portion of the food. The meaning is that he offers after having set aside [a portion] from the food prepared for the feeding of the Brahmins. In this regard, instead of the word “*amuṣmai*,” one should mention the name of the father in the first two [verses], that of the grandfather in the middle two, and that of the great-grandfather in the last two. According to the rule, “If there be two fathers, one should designate both in each *piṇḍa*” (ĀpŚr 1.27.10), there is a designation of both fathers in the case of a man with two fathers—namely, “*amuṣmā amuṣmā*. At the end, the exclamation *svāhā* is used. Some perform the modification (*ūha*) “*pitarau vṛñjetām*”; others perform a variation of the *ṛc*s. By this, the cases of the grandfather and great-grandfather are explained. Likewise, some perform a modification here also in the phrase “*svāhā pitre*,” while others do not, on the grounds that the state of being a father (*pitṛtva*) is intended here, but the singular number is not. Some perform the offering for the maternal grandfathers as well by means of modification: “*yan me mātāmahī*, *yan me mātuḥ pitāmahī*, *yan me mātuḥ prapitāmahī*, *tan me reto mātāmaho vṛṅktām*,” and so forth. || 21.3 ||
The subsequent offerings consist of clarified butter.

He offers six oblations of clarified butter, beginning with "Svāhā to the father," and so forth. In that regard, because the word *svāhā* occurs at the beginning of the formula "Svāhā to the father," there is no *svāhā* at the end. Regarding this, they say: in the monthly *śrāddha*, the feeding of the Brahmins is the principal rite (*pradhānakarma*), while the offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*) and the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) are its subsidiaries. Consequently, the performance of a *śrāddha* for one whose father is living does not take place, due to the prohibition: "If the father is living, he should not give. Furthermore, the injunction "having performed [the rites] up to the oblation, he should desist" does not apply here, because in that case the oblation is a subsidiary to the feeding, whereas in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* the oblation is the principal act. Others, however, say that the son should offer to the very same ancestors to whom his father would have offered.

Another says: there are three principal elements in the *śrāddha*—the fire-oblation (*agnaukaraṇa*), the feeding, and the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*). Therefore, this rule—"one should desist after having performed the *homa*"—is intended for that [specific case] as well. 21.4.
Or rather, it is the opposite of this. ||21.5||

The meaning is that the first seven offerings consist of clarified butter (*ājya*), and the latter six consist of food (*anna*). The mantras, however, are exactly as they are handed down in the tradition. The ritual procedure (*prayoga*) is as follows: on the previous day, after the evening meal, the invitation is made: "Tomorrow there will be a *śrāddha*. From that point onward, all must observe the vow (*vratacaryā*). (We, however, say that there is no eating on the evening of the previous day, based on the indicative mark [in the scripture]: "If one were to fast without having eaten, he would belong to the ancestors and the gods. Then, on the following morning, the second invitation is made: "It is being performed today. Then, after the oil-massage (*abhyaṅga*), he invites them in the afternoon once they have bathed and performed the purification of the feet. First, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), he addresses an even number—two or four—for the Viśvedevas: "An invitation (*kṣaṇa*) should be made for the Viśvedevas at this monthly *śrāddha*. The response is: "Om, so be it. He leads them to their respective seats with the words: "May you be seated," and they respond: "I am seated. The Brāhmaṇas for the Viśvedevas sit facing east upon Darbha grass whose tips point east; those for the ancestors face north upon Darbha grass that is doubled over and whose tips point south. The young ones sit for the father, the elders for the grandfather, and the oldest for the great-grandfather. Or there may be three for each. In a clean place sloping toward the south, the *śrāddha* hall is enclosed on all sides with its door facing north. In the north-eastern part of it is the *aupāsana* fire. To the south of that is a leveled mound (*sthaṇḍila*) for the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). To the south of that, those intended for the ancestors sit facing north, and behind them, those intended for the gods sit facing east. On that very mound, according to the available space, he places water for the *arghya* offering in three vessels containing sesame seeds for the ancestors, ending toward the south; and in one vessel containing barley for the gods. Having scattered flowers over them and placed them on the Darbha grass, he covers them with Darbha grass. Taking water from his own respective water-pot into another vessel, he pours it into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas seated on their seats, saying: "O Viśvedevas, this is your *arghya*; O Father, this is your *arghya*; O Grandfather, this is your *arghya*; O Great-grandfather, this is your *arghya*," or he does so silently. There is pure water before and after the *arghya*. Then, having honored the twice-born with perfumes and other items and with garments, he requests: "Let the food be set aside, and let it be prepared in the fire. The response is: "As you wish, let it be set aside; as you wish, let it be prepared in the fire. Then, taking cooked food intended for the Brāhmaṇas, setting it down to the west of the fire upon the sacred grass (*barhis*), and having sprinkled it with clarified butter, he performs the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire and ending with the *ājyabhāga* offerings. He then offers thirteen principal oblations (*pradhānāhuti*). *Note: This concludes section 21.5.*
One should touch everything with the subsequent [mantras]. || 21.6 ||

Having thus offered the principal oblations and having offered the *sauviṣṭakṛt* (the oblation to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt), he proceeds with the *jayā* and subsequent rites. When the principal rite together with its ancillaries is performed, the sacred thread is worn over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) in all cases. Others, however, maintain that the *jayā* and following rites are not included. Having performed the rites up to the sprinkling around (*pariṣecana*) and having released the *praṇītā* water, he then places all the food and what is to be offered into the fire, and having poured the remains of the offering into that [food], he should touch it with the following verses beginning with "This honeyed [portion] is for you, O father," and so on. Here too, there is an adaptation (*ūha*), such as "This honeyed [portion] is for you, O maternal grandfather," and so forth. 21.6.
Or they may be prepared separately for each individual. || 21.7 ||

Alternatively, he should touch separately, according to the respective gender, the various kinds of cooked rice prepared in the eating vessels for each individual. In that regard, the first mantra is repeated as many times as there are persons fed on behalf of the ancestors; "the same applies to the two following [mantras]. Then, [he touches] the remnants of food placed in the vessels. (21.7)
Having caused him to touch [the water] with the subsequent Yajus formula. || 21.8 ||

Having caused the Brahmins to touch [the food] with the subsequent *yajus* formula, “The earth is your vessel” (*pṛthivī te pātram*, MP 2.20.1), he should feed them; this is the remainder of the sense. And although in that context the plural number is seen in the phrases “you for the Brahmins” (*brāhmaṇānāṃ tvā*) and “may you not fail them” (*mā eṣāṃ kṣeṣṭhāḥ*), nevertheless, there is a repetition of the mantra for each individual person, as in the case of the *uparava* mantras and the *vatsāpākaraṇa* mantra. In that regard, first comes the touching for the gods with the verse beginning “O All-Gods” (*viśve devāsaḥ*), because it is seen in another *smṛti*; others say it is with the verse addressed to Viṣṇu. At the end of “This Viṣṇu” (*idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*), he says, “O Viṣṇu, protect the offering” (*viṣṇo havyaṃ rakṣasva*). Likewise, among those for the ancestors, at the end he says, “O Viṣṇu, protect the ancestral offering” (*viṣṇo kavyaṃ rakṣasva*). While they are eating, he turns away. He causes them to hear mantras that destroy demons, those for the ancestors, those for Viṣṇu, and other purifying, righteous mantras, as well as the *dharmaśāstra*, *itihāsas*, and *purāṇas*.
Then, knowing them to be satisfied, he should cause [the Brahmins] to recite the *Madhumatī* verses and the verse beginning with *akṣann amīmadanta*. Then he scatters food upon the ground, saying:

"Those who were consumed by fire and those who were not consumed by fire, and those who are born in my family—may they, satisfied by this ball of food (*piṇḍa*) given on the ground, attain the supreme goal."

Then, after they have sipped water, he again gives them water and causes those for the ancestors to say, “It is well-tasted” (*svaditam*), and those for the Viśvedevas to say, “It is pleasing” (*rocata*). Then, having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his faith, and having set aside from all the remaining food portions what is intended for the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) and for eating, he should ask the remainder: “What shall be done with the remnants of the food? The reply is: “Let it be enjoyed together with those we love.
“May our givers increase; may our Vedas and our progeny flourish;
may our faith not depart, and may there be much for us to give.”

Thus he makes the request. The response is with the modification: "May your donors prosper. Having circumambulated those who have eaten, he performs a salutation. "Oṃ svadhā" for the ancestors; "May the Viśvedevas be pleased" for the Viśvedevas. In that regard, among all rites, the Vaiśvadeva offerings take place first and the ancestral (pitrya) offerings afterwards. At the time of dismissal, however, the order is reversed. From the pouring of the oblation until before the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas), he wears the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), because of the observation of other ritual manuals (kalpas). 21.8.

When [the guests] have eaten, he should follow them, circumambulate them from left to right, and spread darbha grass with its tips pointing south in two rows. Having poured water over them with the subsequent [mantras], and having offered the rice-balls (piṇḍas) ending toward the south with the subsequent [mantras], he should pour water as before with the subsequent [mantras]. Having performed the worship with the subsequent [mantras], he should sprinkle water three times counter-clockwise around [the area] with a water-pot using the subsequent [mantra]. Having turned the vessels upside down and recited the subsequent Yajus formula without pausing for at least three breaths, he should sprinkle the vessels and lift them up two by two. Taking portions from all [the food], he should offer the best portion of the remainder as a mouthful with the subsequent Yajus formula.
He should consume it. || 21.9 ||

Then, having followed them after they have eaten, having circumambulated them, and having returned, he—wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*)—spreads *darbha* grass with the tips pointing south at the place where the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) are to be offered; "in two parts" means in two separate places, so that they do not overlap. There, he spreads [the grass] first for the fathers and afterwards for the mothers. Thus says Āśvalāyana: "Some [place them] in trenches—either two or six; he should offer to the fathers in the eastern ones, and to the women in the western ones" (ĀśGṛ 1.56.7–8). Because the rule "with tips pointing south in rites for the ancestors" (ĀpGṛ 1.7) refers specifically to the act of strewing [grass], the term "pointing south" (*dakṣiṇāgra*) is used here. Having strewn [the grass], he pours water upon them with the subsequent mantras beginning with "May my fathers cleanse themselves" (MP 2.20.2). The phrase "as before" implies that the mantras to be mentioned later are also drawn back [to this point]. He offers a rice-ball as before; the meaning is that it is the same as the offering of the rice-ball performed in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. By this, the specific details such as "three handfuls of water" and so forth also apply here. Among those, he offers to the fathers on the grass spread for them using mantras containing words indicative of the fathers, and to the mothers on the grass spread for them using mantras containing words indicative of the mothers.

Having thus given water, he then offers rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) upon those *darbha* grasses—both for the fathers and for the mothers—with the subsequent mantras beginning with “This for you, father, O so-and-so” (*etat te tatāsau*), etc., according to their respective designations. In every instance where the word “so-and-so” (*asau*) occurs, the name is to be inserted according to the gender. Here too, because of the connection with the previous rule, the injunction beginning with “having bent the left knee and having placed the hand downwards” (*savyaṃ jānv ācyāvācīnapāṇiḥ*) applies here as well. Regarding the modification for one who has many fathers, the *Paiṅgi-sūtra* states: “‘This for you two, fathers, Yajñaśarman and Viṣṇuśarman, and for those who follow you; this for you two, grandfathers,’ and so forth. And: “‘This for you two, mothers, O so-and-so, and for those who follow you,’ and so forth. It is said that they are “ending toward the south” (*dakṣiṇāpavargān*) so that both sets of rice-balls may be arranged separately, ending toward the south. Therefore, the mother’s rice-balls do not come to the south of the father’s rice-balls; rather, they are behind them.

Having thus given the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), he offers water with the subsequent [mantras] as before, for both the fathers and the mothers. This is because these mantras—“May my fathers cleanse themselves,” etc. (MP 2.20.14)—are taught again [in this context]. Although the result is already established by the statement “having offered water with the subsequent [mantras],” the reference “as before” is intended to point back to the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* ritual—[applying it] to both the rice-balls and the handfuls of water. Then, with the subsequent mantras, he pays homage to them according to their respective characteristics: “And those who are yours here” for the fathers; “And those women who are yours here” for the mothers; “May they carry you across” for the fathers; “May they carry you across” for the mothers; “May you be satisfied, sirs” for the fathers; “May you be satisfied, ladies” for the mothers; and “Be satisfied, be satisfied, be satisfied! for both.

Then, with the following ṛc, “sons and grandsons,” he sprinkles the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) three times from right to left (*prasavyam*) using a water-vessel. Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the phrase “may they both sprinkle around,” the sprinkling of the rice-balls is performed together. The mention of the “water-vessel” is so that [he does not do it] with his hand. The mention of “from right to left” is a restatement (*anuvāda*) so that there may be a single continuous sprinkling performed three times in succession, and not three separate sprinklings as in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. Having sprinkled in this manner, he then turns over—making them face downwards—the vessels that were used here: the three *arghya* vessels, the vessel for sprinkling, the water-pot, and that in which the food was taken out for the rice-balls. Then, with the subsequent *yajus*, “be satisfied, be satisfied, be satisfied,” he recites this three times without pausing or taking breath; this is called *tryavarārdhyam*. The mention of *yajus* is to indicate that the formula “be satisfied,” though repeated three times when recited, constitutes a single *yajus*. When that is repeated three times, there is a ninefold repetition. Having thus repeated it and sprinkled the turned-over vessels, he lifts them up two by two. By the word “up” (*abhi*), the meaning is that he brings them forward toward the subsequent rite. According to some, because of this, those same vessels are used in the subsequent *śrāddha* rite; according to others, they are not. Having thus lifted them up, he should eat a portion of the remaining food—a “portion as the minimum” (*grāsavarārdhyam*); the short vowel is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). He eats it with the subsequent *yajus*, “I offer nectar, established in the vital breath,” taking from all—that is, from all the remnants of the *śrāddha* food. This eating is an integral part (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*, not a restrictive rule for ordinary daily eating. Therefore, even in that case, the sacred thread is worn over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*). However, during the sipping of water (*ācamana*), the sacred thread is worn over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*) because it is not a part of that specific act. Thereafter, the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) proceeds. 21.9.
The eighth day after the full moon of Māgha, which coincides with the constellation Jyeṣṭhā, is called Ekāṣṭakā. || 21.10 ||

The rule for faith has been explained. Now, the *aṣṭakā*, a domestic sacrifice (*pākayajña*) dedicated to the ancestors, which is to be performed year after year, is being taught. This is its rule regarding time: the two *aṣṭakās* following the full moon of Māgha constitute the dark fortnight; the eighth day of that [fortnight] is called the *ekāṣṭakā*. If it coincides with or is joined by the *jyeṣṭhā* [nakṣatra], they call that too the *ekāṣṭakā*; thus there are these two applications. Otherwise, when the eighth day following the full moon is joined by the *jyeṣṭhā* [nakṣatra], they call that the *ekāṣṭakā*; this much is established. Why then say "the two *aṣṭakās* in that [dark fortnight]"? Therefore, even in the absence of a conjunction with *jyeṣṭhā*, the eighth day possesses the status of being the *ekāṣṭakā*. The purpose of mentioning "the two *aṣṭakās*" remains to be sought. For what purpose does it say "it coincides with the *jyeṣṭhā*"? It is so that when the eighth day occurs on two days [consecutively], the ritual may take place on the one joined with *jyeṣṭhā*. (21.10)
In the evening, his tent-city (aupakārya) was pitched for her.
He cooks a cake made from four measures of parched grain. 21.12.

That which is performed near (*upa*) is called an *aupakārya* (preparatory rite). That which occurs therein is the *aupakārya*. The grammatical connection is: "the *aupakārya* belonging to that [Ekāṣṭakā]. Whatever rite is performed near that Ekāṣṭakā—namely, on the preceding day, the seventh lunar day—therein one cooks a cake (*apūpa*) in four cups (*catuśśarāva*). The meaning is that on the evening of the seventh day, when the sun has set, the rite consisting of the cake-oblation must be performed. Thus, the word *aupakārya* is intended to prescribe the time. If the connection were "on the evening of that [Ekāṣṭakā]," then the cake would fall on the eighth day, the animal sacrifice on the ninth, and the *anvaṣṭakā* on the tenth; however, this is not well-known in the scriptures. Furthermore, the word *aupakārya* would be rendered meaningless. (21.11–12)
Some say it is on eight potsherds. || 21.13 ||

Thus ends the twenty-first section in the *Gṛhyapraśna* of Āpastamba. Some maintain that the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is a cake on eight potsherds (*apūpāṣṭākapāla*) offered in the evening. A cake prepared on eight potsherds is called "eight-potsherd. According to this view, the cooking is performed according to the ritual procedure for a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). However, according to the former view, it is cooked according to the procedure for an ordinary cake (*laukikāpūpa*). In both cases, the cooking takes place on the *aupāsana* fire. And although this is a rite that is an auxiliary to the ancestral rites (*pitrya*), it is not itself an ancestral rite; therefore, the wearing of the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) and other such requirements do not apply. 21.13.
Thus ends the twenty-first section in the *Anākula*, a commentary on the *Gṛhyasūtra* composed by the venerable Hara-datta Miśra.
Now begins the twenty-second section.
As at the Pārvaṇa rite, after the Ājyabhāga offerings, he offers cakes with his joined palms while reciting the following verse. 22.1.

When the *pratiṣṭhitābhidhāraṇa* has been performed, having completed the rites from the kindling of the fire up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he offers from the cake with his joined palms (*añjali*) using the subsequent verse, "yāṃ janāḥ pratinandanti" (MP 2.20.27), according to the procedure for the portions (*avadāna-kalpa*) as in the *Pārvaṇa* rite. By implication, there is another performer for the spreading of the base (*upastaraṇa*), the pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*), and the taking of the portion (*avadāna*). The mention of the limit at the *ājyabhāga* offerings is for the purpose of establishing the *tantra* (the common framework of the ritual). This very point indicates that this rite is not one pertaining to the ancestors (*pitrya*). Otherwise, since it has been stated that just as the *tantra* proceeds in the monthly *Śrāddha* and the *Aṣṭakā* even in the absence of specific effort, so too the *tantra* would be established here even in the absence of specific effort regarding ancestral rites.
