The mention of "like the *Pārvaṇa*" is for the purpose of obtaining the procedure for the portions, because the *añjali-homas* do not adopt the [standard] rules; thus, while offering with the joined palms, he offers according to the procedure for the portions as in the *Pārvaṇa*. The placing down (*sādana*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and wiping (*saṃmārjana*) do not apply to the joined palms. 22.1.
The *siddha* portion, having divided it into eight parts, he offers to the Brahmins. || 22.2 ||

The remainder of the *tantra* is established as being unmodified; this is the meaning. By the rule "he offers with joined palms," both [the ladle and the pouring] are excluded from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; this is the meaning. Therefore, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* with the ladle according to the procedure for portions (*avadāna-kalpa*), and having placed twenty-one fuel-sticks (*samidh*) on the fire, he proceeds with the *jaya* and subsequent rites. When the eating of a single portion by [the sacrificer] would follow from the rule "with that [remnant] mixed with clarified butter, [he feeds] a Brāhmaṇa," the distribution to eight [Brāhmaṇas] is prescribed. Therein, having announced [the food] to those Brāhmaṇas who are to eat on the following day, he observes the fast. 22.2.
On the following day, he dedicates the cow with darbha grass, saying: "I dedicate you, acceptable to the ancestors. || 22.3 ||

In the phrase "with a *darbha* [blade]," the singular number is not intended to be restrictive. "A cow" means a female, as indicated by the grammatical gender (*liṅga*). She stands facing west in front [of the sacrificer], because that is seen to be the case in the Śrauta ritual. This is a rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*), namely the *aṣṭakā* ceremony, as seen in the formula "thee, acceptable to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyas tvā juṣṭām*). It was stated previously that in ancestral rites, the ritual framework (*tantra*) proceeds even without a formal effort [to establish it]. Therefore, once the *tantra* has been performed up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, the procedure beginning with the dedication (*upākaraṇa*) commences. We shall state the authority for this later. Furthermore, the time is "the afternoon of the dark fortnight is better. In all such cases, the sacred thread is worn over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*). 22.3.

Having silently offered five oblations of clarified butter and having cooked its omentum, he offers it—after spreading a base of ghee and pouring ghee over it—with either a middle or a terminal leaf of the *palāśa* tree, reciting the following verse.

If the word *tūṣṇīm* (silently) were not stated, since there would be no recipient (*saṃpradāna*) for the offering, and thus the act of offering (*homa*) would not take place, it would follow that one must assume a deity. Under such circumstances, one might understand the phrase to refer to those five animal-offerings prescribed for the *Paśubandha* sacrifice—those enjoined by the rule “having brought [the victim] near, he offers five”—thinking, “these are those [offerings]. Consequently, even though the mantras would have been applicable, the word *tūṣṇīm* is stated. By saying this, he shows that this is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the animal even when it follows the procedure (*āvṛt*) of a Vedic animal sacrifice. Therefore, specific details such as “standing in front, facing west,” and so forth, also apply here. The mention of *tasyāḥ* (of that) is for the purpose of ensuring that the specific rules enjoined here—such as cooking (*śrapaṇa*) and so on—apply only to that omentum (*vapā*), and not to the cutting of portions (*avadāna*). Thus, the preparation of meat, rice, and so on, occurs in another fire, just as in the case of the monthly *Śrāddha*. The inclusion of the word *ājya* (clarified butter) is redundant; however, it is established as in the case of the rule “he offers with the subsequent [verse],” and it is included for the sake of providing an indicator (*jñāpaka*). This indicates that once the ritual framework (*tantra*) is completed at the end of the *Ājyabhāga* offerings, the bringing near of the animal (*upākaraṇa*) and so forth occur. How does it serve as an indicator? In all cases where there are multiple primary oblations (*pradhānāhuti*) involving sacrificial materials (*havis*) possessing the same characteristics within the ritual framework, a qualification is observed, such as “an offering of clarified butter from the food consisting of the *sthālīpāka*. That is seen here as well. This indicates that the oblations are offered with the very clarified butter belonging to the ritual framework. Furthermore, the immediate sequence between the bringing near and these [offerings] is observed in the text: “Having brought [the victim] near, he offers five” (TS 3.1.5). Therefore, it is established that the bringing near of the animal takes place at the end of the *Ājyabhāga* offerings. Thus, having offered the five *ājya* oblations, having quieted the animal silently, having silently extracted the omentum with the two omentum-spits, having cooked it on the *aupāsana* fire, having sprinkled it with clarified butter, having placed it on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), having sprinkled it again, and then, having spread a base of butter and sprinkled it over it, he offers it with the middle or the last leaf of a *palāśa* branch using the subsequent verse, “Carry the omentum” (*vaha vapām*). The placing down of the leaf and the two omentum-spits along with the vessels and so forth is performed.
One should offer meat-rice with the [verses] beginning with "uttarābhiḥ. || 22.5 ||

When the omentum has been offered, having caused the animal to be dissected, one cooks—for the sake of the Anvaṣṭakā—[the meat] in the houses, along with other sacrificial grains such as boiled rice (*odana*), and having sprinkled them with clarified butter (*ājya*) and placed them upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), one sprinkles them again and offers them with a ladle (*darvī*) according to the procedure for the cutting of portions (*avadāna*). Here, the procedure of a single supplementary offering (*upaghāta*) does not apply, because of the prohibition regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. This is because there is no clarified butter present, whereas meat and ground rice are present. In this regard, the meat-rice is offered with the seven subsequent verses beginning with “The people who rejoice in her” (*yāṃ janāḥ pratinandanti*, MP 2.20.27). Meat-rice (*māṃsaudana*) is rice mixed with meat. The mixing occurs at the time of the offering, not at the time of cooking, because of the risk of uneven cooking. Eighteen offering-mantras are prescribed for this rite: ten *ṛc*s and eight *yajus*s. Among these, the first *ṛc* is for the cake (*apūpa*), and the next is for the omentum (*vapā*). The mention of the feminine gender in the phrase “with the subsequent [verses]” (*uttarābhiḥ*) is significant; he will later state that the ground-rice is offered with the following verse. Thus, the offering of the meat-rice is performed with seven *ṛc*s. (22.5)
He offers flour-cake with the following [verse]. || 22.6 ||
He offers into the milk food prepared from flour with the subsequent ṛc, "And the Ukthya" (MP 2.21.1). || 22.6 ||
The subsequent oblations of clarified butter. || 22.7 ||
The meaning is that he offers oblations of clarified butter with the eight subsequent mantras beginning with "Bhūḥ pṛthivy agnir ṛcā" (MP 2.21.2). || 22.7 ||
From the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the procedure is the same up to the placing of the rice balls (*piṇḍa*).

The meaning is that the entire ritual procedure, beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and ending with the placement of the *piṇḍas*, should be performed here as well, just as in the monthly *śrāddha*. In this case, the *sviṣṭakṛt* is offered from the meat-rice and the flour; thereafter follow the *jaya* offerings and so forth. Then follows the seating of the Brahmins, the bringing of water-vessels to their hands, and their adornment. Then begins the section starting with "He should touch everything with the subsequent [mantras]" and ending with "He should eat a portion no larger than a mouthful. This alone is the meal on this day, and nothing else. Furthermore, once begun, there is no eating until its completion, and the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) are suspended. (22.8)
Some teachers prescribe the offering of the rice-balls specifically on the Anvaṣṭakā day.

If it were stated that "the placing of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) [is not required]," then there would be no placing of the rice-balls even at the *anvaṣṭakā* ceremony. However, the *aṣṭakā* is the subject under discussion; therefore, what occasion is there for [the rule] not to apply to the *anvaṣṭakā*? In that case, this indicates that here there is an option (*vikalpa*), and this is the injunction. Consequently, the entire ritual—including both the one with the cake (*sāpūpa*) and the one with the *anvaṣṭakā*—becomes the scope of the rite. For this reason, some say that the handful of curd (*dadhyañjali*) is optional because it is performed as part of the complete *ekāṣṭakā* rite, being [alternatively] accompanied by the cake or the *anvaṣṭakā*. We, however, say: this statement is intended precisely for the purpose that if the *aṣṭakā* has not been performed, he must not eat. Thus, the offering of the rice-balls which occurs at the *anvaṣṭakā* is [already included] here; it need not be performed separately in this ritual. (22.9)
Then he offers this other [oblation] with his joined palms of curd alone, just as he did with the cake.

Thus has the primary ritual procedure (*mukhya-kalpa*) for the Aṣṭakā been shown. Now follows the secondary procedure (*anukalpa*). With the verse with which one offers—namely, "yāṃ janā" (RV 10.62.8)—one offers with a full handful (*añjali*) of curd. Because of the prescription of a single ritual framework (*tantra*) and because the offering is made with a handful, this handful of curd is a unique rite (*apūrva*). By the explicit mention of "with a handful," the ladle (*darvī*) is excluded. Furthermore, there is no double ritual framework (*tantradvaya*). What, then, is its time? It is the eighth day (*aṣṭamī*), and the performance takes place in the forenoon because it is a rite dedicated to the gods. After the morning oblation (*prātar-homa*), having kindled the domestic fire (*aupāsana*) and strewn grass around it, having silently sprinkled water all around, and having filled his joined palms with curd, he offers it with the verse "yāṃ janā" (MP 2.20.27); there is no *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. Again, there is a silent sprinkling of water. Others, however, desire the preliminary ritual framework and the *sviṣṭakṛt*, but not the *jaya* and other such offerings; the source for this must be sought. This is the time, because it is the practice of the Teacher (*ācārya*). For this indeed is the Teacher’s practice regarding secondary procedures. For example: at the *samāvartana*, "having bathed silently at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*). And this handful of curd supersedes those oblations that belong to the Aṣṭakā, because it is mentioned immediately after them, but not the *apūpa-homa* nor the *Anvaṣṭakā*. The feeding of Brahmins and the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa-nirvāpaṇa*) do take place. This handful of curd is a superseder of the oblation alone. If that is so, then the meaning of the statement here is clarified as: "that which one offers, that [is done] with a handful of curd. [Another says: "It is a superseder of both the *apūpa* and the Aṣṭakā, but not of the *Anvaṣṭakā*. If there were a substitute for the latter as well, then this secondary procedure would have to be stated after mentioning it. Others, however, hold that the handful of curd is a superseder of the entire Aṣṭakā rite, including both the *apūpa* and the *Anvaṣṭakā*. (22.10)
Therefore, having set aside meat that is fit for consumption, on the following day,
the Anvaṣṭakā rite is performed.

Therefore, when this very cow has been slaughtered on the Ekāṣṭakā day, having set aside as much meat as is required for each person according to their need, the rite named Anvaṣṭakā should be performed on the following day, the ninth tithi. The word "eva" (only/this very) is used precisely to exclude the alternatives such as "with more [meat] than that," "with buffalo meat," and so forth. 22.11.
The ritual procedure for that [offering] has been explained by the rules for the monthly śrāddha. || 22.12 ||

The meaning is that the Anvaṣṭakā rite is to be performed like the Māsi-śrāddha. Because of the extension of the ritual procedure (*kalpātideśa*), everything—including the materials and the deities—is obtained here. Regarding the statement, "There he offers the food with the subsequent [verses]," they maintain that this refers to an oblation of food mixed with meat, because such is seen in the case of the Aṣṭakā, and because of the statement here, "meat according to the requirement. Others, however, maintain that because of the extension from the Māsi-śrāddha, there is no oblation of food; rather, meat is used only in those specific rites where it is prescribed in the Māsi-śrāddha, and not here as well.

On this point, some maintain that even in the case of the *añjali* portion of curd, one should perform the *anvaṣṭakā* [offering], because it is prescribed in the middle [of the sequence]. For if this were a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) for the *anvaṣṭakā* as well, then after mentioning that too, it would have had to be stated [explicitly]. Therefore, the connection with what precedes is as follows: "Having set aside meat according to the requirements, on the following day comes the *anvaṣṭakā*; its ritual procedure is explained by the monthly *śrāddha*."

Now follows the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* (the rite dedicated to a single deceased person) according to another treatise: The *śrāddha* which is performed with reference to one deceased person (*preta*) is called *ekoddiṣṭa*. An odd number of Brahmins are invited—one, three, or five. Through an increase [in the number], there is a greater abundance of fruit. In this rite, there is no offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), no formal announcement (*abhiśrāvaṇa*), no prior invitation (*pūrva-nimantraṇa*), no portion for the gods (*daiva*), no incense (*dhūpa*), no lamp (*dīpa*), no utterance of *svadhā*, and no prostration (*namaskāra*). The Brahmins face north. Taking portions from all the food, one by one, and having pushed out embers mixed with ashes toward the south, one should offer oblations into those very embers, saying: "To the deceased (*preta*), to such-and-such a person, and to Yama, *svāhā*. The mention of "to the deceased" is for the purpose of specifying the name of the deceased; they desire the practical application to be: "To Yajñaśarman, the deceased, and to Yama, *svāhā*. Others say: "To Yajñaśarman, the deceased, and to Yama. The receiving of water and the dismissal are performed with the formula: "May there be satisfaction for such-and-such a person. The response is: "There is satisfaction. The assignment is: "May it attend upon such-and-such a person. The offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) takes place in the receptacles, meaning at the place where the meal was eaten. The rinsing is done with: "Be satisfied. This *ekoddiṣṭa* is well-known to be performed for all castes at the end of their own period of impurity (*āśauca*).

Now, there are other *śrāddhas*: the *navaśrāddha*, the monthly (*māsika*), the tri-quinquennial (*traipakṣika*), the six-monthly (*ṣāṇmāsika*), and the annual (*sāṃvatsarika*). That which is performed first is the *navaśrāddha*; it is so called because it is both "new" (*nava*) and a "funeral rite" (*śrāddha*). Its timing follows the sequence of the social classes (*varṇa*):
"In the fourth, fifth, ninth, and likewise the eleventh [day], whatever is given here for a living being is called the *navaśrāddha*. Thus it is said.

Others maintain that for all castes (*varṇas*), there are four types of *navaśrāddhas*. For them, the term "nine" applies to the second and subsequent [funeral rites]. The twelve monthly rites (*māsika*) are to be performed on the anniversary of death every month. However, the first is performed at the end of one's own period of impurity (*āśauca*). The last is performed together with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the very day of death. The three-monthly, six-monthly, and annual rites are likewise performed on the anniversary of death in the second and subsequent years; thus, these sixteen are *ekoddiṣṭa* rites. Regarding the annual rite, there is an option between the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure and [the *pārvaṇa*] for the *kṣetraja* and *jāraja* sons. For others, however, there is only the *ekoddiṣṭa*. For those who desire the combination of the nine *śrāddhas*, even the well-known designation of "sixteen *ekoddiṣṭas*" would be difficult to justify. On this point, they recite:
The perpetual *śrāddha* should be performed month after month; if that is not possible, it may be done every season, or every twelve days, or even all twelve at a single day.

Now, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* [rite] takes place either after one year, or in the eleventh, fourth, third, or third-fortnightly month, or in the half-month, or on the twelfth day, or upon the attainment of the *upanayana* or an auspicious occasion (*abhyudaya*). In that case, there is a combination of the *ekoddiṣṭa* and the monthly *śrāddha*. For the deceased, there is the *ekoddiṣṭa*; for his ancestors, beginning with the father, there is the monthly *śrāddha*, and there is no modification whatsoever in the mantras. In such passages as "yan me mātā" (MP 2.19.1), just as those [mantras] were previously employed by the deceased father, so too must they be employed by the son. No one other than a son has the authority to perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, because there is no monthly *śrāddha* for others, and because the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is a modification of the procedure of the monthly *śrāddha*. Therefore, for a deceased person who is sonless, the wife performs the monthly *śrāddha* for her husband according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite alone for as long as she lives. A son who is unmarried also does exactly the same. Once he begins the monthly *śrāddha* after marriage, he then begins it together with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of his father.

Others, however, perform this rite differently. In that case, for the deceased father, the oblation is poured into the ashes as before; for the others, it is performed with food and clarified butter according to the *māsi-śrāddha* ritual. Regarding the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*): having offered the rice-balls according to the *māsi-śrāddha*, one offers a rice-ball for the deceased on separate *darbha* grass spread near them. Having offered water as before, he should pour half of the *arghya* water from the vessel of the deceased into the vessels of the ancestors with the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ. He should then merge the rice-ball of the deceased into the other rice-balls. This is the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. When this is performed, the deceased attains the status of an ancestor (*pitṛ*). And the fourth [deceased] becomes authorized and released.

Regarding this, there is a disagreement: some mix the vessel and the *piṇḍa* of the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) with those of the others. He alone is called by the word "preta," because he has departed (*preta*) in an eminent sense; for it is he who is authorized here. However, the established practice is that the one for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed is the "preta," and it is his vessel and *piṇḍa* that are mixed with those of the others. Even so, the authorization remains with the great-grandfather alone.

In the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for the mother, if she was an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) or married through the Āsura or other such forms of marriage, then there is a merging of her with the *piṇḍas* of the maternal grandfather and others. Regarding the merging of her *piṇḍa* with another, some establish the rule that it is with the *piṇḍa* of the mother-in-law and so forth; however, for one who has ascended the same funeral pyre as her husband, it is with the husband’s *piṇḍa*. The performance of the rite should be carried out in accordance with established custom. On this point, some recite:
"The brother, or the brother's son, a *sapiṇḍa*, or even a disciple—having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* together, he should thereafter perform the *abhyudaya* (prosperity) rite."
Likewise:
"But when [the wife] has died without a son, the husband shall perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
Now, regarding the *nāndīśrāddha*, Bodhāyana says:

Now, in rites for prosperity (*abhyudayika*), the procedure is performed from left to right (*pradakṣiṇa*); the sacred thread is worn over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*); the *darbha* grass blades have their tips pointing eastward; an even number of Brahmins are invited; barley takes the place of sesame seeds; and the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*). With a vessel containing water, one receives the water while reciting, "May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased," and performs the mixing (*saṃsarjana*). The offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*) and the assignment of portions (*anudeśana*) are performed with the formula, "Svāhā to the Nāndīmukha ancestors. When the pits have been swept and strewn with *darbha* grass, the offering is made by pouring speckled butter over them, saying, "To the Nāndīmukha ancestors, speckled butter; to the Nāndīmukha ancestors, Svadhā! Homage! All this is done twice each.

In that same work, in another section: When they have finished eating, at the place for the *svadhā* offering, he murmurs this *yajus*: "I shall conceive honey; I shall bring forth honey," and pours out water with the words, "May the *nāndīmukha* ancestors be pleased. This is what is called the *svadhā*. They do not perform the rites for the gods and the ancestors on the same day; for him who performs the ancestral and divine rites on the same day, his offspring will be short-lived. Therefore, the rite for the ancestors is performed on the preceding day, and that for the gods on the following day. (Baudhāyana Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa 1.3.10–11)
Likewise, having smeared [the ground] with barley mixed with flowers, fruits, and unbroken grains, one should scatter curd-rice in place of the sesame seeds.

Among these, the *māsi-śrāddha* (monthly ancestral rite) is the archetype for all ancestral rites (*pitrya*). Our specific details, however, are to be understood from other scriptures. Therefore, everything beginning with "the announcement on the previous day" applies here as well. There are an even number of Brahmins—either eight or sixteen. If there are eight, two are for the gods and two for each of the ancestors. If there are sixteen, four are for the gods and twelve for the ancestors, and so forth. Barley serves the purpose of sesame; whatever function sesame performs in the *māsi-śrāddha*, such as in the *arghya* offerings and so on, that must be done here with barley. There is also the mixing with flowers and other items, because of a statement in another section. The sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*). Some say it is mixed with meat and rice like the *pṛṣadājya*; others say it is plain. "With the *upayāma*" means that the vessel in which the *arghya* is given is held under by another vessel. "May the *nāndīmukha*s be pleased"; but for the gods, "may the Viśvedevas be pleased. In this rite, there is one vessel for the ancestors, not three, because no distinction is taught for the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, and because in all the mantras the instruction is "the *nāndīmukha* ancestors. Therefore, there is only one vessel for the ancestors and one for the gods. There, having seated the Brahmins, the installation of the fire and the two *arghya* vessels takes place. And the fire is specifically the *aupāsana* fire, since it is impossible [to use] the marriage fire. Having offered the *arghya* and adorned them with perfumes and so forth, being permitted, he draws out the oblation, mixes it with *pṛṣadājya*, sprinkles it with clarified butter, and at the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he offers one principal oblation with the mantra "To the *nāndīmukha* ancestors, Svāhā! He should offer the second oblation for *Sviṣṭakṛt* with plain *pṛṣadājya*. Having completed the remainder of the ritual procedure, he assigns the portions to the ancestors with the mantra "To the *nāndīmukha* ancestors, Svāhā! according to the principle of "or prepared separately for each person," and to the gods with "To the Viśvedevas, Svāhā! Those mantras used for the oblations and the assignments in the *māsi-śrāddha* are omitted here. However, the act of touching the water (*upasparśana*) still occurs, as there is no substitute for it. Regarding "The earth is your vessel... when the receptacles have been swept," this refers to the receptacles—the places of eating—having been swept clean by sweeping; there, the offering of the *piṇḍa* is made with the oblation mixed with *pṛṣadājya*, or with *pṛṣadājya* alone, using the mantra "To the *nāndīmukha*s, Svadhā! Namah! Thus, everything is done twice, twice; the meaning is that a double effort must be made in the giving of seats and so forth. Having smeared the ground and scattered curd-rice, that [offering] takes the place of the verse "Those who were burnt by fire... Then, having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the dismissal is performed with "May the *nāndīmukha* ancestors be pleased. Then, near the water-vessel, having murmured the Yajus formula "Madhu maniṣye," he pours the water into the vessel upon the sacred grass (*barhis*) with the two dismissal mantras and turns it face down. Thus, this *nāndī-śrāddha* is to be performed wherever the performance of the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajyā*) is to take place on the following day.
However, some read it otherwise:
"The śrāddha for the mother should come first, followed immediately by that for the paternal ancestors;
then for the maternal grandfathers—thus they know there are three śrāddhas at a vṛddhi ceremony."

In this view, there are two for each of the mother and the others; likewise for the father and the others, and likewise for the maternal grandfather and the others. With two for the sake of the deities, there are twenty twice-born men (*dvija*). And so it has been shown by Manu in another passage:
"The neighbor and the next-door neighbor [should be invited] at a *kalyāṇa* [rite] among twenty twice-born men" (MDh 8.392).
When a journey-śrāddha or an auspicious (*abhyudaya*) śrāddha takes place, that *kalyāṇa* rite consists of twenty twice-born men.
And they recite again:
"In the birth of a son, at the first feeding, the tonsure, the ritual bath, the taking of the hand [in marriage],
the establishment of the sacred fires, and likewise at the Soma sacrifice— in these ten occasions, an *abhyudaya* (prosperity rite) is prescribed."

The ritual procedure is exactly like that of the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha; the difference here is this much: an even number of Brāhmaṇas, circumambulation from the left, the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*), and barley in place of sesame seeds. (22.12)
Now he explains the rites for which the remaining mantras are to be employed:
having recited "sanim" and the subsequent [verses], he should state his purpose. (22.13)

Having gone to the giver for the sake of wealth—wealth that is obtainable by begging is called *san*—and having approached the giver (*sanim*), he should mutter the seven subsequent mantras beginning with “May I be visible to you like food” (MP 2.21.10). He should then announce the purpose for which he has come. In the seventh mantra, at the word *asau*, he should utter the name of the giver in the vocative case. 22.13.
Now, if chariots and other such items are obtained through begging, by what procedure are they to be accepted? Thus, the subsequent rules are commenced.
Having obtained a chariot, having harnessed it, and having stationed it facing eastward, he touches the two wheels of the chariot—or the two side-pieces—with the following verse. 22.14.

If a chariot is obtained, then having obtained it, he has it yoked by laborers; he attaches the yoke to the poles. Having stationed it facing the east, he touches both wheels of the chariot simultaneously with both hands using the following verse: “The two hooks, the two descending ones, on both sides” (MP 2.21.17). Alternatively, he touches the two side-pieces (*pakṣasī*); the word “of the chariot” is understood as the remainder. Others say they are the two side-boards (*phalaka*); others say they are the two rims (*nemi*). The mantra is recited only once. The touching is performed with both hands. Thus says Āśvalāyana: “One about to mount the chariot should touch the two wheels separately with both hands” (ĀśGṛ 2.6.1). || 22.14 ||
Having mounted [the vehicle] with the northern *yajus*, and having set out toward the eastern or northern direction with the northern [verse], he should proceed according to his purpose. || 22.15 ||

Then, with the *uttaraṇa-yajus* mantra, "O Lord of paths, [lead us] on the paths" (MP 2.21.18), he mounts his own chariot; then with the following verse, "This chariot of yours, O Aśvins... (MP 2.21.19). Having set out toward either the eastern or the northern direction, he should proceed as required—that is, he should go wherever there is a purpose. The long reading *adhīruhya* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) form. This procedure applies even to a chariot obtained through purchase or other means when it is being mounted for the first time; however, it does not apply to the second mounting and subsequent ones, because of the word "having obtained" (*labdhvā*). 22.15.
One should mount the horse with the following verses. || 22.16 ||

The word "having obtained" (labdhvā) carries over from the previous context. By means of the eleven [mantras] uttered [subsequently], beginning with "Thou art a horse, thou art a steed," the obtaining of the horse is explained in the same manner as the obtaining of the chariot. || 22.16 ||
[He should touch] the elephant with the [next] verse. || 22.17 ||

"Having obtained [it], he should mount"—this is understood from the context. With the following verse, "O you who are as glorious as an elephant" (MP 2.21.31), [he mounts]. In that [verse], "asau" refers to the naming of the elephant. "I place [my foot] upon the lord of elephants"—having mounted, he should silently name the goad. And in the mantra, "I place" (*abhinidadhāmi*) is to be understood [as the action]; thus, there is no contradiction with the grammatical gender in the mantra. || 22.17 ||
With those two [mantras], in case of injury, he should touch the earth as before. || 22.18 ||

When those two, the horse and the elephant, have caused a noise or bodily injury, he should touch the earth as before—just as during the descent for winter—with these two verses: “O Earth, be pleasant” (MP 2.18.8) and “Thus indeed” (MP 2.18.9). By the phrase “as before,” the *jātakarma* (birth-rite) is not included, because of the interruption. 22.18.
When about to enter into conversation, he takes up his parasol and staff with his left hand.

Thus ends the twenty-second section in the *Gṛhyapraśna* of Āpastamba. The place where one converses with opponents for the sake of a matter or other such purposes is called a "debate" (*saṃvāda*). Approaching that place in order not to be defeated therein, he takes up an umbrella and a staff with his left hand. The mention of "taking" (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) is for the sake of what follows; however, in this case, it is already established by the fact that the action consists of taking them up. Therefore, the *phalīkaraṇa-homa* (the offering of husks) must be performed with the hand alone, and not with a vessel. Otherwise, since the word *muṣṭi* is seen to denote a specific measure as well, its application here would be precluded. 22.19.
Thus ends the twenty-second section in the *Anākula*, a commentary on the *Gṛhya-sūtra* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
Now begins the twenty-third section.
Having offered a handful of husks with the southern [hand] while reciting the following verse, he should go and mutter the next one. || 23.1 ||

Holding the handle of the umbrella with his left hand, he offers a handful of *phalīkaraṇa* husks with his right hand, using the subsequent verse, "O Jihvaka, go down" (MP 2.21.32). In that [verse], the name of the opponent is to be inserted in the nominative case as "asau. This oblation is *apūrva* (unprecedented). The kindling of the fire, the strewing of grass, and the sprinkling of water on both sides are performed silently; these are all that is required. Then, having entered into conversation and having seen the opponent, he should mutter the subsequent verse, "Into your mouth [I place] speech" (MP 2.21.33). Here too, the name of the opponent is to be inserted as "asau," but in the vocative case. The offering is made with the fist turned downward, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the word "avayaja. The mention of "with the right hand" is for the purpose of holding the umbrella and its handle with the left hand at the time of the oblation—since the left hand is occupied, the offering is made with the right hand alone. 23.1.
One should consecrate an angry person with the two verses beginning with "uttarābhyām"; he becomes free from anger. || 23.2 ||

By the two following [verses], namely these two beginning with "That which is this on your forehead" (MP 2.21.1). Since there is no distinction in the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the two mantras, the indicative mark "when angry" (*kruddhe*) is not intended to be restrictive. Therefore, it applies even to a woman, and it also applies to Śūdras and others. Others say "no"; for they hold that since this is an occasional rite (*naimittika*) to be performed as a rule upon seeing someone who is angry, [the mantra] should be used only when the person seen is angry. To this, he says: "He becomes free from anger. The meaning is that it should be performed toward one whom one desires to bring to the cessation of anger. And this anger may be directed toward oneself or toward another. 23.2.

Desiring to cause the non-existence of others, one should have coarse *āḍhārikā* life-powders prepared and, with the following [verse], scatter them into the private parts of a sleeping woman. || 23.3 ||

(Desiring non-union, desiring non-sexual intercourse. "Union" (*sambhava*) means sexual intercourse. And it is heard [in scripture]: "Let us unite at will until procreation" (TS 2.5.5). The absence of that is "non-union" (*asambhava*). Desiring non-union with other men, one uses the *āḍhārikā*, a species of reptile, or one with a hundred feet. It is of two kinds: thick and thin. The thick variety is found in forests, while the thin variety is found elsewhere. Regarding the thick variety, while it is still alive, the practitioner himself has it ground into powder. Having had it ground, when his wife sleeps, he should scatter it into her *saṃbādha*—that is, her vulva—while reciting the following verse: "As one unstrings the bowstring... (MP 2.22.3). When this is done, the *saṃbādha* is no longer fit for enjoyment. This is intended for cases where there is suspicion of infidelity, or it concerns a prostitute.
Now, when suspicion of another man has departed, then for the sake of accomplishing the production of one's own semen, a medicinal remedy is prescribed:
for the sake of success, one should wash with the urine of a brown cow. 23.4.

The meaning is: for the sake of success—that is, for the prayer for the accomplishment of a task, or when desiring a state of being fit for enjoyment. At that time, one should perform the washing of the afflicted [organ] with the urine of a *babhru* cow; the meaning is that this is the medicine here. A *babhru* is a cow of tawny color. (23.4)

Now, he describes the rite to be performed for the sake of success—that is, for the sake of success in trade—for the purpose of profit through lowering prices and so forth, for that Vaiśya or twice-born man following the occupation of a Vaiśya who has in his house merchandise to be sold, such as grain, jewels, and other non-living goods, even alkaline substances, salt, and the like:
"For the sake of success, whatever merchandise he may have in his house, he should offer it with the subsequent [verse]. (23.5)

For the sake of the success of whatever goods, merchandise, or articles for sale are in the house of this householder—so that their success may be achieved through methods such as reducing the price by half—one should take a portion from those goods and offer an oblation with the following verse, "Whatever I [have gained] through wealth" (MP 2.22.4). Success is thereby attained. In this case, the offering of even alkaline substances, salt, and the like is permitted. The optional rites have been described according to the instruction. Among them, a wooden ladle (*darvī*) is used for liquid substances, while for others, the hand is used. And like the offering of husks (*phalīkaraṇa*), this is for the sake of an unprecedented result (*apūrvārtha*). The use of the word "his" (*asya*) is so that the offering may be performed by anyone else who desires his welfare regarding whatever merchandise is in his house. Nor is there a contradiction with the word "I" (*aham*) in the mantra; for it is he himself who, having become that [agent], performs the act. Because of the expression "merchandise in the house," this does not apply to fields and the like. The repetition of the phrase "for the sake of success" is for the purpose of indicating that this is a separate ritual act; otherwise, it might be suspected of being merely an alternative rule (*vikalpavidhi*) for the preceding rite. || 23.5 ||

If one should desire, "May this man not be cut off," one should pour one's own urine onto the horn of a living animal while it is asleep and sprinkle him three times from right to left with the two following verses. 23.6.

If one should desire of a servant: "May he not be cut off from me," "May he not depart," [but rather] "May he remain dependent on me for as long as he lives," then, having that desire, one should take the horn of a living cow that has fallen off by itself, bring its urine, and while the servant is asleep, one should sprinkle him three times counter-clockwise with those two verses beginning with "Around you, O mountain" (*pari tvā gireram*, MP 2.22.5). The mention of "living" is for the purpose of excluding one who is dead. The word "cow" is an instruction [that it must be a cow]. Because of the expression "having brought," one should first urinate into another vessel, perform purification, and then bring the horn. This does not apply to women, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the mantra: "You are sprinkled around" (*pariṣīto 'si*). 23.6.
Some say this refers to the master’s duty regarding his servants. Now, he states the ritual for one who desires the return of servants and others who have fled:
"On the path by which the slaves and laborers have fled, having piled up fuel, he should offer the subsequent oblations. (23.7)

Now, regarding those who perform work for the purpose of bringing back servants who have fled—whether they be slaves or others—they are called *dāsakarmakāra*s. Having placed wooden fetters (*iṇvāni*) on that path by which they might flee, and having kindled them, he should offer four subsequent oblations (*āhuti*s) into that fire with these [verses]: “*Āvartana vartaya*” (MP 2.22.7). Regarding this, some say that the placing of the four fetters on the path is done separately in sequence, and the mantras are likewise recited in sequence. Others say that there is a single placement of many fetters at once, and the oblation is offered in that very same place. This oblation takes place even when one or two have fled, not only when many; for the plural form is used due to the grammatical rule of *ekaśeṣa* (e.g., *dāsakarmakaraś ca*, *dāsakarmakarau ca*, *dāsakarmarāś ca*, *dāsakarmakarāḥ*). Furthermore, the plural number is employed when the matter is uncertain, as in the question, “How many sons do you have? Moreover, the plural in the mantras, such as “*parikrośo va*,” is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), because the focus is on the deity. This too is an unprecedented (*apūrva*) oblation. In all these cases, the fire is the *aupāsana* fire, as far as possible. 23.7.

If fruit should fall from a tree upon him, or a bird should alight [upon him], or a drop of water should fall where rain is not expected, he should wash himself with the subsequent [mantras] according to their respective indications. || 23.8 ||

If a fruit fallen from a tree should fall upon this *snātaka*, or if a bird—such as a crow or the like—should alight upon him, either on his head or another part of his body; or if, at a time or in a place where rain is not expected, a drop of water—a small amount of water—should fall upon him, then he should wash that limb with water according to the specific characteristics of each case, using the following verses beginning with “*yadi vṛkṣāt*. The verse “*yadi vṛkṣāt*” (MP 2.22.11) is for the fruit; “*ye pakṣiṇaḥ*” (MP 2.22.12) is for the bird; and “*divo nu mā bṛhata*” (MP 2.22.13) is for the drop. These three mantras are provided according to their respective indicative marks so that they do not all apply to a single occasion. [Otherwise], there would be the contingency of them applying simultaneously, as in the case of crossing a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) and other such instances, because the injunction (*vidhi*) is more powerful. 23.8.
Now follows the expiation for portents:

if a pillar of the house sprouts, if bees settle [there], if the footprints of a pigeon are seen on the floor, if the bodies of relatives are emaciated, or upon other such extraordinary portents, one should perform the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire at night on the new moon day—at a place where the sound of water cannot be heard—concluding with the *ājyabhāga* offerings, and having offered the subsequent oblations, one proceeds with the *jaya* and following rites. (23.9)

Now follows the expiation for portents (*adbhutotpāta*). A portent (*adbhuta*) is something unprecedented, never seen before. Its "occurrence" (*utpāta*) is its appearance; or rather, specific portents that arise from above—namely celestial and atmospheric—are themselves called "portents" (*utpāta*). Examples include a rainbow at night, a red sky, or the sight of a meteor during the day, and so forth. In this view, by the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*govālīvardanyāya*), the word "portent" (*adbhuta*) refers to terrestrial occurrences. Furthermore, the compound is a *dvandva* (copulative). He shows some examples of these portents in the form of illustrations: "the pillar of the house," etc. "Sprouting" (*virohaṇa*) means the production of sprouts. Because of the mention of the "house" (*agāra*), this does not apply even to one's own houses belonging to *śūdras* and the like. Regarding the settling of honey, it applies only to the house. "Hearth" (*kuptuḥ*) and "oven" (*cullī-bhrāṣṭra*) are synonymous. Regarding the "sight of the footprints of a pigeon"—that is, a wild bird—in the cooking-house, the meaning is when it has entered therein. "Attendants" (*amātya*) refers to sons and others. When many of them simultaneously suffer bodily affliction (*reṣaṇa*), or disease, or death; and in other such cases, such as anthills and the like, or rainbows and the like. By the use of the word "others," even the bodily affliction of attendants is understood only when it takes the form of a portent; it does not apply if only one or two are afflicted, nor if it occurs at different times. The expiation here is as follows: On the new moon night, the night being divided into four parts, the third part is "night. In a place where one would not hear the sound of water-jars being carried to the reservoirs, in that place one should perform the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire, followed by the eleven oblations starting with "This [I offer] to you, O Varuṇa" (*imaṃ me varuṇa*). The verse "O Prajāpati, none other than you... (*prajāpate na tvad etāni*, MP 2.22.19) is to be taken, because of its well-known usage, and not the verse "O Prajāpati, you are the guardian of treasures" (*prajāpate tvaṃ nidhipā*). Having offered the oblation "O Prajāpati, none other than you," he proceeds to the remaining ritual procedure (*tantra-śeṣa*) by performing the principal oblations. Since the completion of the ritual procedure is established by the rule ending with the "portion of clarified butter" (*ājyabhāga*), the specific mention of "kindling of the fire" and so forth is intended to mean the kindling of the fire itself. Therefore, in the absence of the *aupāsana* fire, it may be performed even in the common (*laukika*) fire. This effort to prescribe the fire at the very end is intended to demonstrate that these occasional rites (*naimittika*) and those with visible results, such as the *paṇyahoma*, may proceed in any fire whatsoever. The mention of the *jaya* oblations and so forth is for the sake of immediate sequence: immediately after the principal oblations, one proceeds to the *jaya* oblations and the rest; it means that the oblations seen in other *sūtras* are not to be offered in this ritual system (*tantra*). What then are they? "If a pigeon should strike the house or alight upon it, one should offer oblations or recite verse by verse the hymn 'The pigeon, O gods... (*kapotaś ced agāram upahanyād anupated vā devāḥ kapotaḥ*, ĀśGṛ 3.7.7).

Thus says Āśvalāyana. By the very mention of the *jayas*, there is a prohibition against the combination of ritual procedures (*tantrasamuccaya*). That expiation (*prāyaścitta*) also occurs optionally when the ritual procedure is separate (*pṛthaktantra*). In that case as well, the *śamyā* serves the purpose of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), because this expiation is taught in this very scripture. (23.9)
Having performed the rites up to the final sprinkling, he places a stone as a boundary-marker to the south for those who have perished, using the next verse; he places it. 23.10.
Thus the eighth chapter, being the conclusion, is completed;
this Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra is finished.

Therefore, regarding this extraordinary rite for the search for the bodies of ministers, there is a specific distinction: those whose ancestors, descendants, and kin have died in succession are called *abhimṛta*. For their sake—that is, for the purpose of pacifying their deaths—one performs this subsequent ritual oblation (*homa*). At the conclusion of the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*), one establishes a stone as a boundary (*paridhi*) and as a barrier (*antardhāna*) to ward off death, using the subsequent verse, "This [stone] for the living" (*imaṃ jīvebhyaḥ*). The repetition indicates the completion of the inquiry. Because of the mention of the "boundary" (*paridhi*), that stone must not be moved; it remains established right there. 23.10.
Thus ends the twenty-third section in the *Anākula*, a commentary on the *Gṛhya-sūtra* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra; here the *Anākula-vṛtti* is complete.
